arXiv:1903.11115v1 [hep-th] 26 Mar 2019

JT gravity as a matrix integral

Phil Saad,a Stephen H. Shenker,a and Douglas Stanfordb

a Stanford Institute for Theoretical Physics,

Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305

bInstitute for Advanced Study, Princeton, NJ 08540

Abstract

We present exact results for partition functions of Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity on two-dimensional surfaces of arbitrary genus with an arbitrary number of boundaries. The boundaries are of the type relevant in the NAdS2/NCFT1 correspondence. We show that the partition functions correspond to the genus expansion of a certain matrix integral. A key fact is that Mirzakhani’s recursion relation for Weil-Petersson volumes maps directly onto the Eynard-Orantin “topological recursion” formulation of the loop equations for this matrix integral.

The matrix integral provides a (non-unique) nonperturbative completion of the genus expansion, sensitive to the underlying discreteness of the matrix eigenvalues. In matrix integral descriptions of noncritical strings, such effects are due to an infinite number of disconnected worldsheets connected to D-branes. In JT gravity, these effects can be reproduced by a sum over an infinite number of disconnected geometries – a type of D-brane logic applied to spacetime.

1 Introduction

Studies of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model [1, 2, 3] have led to a resurgence of interest in Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity [4, 5, 6]. This is because the low energy dynamics of the SYK model is described by the 1D Schwarzian theory [3, 7] which in turn is the boundary description of bulk 2D JT gravity [8, 9, 10]. In particular, the low energy limit of the thermal partition function of the SYK model ⟨Z⁡(β)⟩=⟨Tr​e−β​HSYK⟩\langle Z(\beta)\rangle=\langle{\rm Tr}e^{-\beta H_{\text{SYK}}}\rangle is approximated by the Schwarzian theory on the circle, which is dual to JT gravity on the Euclidean disk.

Several studies have pointed to the importance in JT gravity of surfaces of other topologies [11, 12, 13]. In particular, recent work on random matrix statistics in SYK [13] showed that the “ramp” region of the spectral form factor ⟨Z⁡(β+i​T)​Z​(β−i​T)⟩\langle Z(\beta+iT)Z(\beta-iT)\rangle is described by the “double cone” geometry with the topology of the cylinder. This, as well as other hints described in [13], led us to study JT gravity on surfaces of arbitrary topology.

The main result in this paper is the calculation of the the Euclidean JT gravity partition functions ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}} corresponding to surfaces with nn Schwarzian boundaries and arbitrary numbers of handles. These can be computed from a certain double-scaled matrix integral that we will discuss. The topological expansion of this integral gives the sum over handles in JT gravity. The matrix integral supplies a (non-unique) nonperturbative completion of this expansion, which among other things gives an explanation of the “plateau” in the spectral form factor.

We now give a brief summary of this paper.

In section two we review the topological expansion of Hermitian matrix integrals. We start by describing a conventional integral over L×LL\times L Hermitian matrices with potential V⁡(H)V(H):

𝒵=∫d​H​e−L​Tr​V​(H).\mathcal{Z}=\int dH\,e^{-L{\rm Tr}V(H)}. (1)

We will think of the random matrix HH as the Hamiltonian of the boundary theory. A natural observable to consider is the thermal partition function Z⁡(β)=Tr​e−β​HZ(\beta)={\rm Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}. In practice, when studying matrix integrals, it is more convenient to work with the “resolvent” function R⁡(E)=Tr​1E−HR(E)={\rm Tr}\frac{1}{E-H}. The two are related by a simple integral transform.

For a rather general V⁡(H)V(H), the matrix ensemble correlation functions ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}} and ⟨R⁡(E1)​…​R​(En)⟩conn.\langle R(E_{1})...R(E_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}} are of a very constrained type. In particular, a set of equations known as the “loop equations” [14] determine all orders in the 1/L21/L^{2} expansion of these quantities in terms of a function ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E). This function is simply the leading density of eigenvalues that characterizes the infinite LL theory.11 1 For example, in the Gaussian matrix model, where the potential is chosen to be V⁡(H)=H22V(H)=\frac{H^{2}}{2}, this function would be the Wigner semicircle distribution ρ0​(E)=12​π​4−E2\rho_{0}(E)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-E^{2}}. This has been normalized so that the integral is one; the actual density of eigenvalues would be L⋅ρ0​(E)L\cdot\rho_{0}(E). So if one knows ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E), correlation functions are fixed to all orders in 1/L21/L^{2}. And, in fact, this is a practical tool: the procedure of implementing the loop equations was streamlined by Eynard [15] into simple recursion relation, which is part of the more general theory of “topological recursion” [16].

The type of matrix ensemble that will be relevant to JT gravity is not quite of the type described in (1). It is, formally, a matrix integral in which ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) is not normalizable. This type of problem is known as a “double scaled” matrix integral [17, 18, 19], and it can be understood as a limit of a conventional matrix integral. In this limit, LL is taken to infinity, the potential is tuned in a certain way, and one focuses attention near the edge of the eigenvalue distribution, where the density of eigenvalues remains finite. We refer to this density as eS0e^{S_{0}}. The loop equations commute with this limit, and they lead to an expansion of correlation functions in powers of e−2​S0e^{-2S_{0}}.

In section three, we will see that the JT gravity correlation functions ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}} are consistent with the matrix integral recursion relation described above, to all orders in e−S0e^{-S_{0}}. Let’s briefly describe how this arises. JT gravity is a theory of a two dimensional metric gμ​νg_{\mu\nu} and a dilaton field ϕ\phi, with Euclidean action

I=−S02​π​[12​∫ℳg​R+∫∂ℳh​K]⏟topological term =S0​χ​(ℳ)−[12​∫ℳg​ϕ​(R+2)⏟sets R=−2+∫∂ℳh​ϕ​(K−1)⏟gives action for boundary].I=-\underbrace{\frac{S_{0}}{2\pi}\left[\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{g}R+\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{h}K\right]}_{\text{topological term $=S_{0}\,\chi(\mathcal{M})$}}-\bigg[\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{g}\phi(R+2)}_{\text{sets $R=-2$}}+\underbrace{\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{h}\phi(K-1)}_{\text{gives action for boundary}}\bigg]. (2)

To study ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle in this theory, we impose boundary conditions that the manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} should have nn boundaries, with regulated lengths β1/ϵ,…,βn/ϵ\beta_{1}/\epsilon,...,\beta_{n}/\epsilon and with ϕ=γ/ϵ\phi=\gamma/\epsilon at each boundary. We regard ϵ\epsilon as a “holographic renormalization” parameter that should be taken to zero. With boundary conditions of this type, geometries of various topologies will contribute to the JT path integral. The first term in (2) is proportional to the Euler characteristic of ℳ\mathcal{M}, and it implies that different topologies will be weighted by (eS0)χ(e^{S_{0}})^{\chi}. For example, with a single boundary, the first three topologies are

(3)

A surface with one boundary and gg handles, of genus gg, has Euler characteristic χ=1−2​g\chi=1-2g, so the weighting is e(1−2​g)​S0e^{(1-2g)S_{0}}.

The sum over topologies is of the same form as a perturbative string expansion with “string coupling” gs=e−S0g_{s}=e^{-S_{0}}. Our perspective is different, though. In string perturbation theory these diagrams represent the perturbative splitting and joining of closed strings, the amplitude determined by the perturbative coupling gsg_{s}. In the JT context these diagrams represent the nonperturbative splitting and joining of closed JT “baby universes,” the amplitude controlled by e−S0e^{-S_{0}}, nonperturbative in the gravitational coupling GN∼1S0G_{N}\sim\frac{1}{S_{0}}. Such an expansion in multiple “baby universes” is sometimes referred to as a “third quantized” description.

Our basic claim is that the JT gravity answer for the geometries (3), and their generalizations with nn boundaries, are precisely consistent with the recursion relations of a double-scaled matrix integral. To check this, a first step is to compute the analog of ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E). For this, one has to compute the leading (genus zero) contribution to ⟨Z⁡(β)⟩\langle Z(\beta)\rangle, and then interpret it as a Laplace transform of a density of states eS0​ρ0​(E)e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}(E). A nice feature of JT gravity is that this can be evaluated exactly. One can think about doing the JT path integral in two steps, where we first integrate over the dilaton ϕ\phi. If we do this integral along a contour parallel to the imaginary axis, the dilaton functions as a Lagrange multiplier setting R=−2R=-2 everywhere. This implies that ℳ\mathcal{M} is a rigid constant-negative-curvature surface. At genus zero with one boundary, this is simply a piece of the hyperbolic disk. Since the boundary conditions only fix the length of the boundary, we have to integrate over the “cutout shape” of the geometry within the hyperbolic disk [9]. The action for this integral comes from the final extrinsic curvature term in (2). The resulting path integral is the partition function of the Schwarzian theory, which has been computed by several different methods [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25] and it leads to the expression22 2 Up to a multiplicative ambiguity that can be absorbed into S0S_{0}. In this paper, unless stated otherwise, we take x\sqrt{x} to be positive for real positive xx and branched along the negative real xx axis.

ρ0​(E)=γ2​π2​sinh⁡(2​π​2​γ​E).\rho_{0}(E)=\frac{\gamma}{2\pi^{2}}\sinh(2\pi\sqrt{2\gamma E}). (4)

Below, we will often set our units of energy so that γ=12\gamma=\frac{1}{2}.

A next step is to compute higher genus contributions to correlation functions such as ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle, and see if they satisfy the matrix integral recursion relation of [15], with the leading density (4) as input. For example, suppose we are trying to compute ⟨Z⁡(β)⟩\langle Z(\beta)\rangle in JT gravity. Then we we should consider geometries with one asymptotic region and a boundary of length β/ϵ\beta/\epsilon. The first three topological classes of orientable geometries33 3 See [26] for treatment of the nonorientable case relevant for other matrix ensembles. are the ones sketched in (3). The constraint R=−2R=-2 coming from the integral over ϕ\phi simplifies the path integral within each topological class significantly. However, there is still some work to do. For each geometry, we have to do a path integral over the cutout shape of the regulated boundary, with the Schwarzian action induced by the final extrinsic curvature term in (2). For all but the first (genus zero) case, we also have to do a finite dimensional integral over some moduli associated to the surface. It is convenient to divide this into two steps.44 4 A related approach was proposed in [27]. First we fix the length of the minimal geodesic that circles the neck of the geometry to be bb. This geodesic separates a hyperbolic “trumpet” from a Riemann surface with boundary:

(5)

Holding bb fixed, we integrate over all of the moduli of the Riemann surface, and also over the wiggles at the boundary of the trumpet. Finally, we integrate over bb. As we will explain in detail in section (3), this leads to an expression

⟨Z⁡(β)⟩≃eS0​ZSchdisk​(β)+∑g=1∞e(1−2​g)​S0​∫0∞b​𝑑b​Vg,1​(b)​ZSchtrumpet​(β,b).\langle Z(\beta)\rangle\simeq e^{S_{0}}Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{disk}}(\beta)+\sum_{g=1}^{\infty}e^{(1-2g)S_{0}}\int_{0}^{\infty}b\,db\ V_{g,1}(b)Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta,b). (6)

Here the first term comes from the disk topology, and the others are from genus gg. The ZSchZ_{\text{Sch}} expressions come from doing the path integral over the wiggly boundary of the disk and the trumpet. These are explicit functions

ZSchdisk​(β)=γ3/2​e2​π2​γβ(2​π)1/2​β3/2,ZSchtrumpet​(β,b)=γ1/2​e−γ​b22​β(2​π)1/2​β1/2.Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{disk}}(\beta)=\frac{\gamma^{3/2}e^{\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma}{\beta}}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta^{3/2}},\hskip 20.0ptZ_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta,b)=\frac{\gamma^{1/2}e^{-\frac{\gamma b^{2}}{2\beta}}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta^{1/2}}. (7)

The only non-explicit part of this formula is the factor of Vg,1​(b)V_{g,1}(b). This is the Weil-Petersson volume of the moduli space of hyperbolic Riemann surfaces with genus gg and one geodesic boundary of length bb. The “≃\simeq” symbol will be commented on below.

If we were studying instead ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}}, we would have a similar integral to do involving Vg,n​(b1,…,bn)V_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n}), the Weil-Petersson volume of the moduli space of a genus gg surface with nn geodesic boundaries of lengths b1,…,bnb_{1},...,b_{n}. These volumes were shown by Mirzakhani [28] to satisfy a recursion relation.55 5 The first general procedure for calculating Weil-Petersson volumes used topological gravity techniques and the associated matrix integral constructions [29, 30, 31]. For a recent discussion see [32]. This was later shown by Eynard and Orantin [33] to be closely related to the “topological recursion” that determines the genus expansion of a matrix integral. As we described above, the matrix integral recursion relation depends as input on a leading expression for the density of states ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E). It turns out that if one plugs in the leading answer computed from the disk contribution to JT gravity (4), then the two recursion relations agree with one another. To summarize: to all orders in e−S0e^{-S_{0}}, and for arbitrary correlators ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle, the JT gravity answer coincides precisely with the expected answer if we say that Z⁡(β)=Tr⁡(e−β​H)Z(\beta)={\rm Tr}(e^{-\beta H}) and HH is drawn from a double-scaled random matrix ensemble with leading density of states given by (4).

In section four, we briefly review an older connection between 2D gravity and random matrices [34, 35, 36, 37, 17, 18, 19] 66 6 For reviews see [38, 39] and for some more recent work see [40]., the c<1c<1 “minimal string.” In this body of work, it was argued that Liouville gravity coupled to a (2,p)(2,p) minimal model (where pp is odd) is related to a matrix integral with [41]

ρ0​(E)=sinh⁡[p2​arccosh​(1+Eκ)]=E​(a0+a1​E+a2​E2+…+ap−12​Ep−12).\rho_{0}(E)=\sinh\left[\frac{p}{2}\text{arccosh}\left(1+\frac{E}{\kappa}\right)\right]=\sqrt{E}\left(a_{0}+a_{1}E+a_{2}E^{2}+...+a_{\frac{p-1}{2}}E^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\right). (8)

In the limit p→∞p\rightarrow\infty, this agrees with (4) after rescaling EE. Since both JT gravity and the minimal string are supposed to be dual to matrix integrals, matching ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) implies that their partition functions agree on surfaces with arbitrarily many boundaries and handles. This suggests that JT gravity is the large pp limit of the (2,p)(2,p) minimal string. Further work on this is in progress [42].

From the perspective of a matrix integral, the e−S0e^{-S_{0}} expansion is a perturbative expansion. Matrix integrals also contain nonperturbative effects, and in section five, we review these and give a tentative JT gravity interpretation. One can motivate the need for these effects from Eq. (6). This was written with a “≃\simeq” symbol because the sum over genus is an asymptotic series, due to the (2​g)!(2g)! growth of the volume of moduli space with genus gg [43, 44, 45]. To make sense of this formula, one would like to find a nonperturbative completion of this series. This (2​g)!(2g)! behavior is generic in string theory [44] and the e−1/gse^{-1/g_{s}} nonperturbative effects it points to are due to D-branes [46]. In the context of matrix integrals, these effects are related to the dynamics of single eigenvalues and there are procedures for computing them. In the Liouville-minimal string context these effects have been connected to two types of branes, ZZ branes and FZZT branes [47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 53, 40].77 7 There has been an important parallel line of development investigating nonperturbative “brane” effects in the topological string. See, for example, [56, 57, 32]. In JT gravity we can imitate this connection and give these matrix phenomena a spacetime interpretation. In doing so, we will again encounter two different types of nonperturbative effect.

The first is called, in the matrix literature, a “one-eigenvalue instanton” [58, 59, 60, 44].88 8 For a review see [61]. This represents a configuration in the matrix integral where one out of the LL eigenvalues has been displaced away from the rest. In JT gravity, this can be interpreted as a type of D-brane effect which in Liouville theory is called a ZZ brane. In JT gravity there is a similar construction where the spacetime plays the role of the worldsheet. The spacetime is allowed to end at a new type of boundary associated to the location of the eigenvalue. By the usual rules of D-branes [46], we can allow other disconnected spacetimes to also end at the same boundary condition. These disconnected spacetimes exponentiate, adding up to a tiny prefactor that makes the contribution proportional to e−(const.)​eS0e^{-\text{(const.)}e^{S_{0}}}. In fact, as we will see, this contribution also comes with a prefactor of ii, indicating that in the interpretation of JT gravity as a matrix integral, it is one which is expanded about a metastable point. Such a model can be defined nonperturbatively on an appropriate contour, but it doesn’t have the reality properties of a conventional matrix integral.

The second type of effect corresponds to adding a “probe brane,” and is analogous to the FZZT brane in the Liouville context. These branes are characterized by a parameter EE, and they correspond go an insertion of det(E−H)\det(E-H) in the matrix integral. (An insertion of 1/det(E−H)1/\det(E-H) will be referred to as a “ghost brane.”) In the JT gravity interpretation, this object involves an infinite set of disconnected spacetimes. To see this, one can write

det(E−H)\displaystyle\det(E-H) =exp⁡(Tr​log⁡(E−H))\displaystyle=\exp({\rm Tr}\log(E-H)) (9)

Each trace corresponds to a boundary of the spacetime, so after expanding out the exponential, this object involves an infinite number of boundaries. At leading order in the genus expansion, each trace is associated to its own disconnected geometry with the topology of a disk, with a boundary condition that depends on EE. As in the ZZ brane case, this is formally equivalent to a D-brane calculation [46].

These probe branes can be related to more familiar quantities like the resolvent using

Tr​1E−H=∂Edet(E−H)det(E′−H)|E′→E.{\rm Tr}\frac{1}{E-H}=\partial_{E}\frac{\det(E-H)}{\det(E^{\prime}-H)}\bigg|_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}. (10)

This expresses the resolvent as a “dipole” of a brane and ghost brane. It is a trivial equality for matrices, but in the semiclassical approximation to the matrix integral, it is quite surprising. In particular, the infinite number of disconnected spacetimes do not quite cancel out of the RHS. These are interpreted as a nonperturbative contribution to R⁡(E)R(E).

One of the motivations for this work was to understand the origin of random matrix statistics in the SYK model [62, 63, 20, 13] from the gravitational perspective. The eigenvalue pair correlation function ⟨ρ⁡(E)​ρ​(E′)⟩\langle\rho(E)\rho(E^{\prime})\rangle can be extracted from the two resolvent correlator ⟨R⁡(E)​R​(E′)⟩\langle R(E)R(E^{\prime})\rangle. This in turn can be extracted from a four determinant expectation value similar to (10), and this can be related to a FZZT brane type expression in JT gravity. These contain effects that are nonperturbative in the “string” coupling, of order ei​eS0e^{ie^{S_{0}}}, which explain the rapidly oscillating part of the sine kernel formula for the pair correlator. This oscillating behavior, a D-brane effect, is responsible for the “plateau” in the spectral form factor which occurs at exponentially late times, t∼eS0t\sim e^{S_{0}}.99 9 Essentially the same method was used in the semiclassical quantum chaos literature to derive the plateau from a sum over periodic orbits [64, 65, 66, 67, 68].

Our analysis of these nonperturbative effects is not rigorous so it is important to make a check. In principle, Borel resummation of the perturbative series gives another way to determine nonperturbative effects (up to a choice of Borel contour). Nonperturbative effects are associated to singularities in the Borel plane, and the closest singularity to the origin encodes the large-order asymptotics of the perturbative series. We can therefore use the nonperturbative effects described above to make a prediction for the large genus behavior of the perturbative series.1010 10 For a review see [61]. In particular, this gives a prediction for the large genus behavior of the volumes of moduli space. For Vg,0V_{g,0} and for Vg,1​(b)V_{g,1}(b) with b≪gb\ll g, this prediction agrees with the Zograf conjecture [69].1111 11 Parts of this conjecture have been established rigorously [31, 70, 45]. For Vg,1​(b)V_{g,1}(b) at general b/gb/g, this method provides a new conjecture, which appears consistent with extrapolation to g=∞g=\infty of results up to g=20g=20 kindly provided to us by Peter Zograf.

In section six we discuss some open questions.

2 Review of the genus expansion in matrix integrals

For the purposes of this paper, a matrix integral means an integral over Hermitian L×LL\times L matrices HH with a weighting that is determined by a potential function V⁡(H)V(H):

𝒵=∫d​H​e−L​Tr​V​(H),H=L×L​ Hermitian matrix.\mathcal{Z}=\int dH\,e^{-L{\rm Tr}\,V(H)},\hskip 20.0ptH=L\times L\text{ Hermitian matrix}. (11)

We use the curly “𝒵\mathcal{Z}” to refer to the matrix integral partition function, not to be confused with the partition function Z⁡(β)=Tr​e−β​HZ(\beta)={\rm Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}, which is an observable in this matrix ensemble. Expectation values of such observables are given by e.g.

⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩=1𝒵​∫d​H​e−L​Tr​V​(H)​Z​(β1)​…​Z​(βn).\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\int dH\,e^{-L{\rm Tr}\,V(H)}Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n}). (12)

Matrix ensembles of this type have been widely studied. They are solvable in the infinite LL limit, in the 1/L1/L expansion, and in some cases beyond. For reviews, see [39, 71, 72]. In this section, we will review the 1/L1/L expansion, so that we can recognize the same structure when it appears in the context of JT gravity.

In the matrix integral literature, a quantity that is commonly studied is the matrix resolvent

R⁡(E)=Tr​1E−H=∑j=1L1E−λj.R(E)={\rm Tr}\,\frac{1}{E-H}=\sum_{j=1}^{L}\frac{1}{E-\lambda_{j}}. (13)

Here EE is an arbitrary complex number. For a fixed matrix HH, this function is a sum of poles in EE corresponding to the eigenvalues λj\lambda_{j}. But after taking the expectation value over matrices, the poles are smeared into a branch cut. To specify the resolvent one has to indicate which side of the cut one is studying; the discontinuity across the real axis given by

R⁡(E+i​ϵ)−R⁡(E−i​ϵ)=−2​π​i​ρ​(E)R(E+i\epsilon)-R(E-i\epsilon)=-2\pi i\rho(E) (14)

where ρ⁡(E)\rho(E) is the density of eigenvalues

ρ⁡(E)=∑j=1Lδ⁡(E−λj).\rho(E)=\sum_{j=1}^{L}\delta(E-\lambda_{j}). (15)

For a fixed matrix, ρ⁡(E)\rho(E) is a discrete sum of delta functions, but its expectation value over an ensemble of matrices is a smooth function. From either ρ⁡(E)\rho(E) or R⁡(E)R(E), one can compute Z⁡(β)=Tr​e−β​HZ(\beta)={\rm Tr}\,e^{-\beta H} by an integral transform, and vice versa.

Correlation functions of resolvents have a 1/L1/L expansion of the form

⟨R⁡(E1)​…​R​(En)⟩conn.≃∑g=0∞Rg,n​(E1,…,En)L2​g+n−2.\langle R(E_{1})...R(E_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}}\simeq\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\frac{R_{g,n}(E_{1},...,E_{n})}{L^{2g+n-2}}. (16)

Of course, one also has a similar expansion for correlation functions of partition functions Z⁡(β)Z(\beta) or eigenvalue densities ρ⁡(E)\rho(E). The existence of such an expansion follows from the analysis of matrix integral perturbation theory [73] in terms of ‘t Hooft double line diagrams [74]. The parameter gg is called the genus, because it is the genus of the double-line diagrams that contribute to a given term. The ≃\simeq is because the series is asymptotic, and the “conn.” subscript means that we take the connected part, or cumulant.

In the next three subsections, we will illustrate several techniques for studying matrix integrals by showing how to compute R0,1,R0,2,R1,1R_{0,1},R_{0,2},R_{1,1}.

2.1 Computing R0,1R_{0,1}

At infinite LL, matrix integrals of the type described above simplify dramatically. The eigenvalues of the matrix become very finely spaced, and from the perspective of coarse-grained observables like correlation functions of resolvents, they can be approximated as a smooth density. In the large LL limit, this smooth density is non-fluctuating, or “self-averaging” which means that it is the same for all typical matrices drawn from the ensemble.

We will refer to the unit-normalized density of eigenvalues in the large LL limit as

ρ0​(E)=limL→∞1L​⟨ρ⁡(E)⟩.\rho_{0}(E)=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{1}{L}\langle\rho(E)\rangle. (17)

We will focus on the simplest type of problem (the so-called “one-cut” matrix models) where the density is supported in a single interval on the energy axis between a±a_{\pm}. As an example, ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) might look like the following:

(18)

Note that in (17), ρ0\rho_{0} is normalized so that its integral is one. It is related to the leading term R0,1R_{0,1} in the 1/L1/L expansion of the expectation value of the resolvent (16), by

R0,1​(E)=∫a−a+d​λ​ρ0​(λ)E−λR_{0,1}(E)=\int_{a_{-}}^{a_{+}}d\lambda\frac{\rho_{0}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda} (19)

and an inverse expression

ρ0​(E)=−12​π​i​(R0,1​(E+i​ϵ)−R0,1​(E−i​ϵ)).\rho_{0}(E)=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\left(R_{0,1}(E+i\epsilon)-R_{0,1}(E-i\epsilon)\right). (20)

There are several ways to determine ρ0\rho_{0} or R0,1R_{0,1}, starting from the matrix potential V⁡(H)V(H). One way begins by writing the matrix integral in terms of an integral over the matrix eigenvalues,

𝒵=CL∫dLλ∏i<j(λi−λj)2e−L∑j=1LV(λj).\mathcal{Z}=C_{L}\int d^{L}\lambda\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{2}e^{-L\sum_{j=1}^{L}V(\lambda_{j})}. (21)

Here the numerical factor CLC_{L} and the Vandermonde determinant ∏i<j(λi−λj)2\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{2} arise from integrating out the unitary matrix that diagonalizes HH. The leading density ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) can be derived from a mean-field analysis (valid at large LL) of the statistical mechanics problem for these eigenvalues. The idea is as follows: the effective potential that a single eigenvalue feels is a combination of the bare potential and a term coming from the Vandermonde factor:

Veff​(λj)=L​V​(λj)−∑i≠jlog⁡[(λi−λj)2].V_{\text{eff}}(\lambda_{j})=LV(\lambda_{j})-\sum_{i\neq j}\log\left[(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{2}\right]. (22)

After making a continuum approximation to the contribution from all of the other eigenvalues

∑i≠jlog⁡[(λi−λj)2]=L​∫d​λ​ρ0​(λ)​log⁡[(λ−λj)2]\sum_{i\neq j}\log\left[(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{2}\right]=L\int d\lambda\rho_{0}(\lambda)\log\left[(\lambda-\lambda_{j})^{2}\right] (23)

the equilibrium condition is that each eigenvalue should sit at a stationary point of the effective potential [73]:

Veff′​(E)=0⟹V′​(E)=2​∫d​λ​ρ0​(λ)E−λ.V^{\prime}_{\text{eff}}(E)=0\hskip 20.0pt\implies\hskip 20.0ptV^{\prime}(E)=2\int d\lambda\frac{\rho_{0}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda}. (24)

Here the integral should be defined by a principal value prescription, analogous to leaving out the i=ji=j term from the sum (22). Taking this prescription into account (24) can be written as

R0,1​(E+i​ϵ)+R0,1​(E−i​ϵ)=V′​(E).R_{0,1}(E+i\epsilon)+R_{0,1}(E-i\epsilon)=V^{\prime}(E). (25)

To use (25) to get an expression for R0,1​(E)R_{0,1}(E), one can use the following trick [14]. Let’s imagine for a moment that we knew the end points a±a_{\pm}, and let’s define a function

σ⁡(x)=(x−a+)​(x−a−).\sigma(x)=(x-a_{+})(x-a_{-}). (26)

We will define σ⁡(x)\sqrt{\sigma(x)} as a function with a cut between x=a±x=a_{\pm}, so that in particular for large xx, σ⁡(x)∼x\sqrt{\sigma(x)}\sim x. Then, for complex EE away from the cut,

R0,1​(E)\displaystyle R_{0,1}(E) =∮Ed​λ2​π​iR0,1​(λ)λ−Eσ⁡(E)σ⁡(λ)=−∫𝒞d​λ2​π​iR0,1​(λ)λ−Eσ⁡(E)σ⁡(λ)\displaystyle=\oint_{E}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{R_{0,1}(\lambda)}{\lambda-E}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma(E)}{\sigma(\lambda)}}=-\int_{\mathcal{C}}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{R_{0,1}(\lambda)}{\lambda-E}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma(E)}{\sigma(\lambda)}}
=−12∫𝒞d​λ2​π​iV′​(λ)λ−Eσ⁡(E)σ⁡(λ).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{C}}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{V^{\prime}(\lambda)}{\lambda-E}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma(E)}{\sigma(\lambda)}}. (27)

Here 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a contour surrounding the interval [a−,a+][a_{-},a_{+}]. In the first equality we used the residue theorem. In the second we deformed the contour past infinity1212 12 It is clear from the definition that R0,1​(λ)≈1λR_{0,1}(\lambda)\approx\frac{1}{\lambda} at infinity so this is OK. to surround the cut on the real axis. In the third equality we used that σ⁡(λ)\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)} takes the opposite sign on the two sides of the cut. This sign change is canceled by the sign of d​λd\lambda on the two sides, so the net effect is that R0,1​(λ)R_{0,1}(\lambda) can be replaced by its average value on the two sides (25).

As a final step, we need to determine the endpoints a±a_{\pm}. To do this, one can impose that R0,1​(E)∼1ER_{0,1}(E)\sim\frac{1}{E} for large EE. By expanding (27) for large EE, one finds that this implies

0=∫𝒞d​λ2​π​i​V′​(λ)σ⁡(λ),2=∫𝒞d​λ2​π​i​λ​V′​(λ)σ⁡(λ),0=\int_{\mathcal{C}}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{V^{\prime}(\lambda)}{\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)}},\hskip 20.0pt2=\int_{\mathcal{C}}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{\lambda V^{\prime}(\lambda)}{\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)}}, (28)

which gives two conditions for the two endpoints a±a_{\pm}. After solving for the endpoints using these equations, (27) becomes an explicit equation for the resolvent R0,1​(E)R_{0,1}(E), and we can take its discontinuity (20) to get the density of eigenvalues ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E).

2.2 Computing R0,2R_{0,2}

A useful trick for computing R0,2​(E1,E2)R_{0,2}(E_{1},E_{2}) is the following [75, 76]. If we write the potential as a power series

V⁡(M)=∑n=0∞vn​MnV(M)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}v_{n}M^{n} (29)

then it is straightforward to check that an appropriate sum of derivatives of R0,1R_{0,1} gives R0,2R_{0,2}:

R0,2(E1,E2)=−∑n=0∞1E2n+1∂vnR0,1(E1).R_{0,2}(E_{1},E_{2})=-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{E_{2}^{n+1}}\partial_{v_{n}}R_{0,1}(E_{1}). (30)

Since we have a formula (27) for R0,1R_{0,1} in terms of the potential, we can differentiate it with respect to the parameters vnv_{n} and get R0,2R_{0,2}. In taking the derivative of (27), the term where ∂vn\partial_{v_{n}} hits the potential can be simplified using

∑n=0∞1En+1​∂vnV′​(λ)=∑n=0∞n​λn−1En+1=1(λ−E)2.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{E^{n+1}}\partial_{v_{n}}V^{\prime}(\lambda)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{n\lambda^{n-1}}{E^{n+1}}=\frac{1}{(\lambda-E)^{2}}. (31)

One also needs to know the derivative of the endpoints, ∂vna±\partial_{v_{n}}a_{\pm}. These can be determined by taking derivatives of (28). For example, in the symmetric case with a±=±aa_{\pm}=\pm a, one finds after some algebra that

R0,2​(E1,E2)=12​(E1−E2)2​(E1​E2−a2σ⁡(E1)​σ⁡(E2)−1).\displaystyle R_{0,2}(E_{1},E_{2})=\frac{1}{2(E_{1}-E_{2})^{2}}\left(\frac{E_{1}E_{2}-a^{2}}{\sqrt{\sigma(E_{1})}\sqrt{\sigma(E_{2})}}-1\right). (32)

Somewhat miraculously, this depends on the potential only through the endpoints ±a\pm a. This is a very general feature of one-cut matrix integrals [75, 77].

2.3 Computing R1,1R_{1,1}

In order to compute R1,1R_{1,1}, we will introduce the machinery of the “loop equations,” which make it possible to systematically compute all of the Rg,nR_{g,n}. The starting point is the equation

0=∫dLλ∂∂λa[1E−λaR(E1)…R(Ek)∏i<j(λi−λj)2e−L∑jV(λj)].0=\int d^{L}\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_{a}}\left[\frac{1}{E-\lambda_{a}}R(E_{1})...R(E_{k})\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j})^{2}e^{-L\sum_{j}V(\lambda_{j})}\right]. (33)

To get R1,1R_{1,1}, one only needs the first of these equations, with k=0k=0, so no extra resolvents are inserted in the integrand. Evaluating the derivative explicitly in this case, one gets

0=⟨1(E−λa)2+1E−λa​∑j≠a2λa−λj−L​V′​(λa)E−λa⟩.0=\left\langle\frac{1}{(E-\lambda_{a})^{2}}+\frac{1}{E-\lambda_{a}}\sum_{j\neq a}\frac{2}{\lambda_{a}-\lambda_{j}}-\frac{LV^{\prime}(\lambda_{a})}{E-\lambda_{a}}\right\rangle. (34)

After symmetrizing the second term under λa↔λj\lambda_{a}\leftrightarrow\lambda_{j}, combining it with the first term, and then summing over aa, this equation can be rewritten as

⟨(Tr​1E−H)2−L​Tr​V′​(H)E−H⟩=0.\displaystyle\left\langle\left({\rm Tr}\frac{1}{E-H}\right)^{2}-L{\rm Tr}\frac{V^{\prime}(H)}{E-H}\right\rangle=0. (35)

This is an exact equation, but it can be expanded in powers of 1/L1/L. At leading order in the expansion, we find an equation that can be written (after dividing by L2L^{2} and adding terms involving V′​(E)V^{\prime}(E) to both sides of the equation)

(R0,1​(E)−V′​(E)2)2=V′​(E)24−⟨1L​Tr​V′​(E)−V′​(H)E−H⟩0\left(R_{0,1}(E)-\frac{V^{\prime}(E)}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{V^{\prime}(E)^{2}}{4}-\left\langle\frac{1}{L}{\rm Tr}\frac{V^{\prime}(E)-V^{\prime}(H)}{E-H}\right\rangle_{0} (36)

where the zero subscript means the large LL limit. If the potential V⁡(E)V(E) is an analytic function, then the RHS of this equation is also analytic in EE (in fact, if the potential is a polynomial then the RHS is also a polynomial). So if we define the quantity

y=R0,1​(E)−V′​(E)2,y=R_{0,1}(E)-\frac{V^{\prime}(E)}{2}, (37)

then (36) defines a hyperelliptic curve y2=f⁡(E)y^{2}=f(E), where ff is the RHS of (36). This curve is referred to as the spectral curve of the matrix integral. Concretely, it is a double cover of the complex EE plane, with the two sheets differing by y→−yy\rightarrow-y. We define it so that (37) holds on the physical sheet, away from the cut along the positive real axis. Eq. (20) then implies that if we continue to the positive real axis through the upper half plane for EE, we have

y=−π​i​ρ0​(E).y=-\pi i\rho_{0}(E). (38)

If we continue through the lower half plane, we would have the opposite sign.

Correlation functions of resolvents have branch points in the energy plane, but they become single-valued functions on the spectral curve. For example, the same loop equation (35) can be expanded to higher orders in 1/L21/L^{2}. And, at next order, one finds

2​y​(E)​R1,1​(E)=−R0,2​(E,E)−⟨1L​Tr​V′​(E)−V′​(H)E−H⟩12y(E)R_{1,1}(E)=-R_{0,2}(E,E)-\left\langle\frac{1}{L}{\rm Tr}\frac{V^{\prime}(E)-V^{\prime}(H)}{E-H}\right\rangle_{1} (39)

where the subscript on the expectation value in the RHS means the next-to-leading (i.e. 1/L21/L^{2}) term. Note that the RHS is a single-valued function of EE. This implies that R1,1R_{1,1} must be a double-valued function, changing sign in the same way as yy on the two sheets of the spectral curve. So R1,1R_{1,1} can be defined as a single-valued function on the spectral curve.

An alternative way to get a single-valued function related to the resolvents is to multiply them by factors of σ⁡(E)\sqrt{\sigma(E)}, which changes sign in a compensating way between the two sheets. So, for example R1,1​(E)​σ⁡(E)R_{1,1}(E)\sqrt{\sigma(E)} is a single-valued function in the original energy plane. A very important point is that R1,1​(E)​σ⁡(E)R_{1,1}(E)\sqrt{\sigma(E)} is singular only at the endpoints of the eigenvalue distribution E=a±E=a_{\pm}. This follows from the representation

R1,1​(E)=∫a−a+d​λ​ρ1​(λ)E−λR_{1,1}(E)=\int_{a_{-}}^{a_{+}}d\lambda\frac{\rho_{1}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda} (40)

in terms of the 1/L21/L^{2} correction ρ1\rho_{1} to the density of eigenvalues, which is itself analytic away from the endpoints of the cut. It is obvious from this definition that R1,1R_{1,1} is singular only when EE coincides with an endpoint a±a_{\pm}. For example, if EE approaches the real axis somewhere away from the endpoints, the contour can be deformed smoothly to avoid a singularity.

The fact that R1,1​(E)​σ⁡(E)R_{1,1}(E)\sqrt{\sigma(E)} is single-valued and only singular at a±a_{\pm} makes it possible to bypass the fact that we don’t know the second term on the RHS of (39). Following [15], we write a dispersion relation

R1,1​(E)​σ⁡(E)\displaystyle R_{1,1}(E)\sqrt{\sigma(E)} =∮Ed​λ2​π​iR1,1​(λ)​σ⁡(λ)λ−E=−∑±∮a±d​λ2​π​iR1,1​(λ)​σ⁡(λ)λ−E\displaystyle=\oint_{E}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{R_{1,1}(\lambda)\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)}}{\lambda-E}=-\sum_{\pm}\oint_{a_{\pm}}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{R_{1,1}(\lambda)\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)}}{\lambda-E} (41)
=∑±∮a±d​λ2​π​i​R0,2​(λ,λ)λ−E​σ⁡(λ)2​y​(λ).\displaystyle=\sum_{\pm}\oint_{a_{\pm}}\frac{d\lambda}{2\pi i}\frac{R_{0,2}(\lambda,\lambda)}{\lambda-E}\frac{\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)}}{2y(\lambda)}. (42)

The first equality uses the residue theorem, and the second equality uses that R1,1​(λ)​σ⁡(λ)R_{1,1}(\lambda)\sqrt{\sigma(\lambda)} has singularities only at a±a_{\pm}.1313 13 Since R⁡(E)∼LE+Tr​(H)E2+…R(E)\sim\frac{L}{E}+\frac{\text{Tr}(H)}{E^{2}}+... for large EE, a 1E\frac{1}{E} piece appears only in R0,1​(E)R_{0,1}(E), and in particular R1,1R_{1,1} has no pole at infinity. In going to the third line, we used (39) and exploited the fact that the unknown term on the RHS of (39) is not singular at the points a±a_{\pm}.

Eq. (42) relates R1,1R_{1,1} to R0,2R_{0,2}, which was computed in (32). In [15, 72], it is shown how a similar strategy works for higher order quantities Rg,nR_{g,n}. One expands the loop equations in powers of 1/L1/L and gets a set of equations for Rg,nR_{g,n} involving some unknown correlators that include a factor of Tr​V′​(E)−V′​(H)E−H{\rm Tr}\frac{V^{\prime}(E)-V^{\prime}(H)}{E-H}. These unknown terms are not singular at E=a±E=a_{\pm}, so the dispersion relation method in (42) gives a set of equations purely involving Rg,nR_{g,n}. These equations can be solved recursively. We will write a special case of the resulting recursion relation below, after introducing the idea of double-scaled matrix integrals.

2.4 Double scaling

In this paper, we will be interested in an analog of a matrix integral for which the leading density of eigenvalues is of the form

ρ0total​(E)=eS0(2​π)2​sinh⁡(2​π​E),E>0.\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E)=\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\sinh(2\pi\sqrt{E}),\hskip 20.0ptE>0. (43)

Here the superscript “total” is meant to indicate that unlike (17), we are not dividing by LL here, so this density of eigenvalues is normalized so that its integral is LL. Of course, such an equation doesn’t make sense, since the integral of the RHS is not normalized at all. However, (43) can be realized as a limit of an ordinary matrix integral. For finite aa, we can imagine choosing a potential and a value of LL so that

ρ0total​(E)=eS0(2​π)2​sinh⁡(2​π​a2−E22​a),−a<E<a.\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E)=\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\sinh\left(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}-E^{2}}{2a}}\right),\hskip 20.0pt-a<E<a. (44)

Shifting E→E−aE\rightarrow E-a and taking aa large, we recover (43). Note that as aa becomes large, the ratio L/eS0L/e^{S_{0}} also becomes large, in order to keep ρ0total​(E)\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E) normalized to have integral LL. So the total number of eigenvalues is going to infinity. However, this doesn’t mean that the matrix integral becomes trivial. The reason is that in the region of interest, the density of eigenvalues is finite, controlled by eS0e^{S_{0}}, and the 1/L1/L expansion will be replaced by an e−S0e^{-S_{0}} expansion. This procedure is an example of what is called “double scaling,” and what we are saying here is that (43) makes sense as a leading density of eigenvalues for a double-scaled matrix integral. In such an integral, correlation functions of resolvents have an expansion of the form

⟨R⁡(E1)​…​R​(En)⟩conn.≃∑g=0∞Rg,n​(E1,…,En)(eS0)2​g+n−2.\langle R(E_{1})...R(E_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}}\simeq\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\frac{R_{g,n}(E_{1},...,E_{n})}{(e^{S_{0}})^{2g+n-2}}. (45)

Note that we are risking confusion by writing the coefficients of the e−S0e^{-S_{0}} expansion of a double-scaled matrix integral with the same notation Rg,nR_{g,n} as the coefficients of the 1/L1/L expansion of a conventional matrix integral. Similarly, whereas for a conventional matrix integral one defines ρ0=1L​ρ0total\rho_{0}=\frac{1}{L}\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}, for a double-scaled theory we will use

ρ0​(E)=e−S0​ρ0total​(E).\rho_{0}(E)=e^{-S_{0}}\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E). (46)

The double-scaling procedure needed to achieve (43) would be quite complicated at the level of the potential, since we have to tune it carefully as we take the limit. And, in fact, the potential itself diverges in the limit.1414 14 The quantity that remains finite is the effective potential on a given eigenvalue (22), which is the sum of the “bare” potential and the Vandermonde potential from an increasingly large number of other eigenvalues. Fortunately, as we will see in a moment, the e−S0e^{-S_{0}} expansion is determined directly by the leading density of eigenvalues itself, without any explicit reference to the potential.1515 15 The same is also true for the 1/L1/L expansion of a conventional matrix integral.

In practice, double-scaled theories are a little simpler than conventional matrix integrals, since they have only a single endpoint of the eigenvalue distribution, which we take to be at E=0E=0. So for example, a formula that will be important below is the expression for R0,2R_{0,2}. If we start with (32) and shift E1→E1−aE_{1}\rightarrow E_{1}-a and E2→E2−aE_{2}\rightarrow E_{2}-a and finally take aa large, one finds a somewhat simpler expression

R0,2​(E1,E2)=14​z1​z2​(z1+z2)2,zi=−Ei.R_{0,2}(E_{1},E_{2})=\frac{1}{4z_{1}z_{2}(z_{1}+z_{2})^{2}},\hskip 20.0ptz_{i}=\sqrt{-E_{i}}. (47)

This is valid for any double-scaled theory. But in some cases one can say much more. For example, it will sometimes be helpful to have in mind the simple double-scaled theory

ρ0total​(E)=eS0π​E,E>0.\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E)=\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{\pi}\sqrt{E},\hskip 20.0ptE>0. (48)

This theory is dual to topological gravity [29, 30]. For a recent discussion see [32].

The density of eigenvalues (48) can be obtained by starting with the Gaussian matrix integral, for which ρ0\rho_{0} is a semicircle:

ρ0total​(E)=eS0π​a2−E22​a,−a<E<a.\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E)=\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}-E^{2}}{2a}},\hskip 20.0pt-a<E<a. (49)

The condition that ρ0\rho_{0} should have unit normalization implies that L/eS0=(a/2)3/2L/e^{S_{0}}=(a/2)^{3/2}. To take the double-scaled limit, one shifts E→E−aE\rightarrow E-a and takes aa large, recovering (48). In this limit, many quantities can be computed exactly, such as the exact ensemble average of the density of eigenvalues:

⟨ρ⁡(E)⟩=e2​S03​[Ai′​(ξ)2−ξ​Ai​(ξ)2],ξ=−e2​S03​E.\langle\rho(E)\rangle=e^{\frac{2S_{0}}{3}}\Big[\text{Ai}^{\prime}(\xi)^{2}-\xi\text{Ai}(\xi)^{2}\Big],\hskip 20.0pt\xi=-e^{\frac{2S_{0}}{3}}E. (50)

Note that unlike the leading expression (48), this eigenvalue distribution is extended along the entire real axis, although it is nonperturbatively small (in e−S0e^{-S_{0}}) for fixed negative EE.

2.5 Topological recursion

We will now present the recursion relation of [15], which efficiently determines all of the higher Rg,nR_{g,n}. Instead of working with functions of the energy, it will be convenient to define a new coordinate zz by1616 16 The minus sign here is conventional, and we have chosen to define things so that real zz corresponds to the “forbidden” region of negative EE, where the large LL density of eigenvalues vanishes.

z2=−E.z^{2}=-E. (51)

In terms of EE, the functions Rg,nR_{g,n} and the spectral curve quantity yy are double valued. They can be viewed as single-valued functions living on a double cover of the EE plane. For a conventional one-cut matrix integral, this double cover is branched over the endpoints a−,a+a_{-},a_{+}. In the double scaled limit, we move one branch point to the origin and the other to infinity, so we have a double cover of the EE plane branched over the origin. The coordinate zz defined above is a good coordinate on that space. The variable x=−Ex=-E is often used. Then, more precisely, the spectral curve is given by the locus

(x⁡(z),y⁡(z))⊂ℂ2.(x(z),y(z))\subset\mathbb{C}^{2}~. (52)

This curve is uniformized by zz and so is genus 00.1717 17 It can be also be viewed as a degenerate infinite genus curve with degenerations located at each of the infinite number of zeros of y⁡(z)y(z).

Concretely, Rg,nR_{g,n} and yy are single-valued functions of zz. For example, for the case (43), using (38) and (46) one has (up to a minus sign that can be fixed once and for all)

y=sin⁡(2​π​z)4​π.y=\frac{\sin(2\pi z)}{4\pi}. (53)

In the topological gravity case (48), one has y=zy=z. For small zz the two differ by a factor of two that is conventional; it could have been absorbed into a shift of S0S_{0} by log⁡(2)\log(2).

We can now present Eynard’s recursion relation for the expansion of the multi-resolvent correlators Rg,nR_{g,n} defined in (45). We will write this for the special case of a double-scaled matrix integral, with one branch point at the origin. In order to line up with the notation in [78], we define functions Wg,nW_{g,n} by

Wg,n​(z1,…,zn)=(−1)n​2n​z1​…​zn​Rg,n​(−z12,…,−zn2)W_{g,n}(z_{1},...,z_{n})=(-1)^{n}2^{n}z_{1}...z_{n}\,R_{g,n}(-z_{1}^{2},...,-z_{n}^{2})\hskip 20.0pt (54)

except for two special cases where

This was noted and proven in general in work by Eynard and Orantin [33], who showed that after Laplace transform, Mirzakhani’s recursion relation takes the form of (56) with the spectral curve y=sin⁡(2​π​z)4​πy=\frac{\sin(2\pi z)}{4\pi}. This relation provides a link between the loop equations of a matrix integral and the volumes of the moduli space of curves. In the next section, we will see that it implies that JT gravity is dual to a matrix ensemble.

3 The genus expansion in JT gravity

Now that we have reviewed the structure of the genus expansion in matrix integrals, we will see how the same thing arises from an analysis of the path integral in JT gravity. This theory is defined by the Euclidean action

IJ​T=−S02​π​[12​∫ℳg​R+∫∂ℳh​K]−[12​∫ℳg​ϕ​(R+2)+∫∂ℳh​ϕ​(K−1)].I_{JT}=-\frac{S_{0}}{2\pi}\left[\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{g}R+\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{h}K\right]-\left[\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{g}\phi(R+2)+\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{h}\phi(K-1)\right]. (61)

The basic strategy is to compute something like the correlation functions of resolvents studied in the previous section, and show that they satisfy the recursion relation of a double-scaled matrix integral.

More precisely, we will study correlation functions ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}}, where in the matrix integral interpretation, Z⁡(β)=Tr⁡(e−β​H)Z(\beta)={\rm Tr}(e^{-\beta H}) and HH is the random matrix. This is related to the resolvent by an integral transform

R(E)=−∫0∞dβeβ​EZ(β),R(E)=-\int_{0}^{\infty}d\beta e^{\beta E}Z(\beta), (62)

which makes sense for EE less than the ground state energy (which we will set to be zero). The expression can be continued in EE after doing the integral.

We can translate ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}} to a bulk gravity computation using the usual NAdS2/NCFT1 dictionary [9]. Here we think about the random matrix HH as the Hamiltonian of the boundary theory. The way the translation works is as follows. One integrates over 2d geometries with the rule that for each factor of Z⁡(β)Z(\beta), the geometry must have a boundary with length β/ϵ\beta/\epsilon, and where the dilaton has the value ϕ=γ/ϵ\phi=\gamma/\epsilon. (One takes ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 at the end.) In order to compute the connected part of the correlator, we require that the 2d geometry be connected. In what follows we will often take γ=1/2\gamma=1/2, which amounts to a choice of units.

The upshot of this is that to compute ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}}, we are looking for connected geometries with nn boundaries of a specific kind. For a fixed number of boundaries, these are classified topologically1919 19 In this paper we restrict to orientable surfaces, which are appropriate for a Hermitian matrix integral. We are grateful to Edward Witten for comments on nonorientable contributions. See [26] for discussion. by the number of handles (“genus”) g=0,1,…g=0,1,.... The first S0S_{0} term2020 20 We should note that the presence of the topological term in the low energy limit of the SYK model has only been verified for the disk and the cylinder. in the JT action (61) gives a factor of (eS0)χ(e^{S_{0}})^{\chi}, where χ\chi is the Euler character χ=2−2​g−n\chi=2-2g-n. So, summing over different topologies, we get an expression

⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩conn.≃∑g=0∞Zg,n​(β1,…,βn)(eS0)2​g+n−2\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle_{\text{conn.}}\simeq\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\frac{Z_{g,n}(\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n})}{(e^{S_{0}})^{2g+n-2}} (63)

where Zg,n​(β1,…,βn)Z_{g,n}(\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n}) is the JT path integral for a given topology with the S0S_{0} term left out of the action. As an example of the type of geometry involved, we have

Zg=2,n=3​(β1,β2,β3)=Z_{g=2,n=3}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3})\hskip 10.0pt=\hskip 15.0pt\includegraphics[width=93.15147pt,valign={c}]{figures/threeTrumpets.pdf} (64)

where the lengths of the regularized (red) boundaries are fixed to be βj/ϵ\beta_{j}/\epsilon, but they are allowed to take wiggly shapes as we discuss in a moment.

The path integral over such geometries is simplified considerably by the fact that the integral over ϕ\phi with the action (61) imposes a constraint that the metric should be constant negative curvature R=−2R=-2. It is possible to put a metric with R=−2R=-2 on a topology such as (64), and in fact there is an infinite-dimensional space of such geometries, consistent with our boundary conditions. This corresponds to the freedom to make the boundary wiggly, and also a finite-dimensional moduli space associated to the surface itself. The path integral over the metric then becomes an integral over the moduli space, and a path integral over the boundary wiggles. The JT action reduces to the final extrinsic curvature term, and we have

Zg,n​(β1,…,βn)=∫d⁡(bulk moduli)​∫𝒟⁡(boundary wiggles)​e∫∂ℳh​ϕ​(K−1).Z_{g,n}(\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n})=\int d(\text{bulk moduli})\int\mathcal{D}(\text{boundary wiggles})e^{\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\sqrt{h}\phi(K-1)}. (65)

As we will see, the integral over the boundary wiggles is easy to do. The integral over the bulk moduli is difficult to get explicit expressions for, but we will see that Mirzakhani’s recursion relation implies that the result satisfies the recursion of a double-scaled matrix integral.

Since our goal is to compute the quantities Zg,nZ_{g,n} exactly, it will be important to understand the integration measure. As we will see, the measure that follows from the JT path integral is the Weil-Petersson measure on the bulk moduli, and the symplectic measure on the boundary wiggles, with a relation between the normalization of these measures. As a first step we will review the definition of the Weil-Petersson measure for the moduli space, deferring until slightly later an explanation of why it is relevant in JT gravity.

3.1 The Weil-Petersson symplectic form

The Weil-Petersson measure is derived from a symplectic form. This form can be explained very concretely in terms of the “pants” construction of a hyperbolic Riemann surface. This is based on building up surfaces from an elementary building block, which is a hyperbolic surface with genus zero and three geodesic boundaries, of lengths b1,b2,b3b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}. For example, the three shaded pieces here

(66)

can be glued together to give a genus two surface with one geodesic boundary. Such a geometry can be attached to a “trumpet” (shown unshaded above) in order to form a geometry with an asymptotic boundary, but for the moment we will focus on the shaded components only. By gluing together several of these three-boundary building blocks, one ends up with a manifold with some genus gg and some number nn (possibly zero) of leftover geodesic boundaries. In the example, (g,n)=(2,1)(g,n)=(2,1). The space of such manifolds for fixed values of the external boundary lengths is denoted ℳg,n​(b1,…,bn)\mathcal{M}_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n}), and referred to as the moduli space of bordered Riemann surfaces.

A set of coordinates on this space are simply the parameters of the gluing construction, known as Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates. These consist of the lengths b~1,…,b~k\widetilde{b}_{1},...,\widetilde{b}_{k} of the pairs of internal boundaries that were glued together, along with a corresponding set of twist parameters τ1,..,τk\tau_{1},..,\tau_{k}, which represent the proper distance that one boundary is rotated relative to its partner before the two are glued together. So, all together we have 2​k2k coordinates, and one can show that k=3​g+n−3k=3g+n-3, where gg is the genus and nn is the number of fixed leftover boundaries. The Weil-Petersson form is a symplectic form on this space, and in these coordinates it is simply [80]

Ω=α​∑i=13​g+n−3d​b~i∧d​τi,\Omega=\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{3g+n-3}d\widetilde{b}_{i}\wedge d\tau_{i}, (67)

where α\alpha is a numerical constant that depends on convention. In the literature, α=1\alpha=1 is widely used, and we will often use this convention below. The quantity 1k!​Ωk\frac{1}{k!}\Omega^{k} gives a volume form, and one can integrate this to get the volume of the moduli space ℳg,n​(b1,…,bn)\mathcal{M}_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n}).

In practice, a major complication is that the pants decomposition overcounts the moduli space. Because hyperbolic Riemann surfaces have many geodesics on which to cut, one can find different pants decompositions of the same geometrical surface. Although it is not obvious in these coordinates, the form (67) is invariant under such changes in decomposition. But to correctly compute the volume of the moduli space

Vg,n​(b1,…,bn)=vol​(ℳg,n​(b1,…,bn))V_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n})=\text{vol}\left(\mathcal{M}_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n})\right) (68)

one still needs to restrict the integral to a fundamental region that counts each distinct surface once. This is tricky: see e.g. [79] for an example computation.

In [28], Mirzakhani showed that these volumes satisfy a recursion relation that makes it possible to compute them in practice (see [32] for a recent introduction to Mirzakhani’s method). We will not show the recursion relation explicitly, but an important fact for this paper is that it is equivalent to the statement that the Wg,nW_{g,n} defined in (60) satisfy the recursion relation of a double scaled matrix integral, with y=sin⁡(2​π​z)4​πy=\frac{\sin(2\pi z)}{4\pi} [33].

3.2 Optional: the compact case, in the second-order formalism

We will now begin to explain why the Weil-Petersson measure is relevant for JT gravity. In this section we start with an explanation intended to appeal to readers who have background in string perturbation theory; a more complete explanation will be given later.

To avoid the complication of boundary wiggles for the moment, we will assume that we are integrating over closed manifolds, and in order to have a hyperbolic metric, we assume the genus is g≥2g\geq 2. The path integral on a closed genus gg surface gives a contribution to the logarithm of the matrix integral partition function:

log⁡𝒵⊃(eS0)χ​ℱg=∫𝒟​gμ​ν​𝒟​ϕVol​(diff)​e−IJ​T​[gμ​ν,ϕ].\log\mathcal{Z}\supset(e^{S_{0}})^{\chi}\mathcal{F}_{g}=\int\frac{\mathcal{D}g_{\mu\nu}\mathcal{D}\phi}{\text{Vol}(\text{diff})}\,e^{-I_{JT}[g_{\mu\nu},\phi]}. (69)

To evaluate the path integral, one can fix to conformal gauge

ga​b=e2​ω​g^a​b,g​R=g^​(R^−2​∇^2​ω)g_{ab}=e^{2\omega}\widehat{g}_{ab},\hskip 20.0pt\sqrt{g}R=\sqrt{\widehat{g}}(\widehat{R}-2\widehat{\nabla}^{2}\omega) (70)

where g^\widehat{g} is a metric with R^=−2\widehat{R}=-2. The path integral becomes (see, e.g. eq. (3.13) of [81] with d=0d=0 and including the extra JT gravity term)

ℱg=∫modulid⁡(Weil-Pet.)​(detP^1†​P^1)1/2​∫𝒟​ω​𝒟​ϕ​e−26​SL​[ω]​e∫g​ϕ​(R+2).\mathcal{F}_{g}=\int_{\text{moduli}}d(\text{Weil-Pet.})(\det\widehat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\widehat{P}_{1})^{1/2}\int\mathcal{D}\omega\mathcal{D}\phi\ e^{-26S_{L}[\omega]}e^{\int\sqrt{g}\phi(R+2)}. (71)

The integral over moduli is the integral over metrics g^\widehat{g} with R^=−2\widehat{R}=-2. In [81] it is shown that the path integral reduces to the Weil-Petersson measure on this space, times the Fadeev-Popov determinant for the gauge-fixing to conformal gauge, (detP^1†​P^1)1/2(\det\widehat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\widehat{P}_{1})^{1/2}. The operator P^1\widehat{P}_{1} takes vectors to traceless symmetric tensors

(P^1​v)a​b=∇^a​vb+∇^b​va−g^a​b​∇^c​vc,(\widehat{P}_{1}v)_{ab}=\widehat{\nabla}_{a}v_{b}+\widehat{\nabla}_{b}v_{a}-\widehat{g}_{ab}\widehat{\nabla}^{c}v_{c}, (72)

and for a conventional choice of metric, its adjoint acts as (P^1†​α)a=−2​ga​b​∇^c​αb​c(\widehat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\alpha)^{a}=-2g^{ab}\widehat{\nabla}^{c}\alpha_{bc}. SLS_{L} is the Liouville action; it will not play an important role in this theory because the Liouville field will be localized to zero, and the action will give a multiple of the Euler characteristic.

The final term in the action in (71) can be written more explicitly as

∫g​ϕ​(R+2)=∫g^​ϕ​(R^−2​∇^2​ω+2​e2​ω)=2​∫g^​ϕ​(−∇^2+2)​ω+O⁡(ω2).\int\sqrt{g}\phi(R+2)=\int\sqrt{\widehat{g}}\phi(\widehat{R}-2\widehat{\nabla}^{2}\omega+2e^{2\omega})=2\int\sqrt{\widehat{g}}\,\phi(-\widehat{\nabla}^{2}+2)\omega+O(\omega^{2}). (73)

The path integral over ϕ\phi imposes a delta function constraint δ⁡((−∇^2+2)​ω)\delta((-\widehat{\nabla}^{2}+2)\omega) at every point in space. This condition implies ω=0\omega=0, but in doing the integral over ω\omega we get an inverse power of det(−∇^2+2)\det(-\widehat{\nabla}^{2}+2). So the path integral becomes

ℱg\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{g} =e(const.)​χ​∫modulid⁡(Weil-Pet.)​(detP^1†​P^1)1/2det(−∇^2+2)CLOSE\displaystyle=e^{(\text{const.})\chi}\int_{\text{moduli}}d(\text{Weil-Pet.)}\frac{(\det\widehat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\widehat{P}_{1})^{1/2}}{\det(-\widehat{\nabla}^{2}+2)} (74)

In going to the second line, we used that the ratio of determinants in (74) for hyperbolic manifolds is proportional to e#​χe^{\#\chi}. To show this, one can use the constant negative curvature condition and a short calculation to write P^1†​P^1=2​(−∇^12+1)\widehat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\widehat{P}_{1}=2(-\widehat{\nabla}_{1}^{2}+1), where ∇12\nabla_{1}^{2} is the Laplacian acting on vectors. One can then write out the vector Laplacian explicitly, using coordinates d​s2=d​x2+d​y2y2ds^{2}=\frac{dx^{2}+dy^{2}}{y^{2}}. One finds a simple expression after conjugating by a factor of yy:

y−1​∇^12​y=(D−1−100D1−1)y^{-1}\widehat{\nabla}_{1}^{2}y=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}D_{-1}-1&0\\ 0&D_{1}-1\end{array}\right) (76)

acting on two-component vectors with top component vx+i​vyv^{x}+iv^{y} and bottom component vx−i​vyv^{x}-iv^{y}. The differential operators DnD_{n} are defined, following the conventions in [82], as

Dn≡y2(∂x2+∂y2)−2iny∂x.D_{n}\equiv y^{2}\left(\partial_{x}^{2}+\partial_{y}^{2}\right)-2iny\partial_{x}. (77)
