(det12​P^1†​P^1)1/2det(−∇^2+2)=det1/2(−D1+2)​det1/2(−D−1+2)det(−D0+2)=det(−D1+2)det(−D0+2).\frac{(\det\tfrac{1}{2}\widehat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\widehat{P}_{1})^{1/2}}{\det(-\widehat{\nabla}^{2}+2)}=\frac{\det^{1/2}(-D_{1}+2)\det^{1/2}(-D_{-1}+2)}{\det(-D_{0}+2)}=\frac{\det(-D_{1}+2)}{\det(-D_{0}+2)}. (78)

These determinants differ by at most a factor (const)χ(\text{const})^{\chi} where χ\chi is the Euler characteristic, see [82, 83]. Note that we inserted a factor of 12\tfrac{1}{2} in the first expression here. After regularization, this factor also contributes at most a term proportional to (const)χ(\text{const})^{\chi}.

So we find that, up to a factor e(const.)​χe^{(\text{const.})\chi} that can be absorbed into S0S_{0}, the path integral on a compact g≥2g\geq 2 surface reduces to the Weil-Petersson volume of the moduli space.2121 21 Note that this volume also depends on an arbitrary normalization of the form in (67). If we rescale the form by a factor of α\alpha, we will rescale the answer by a factor of α3​g−3=α−32​χ\alpha^{3g-3}=\alpha^{-\frac{3}{2}\chi}, so this factor can also be absorbed into S0S_{0}. The cancellation of the determinants that made this possible was quite specific to the JT theory. We will see this from another perspective below.

3.3 First-order formalism

In order to evaluate (65), we need the measure both for the bulk moduli and the boundary wiggles. And, moreover, we will need a relation between the normalizations of these measures. In order to derive this, it will be convenient to use the first-order formalism for JT gravity, which is a topological B​FBF-type theory.

3.3.1 Basic setup

We start with some equations for first order gravity in two dimensions. The basic objects are the one forms ea=eμa​d​xμe^{a}=e^{a}_{\mu}dx^{\mu} and the spin connection ωba=ϵba​ω\omega^{a}_{\ b}=\epsilon^{a}_{\ b}\omega where ϵ12=1\epsilon_{12}=1, and a,ba,b indices are raised and lowered with δa​b\delta_{ab}, so we don’t need to distinguish up vs. down. The no-torsion condition, which determines the spin connection, is

d​ea=−ωba∧eb.de^{a}=-\omega^{a}_{\ b}\wedge e^{b}. (79)

The curvature two form is

Rba=d​ωba+ωca∧ωbc=d​ωba.R^{a}_{\ b}=d\omega^{a}_{\ b}+\omega^{a}_{\ c}\wedge\omega^{c}_{\ b}=d\omega^{a}_{\ b}. (80)

The first equation is the general definition. The second equation is true in two dimensions, since in this case ωca∧ωbc=−δba​ω∧ω=0\omega^{a}_{\ c}\wedge\omega^{c}_{\ b}=-\delta^{a}_{b}\omega\wedge\omega=0. In general, the curvature two form is related to the Riemann tensor by

Rba=12​eμa​ebν​Rν​ρ​σμ​d​xρ∧d​xσ.R^{a}_{\ b}=\frac{1}{2}e^{a}_{\mu}e^{\nu}_{b}R^{\mu}_{\ \nu\rho\sigma}dx^{\rho}\wedge dx^{\sigma}. (81)

In two dimensions this simplifies because Rμ​ν​ρ​σ=12​R​(gμ​ρ​gν​σ−gμ​σ​gν​ρ)R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}R(g_{\mu\rho}g_{\nu\sigma}-g_{\mu\sigma}g_{\nu\rho}) and we find that

d​ωba=12​R​ea∧eb.d\omega^{a}_{\ b}=\frac{1}{2}Re^{a}\wedge e_{b}. (82)

Now, e1∧e2=e1∧e2=g​d2​xe^{1}\wedge e_{2}=e^{1}\wedge e^{2}=\sqrt{g}d^{2}x, so

g​d2​x​R=2​d​ω 21=2​d​ω.\sqrt{g}d^{2}xR=2d\omega^{1}_{\ 2}=2d\omega. (83)

We can then write the JT action in the first order formalism as

12​∫g​ϕ​(R+2)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\sqrt{g}\phi(R+2) →∫[ϕ⁡(𝑑ω+e1∧e2)+ϕa​(d​ea+ϵba​ω∧eb)]\displaystyle\rightarrow\int\left[\phi(d\omega+e^{1}\wedge e^{2})+\phi_{a}(de^{a}+\epsilon^{a}_{\ b}\omega\wedge e^{b})\right] (84)
=i​∫Tr​(B​F).\displaystyle=i\int\text{Tr}\left(BF\right). (85)

In the first line, we introduced the ϕa\phi^{a} as Lagrange multipliers that enforce the no-torsion condition (79). In the second line we wrote the answer in terms of a matrix of scalars BB and a matrix of one forms AA:

B=−i⁡(−ϕ1ϕ2+ϕϕ2−ϕϕ1),A=12​(−e1e2−ωe2+ωe1)B=-i\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-\phi^{1}&\phi^{2}+\phi\\ \phi^{2}-\phi&\phi^{1}\end{array}\right)\hskip 20.0ptA=\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-e^{1}&e^{2}-\omega\\ e^{2}+\omega&e^{1}\end{array}\right) (86)

where the field strength FF is defined as

F=D​A=d​A+A∧A.F=DA=dA+A\wedge A. (87)

The action can now be recognized as an S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) “B​FBF” theory. Note that we introduced a factor of ii in (85), and a compensating factor of −i-i in (86). With this convention, the purely imaginary contour for our Lagrange multipliers ϕ,ϕ1,ϕ2\phi,\phi_{1},\phi_{2} becomes a real contour for the matrix BB. The action (85) then has the usual factor of ii for a BF theory in Euclidean signature.

The field BB enters the action only linearly, so we can integrate it out, getting a constraint that F=0F=0, in other words that we should integrate only over flat connections.2222 22 Actually, in JT gravity we only want to integrate over one topological component of the space of flat S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) connections (see e.g. footnote 5 of [32]). Global aspects of the space of flat connections will not be important for us, because we view the second order Lagrangian as the definition of the theory, and only use the BF description locally, in order to compute the correct measure about a given configuration. The advantage of the BF theory presentation is that there is a very simple description for the measure on the space of flat connections. This measure arises from the original ultralocal measure for the path integral, after integrating out the nonzero modes. After gauge-fixing and using the Fadeev-Popov procedure, it was shown in [84] for B​FBF theories with compact gauge group that the path integral on orientable surfaces reduces to an integral over flat connections, with the measure induced by the symplectic form on the space of gauge fields

Ω⁡(σ,η)=2​α​∫Tr⁡(σ∧η).\Omega(\sigma,\eta)=2\alpha\int{\rm Tr}\left(\sigma\wedge\eta\right). (88)

Here σ\sigma and η\eta are elements of the tangent space in the space of gauge fields. Concretely, they are one forms that parametrize infinitesimal variations of AA. The constant α\alpha is arbitrary and can be absorbed into a shift of S0S_{0}, as we will see in detail below.

An important point in [84] is that this symplectic form is Kahler-compatible with a metric on the space of one-forms, which can be used together with a similar metric on the space of zero-forms to define the gauge-fixed path integral measure. Concretely, Kahler-compatibility of a metric and a symplectic form means that g⁡(σ,η)=Ω⁡(σ,J​η)g(\sigma,\eta)=\Omega(\sigma,J\eta), where J2=−1J^{2}=-1 and Ω⁡(J​σ,J​η)=Ω⁡(σ,η)\Omega(J\sigma,J\eta)=\Omega(\sigma,\eta). In the case of compact BF theory, one can take J=∗J=*, and the corresponding metric on the space of one-forms is

g(σ,η)=2α∫Tr(σ∧∗η).g(\sigma,\eta)=2\alpha\int{\rm Tr}\left(\sigma\wedge*\eta\right). (89)

Unlike (88), this formula involves a choice of metric on the underlying surface, which is needed to define ∗*, but in the gauge-fixed path integral, this dependence drops out if one uses a similar formula to define the metric on the space of ghost and antighost fields, as explained in [84].

In the noncompact case, (89) is not a positive metric on the space of field configurations, since the Lie algebra metric has negative directions. However, following [85], we can use a non-invariant but positive metric on the Lie algebra in order to define the gauge fixing condition, and also to define the metric in the space of field configurations:

g(σ,η)=2α∫Tr(σ∧∗Tη).g(\sigma,\eta)=2\alpha\int{\rm Tr}\left(\sigma\wedge*T\eta\right). (90)

Here TT reverses the sign of the negative-metric component of the Lie algebra.2323 23 We are grateful to Edward Witten for suggesting this. This metric is also Kahler-compatible with (88), using J=∗TJ=*T. This means that the analysis in the noncompact case continues to apply, and in particular the induced measure on the space of flat connections is the one that follows from (88).

3.3.2 The Weil-Petersson measure from BF theory

An important fact for us is that, on the space of flat S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) connections, (88) is locally the same as the Weil-Petersson form on the moduli space of curves [86]. We will explain this with a simple example in a moment, but first we should explain the formula in more detail.

Suppose we are at a point in the space of flat S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) connections. A symplectic form is a two-form, which is supposed to take as input two vectors in the tangent space to this point. The tangent space can be described (up to gauge transformations) as consisting of gauge fields δ​A\delta A such that A+ϵ​δ​AA+\epsilon\delta A is still flat to linear order in ϵ\epsilon, i.e.

d⁡(δ​A)+A∧δ​A+δ​A∧A=0.d(\delta A)+A\wedge\delta A+\delta A\wedge A=0. (91)

We can stick two such configurations into (88) and get a number Ω⁡(δ1​A,δ2​A)\Omega(\delta_{1}A,\delta_{2}A), so (88) is a two form in that sense. Note also that it is gauge-invariant on the space of flat connections. To see this, suppose we make a gauge transformation of one of the deformations: δ2​A→δ2​A+d​Θ+[A,Θ]\delta_{2}A\rightarrow\delta_{2}A+d\Theta+[A,\Theta]. Then the change in the value of Ω⁡(δ1​A,δ2​A)\Omega(\delta_{1}A,\delta_{2}A) is

2​α​∫Tr⁡(δ1​A∧(𝑑Θ+[A,Θ]))2\alpha\int{\rm Tr}\left(\delta_{1}A\wedge(d\Theta+[A,\Theta])\right) (92)

which vanishes after integrating by parts and using (91). (The possible boundary term in this integration by parts will be important below.)

Let’s now see concretely how the form (88) is related to the Weil-Petersson form (67). To do this we focus on a particular geodesic where two tubes of pants have been glued together. Near this region, we choose coordinates ρ,x\rho,x so that ρ\rho measures the distance to the joining locus (ρ<0\rho<0 is one tube, and ρ>0\rho>0 is the other). The metric is

d​s2=d​ρ2+cosh2⁡(ρ)​[b​d​x+τ​δ​(ρ)​d​ρ]2,x∼x+1.ds^{2}=d\rho^{2}+\cosh^{2}(\rho)\left[bdx+\tau\delta(\rho)d\rho\right]^{2},\hskip 20.0ptx\sim x+1. (93)

The funny term involving δ⁡(ρ)\delta(\rho) is to implement the twist by distance τ\tau. To see that this works correctly, we can write the expression in brackets as 2424 24 It should be clear from context that θ⁡(ρ)\theta(\rho) in the following equation is the step function, not an angular coordinate.

b​d​x+τ​δ​(ρ)​d​ρ=d​y,y=b​x+τ​θ​(ρ).bdx+\tau\delta(\rho)d\rho=dy,\hskip 20.0pty=bx+\tau\theta(\rho). (94)

The metric is smooth in yy, which is a continuous coordinate on the geometry. This means that xx is actually discontinuous: the two spaces have been glued together with a shift by proper length τ\tau in the xx direction.

In S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) gauge theory terms, up to a gauge choice AA is given by (86) with

e1=d​ρ,e2=b​cosh⁡(ρ)​d​x+τ​δ​(ρ)​d​ρ,ω=−b​sinh⁡(ρ)​d​x.e^{1}=d\rho,\hskip 20.0pte^{2}=b\cosh(\rho)dx+\tau\delta(\rho)d\rho,\hskip 20.0pt\omega=-b\sinh(\rho)dx. (95)

We now consider small variations of δi​b,δi​τ\delta_{i}b,\delta_{i}\tau for i=1,2i=1,2 and we compute

Tr​(δ1​A∧δ2​A)\displaystyle\text{Tr}\left(\delta_{1}A\wedge\delta_{2}A\right) =12​(δ1​e1∧δ2​e1+δ1​e2∧δ2​e2−δ1​ω∧δ2​ω)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta_{1}e^{1}\wedge\delta_{2}e^{1}+\delta_{1}e^{2}\wedge\delta_{2}e^{2}-\delta_{1}\omega\wedge\delta_{2}\omega\right) (96)
=12​(δ1​b​δ2​τ−δ2​b​δ1​τ)​δ​(ρ)​d​x​d​ρ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\delta_{1}b\,\delta_{2}\tau-\delta_{2}b\,\delta_{1}\tau)\delta(\rho)dxd\rho. (97)

Integrating over ρ,x\rho,x, the symplectic form (88) is

Ω⁡(δ1​A,δ2​A)=α⁡(δ1​b​δ2​τ−δ2​b​δ1​τ).\Omega(\delta_{1}A,\delta_{2}A)=\alpha(\delta_{1}b\,\delta_{2}\tau-\delta_{2}b\,\delta_{1}\tau). (98)

This coincides with (67) including the normalization factor of α\alpha, which is why we chose the specific normalization in (88).

3.3.3 Boundary conditions

The real advantage to working with the BF formulation is that it is straightforward to use the same symplectic form (88) to get the measure for the integral over wiggly boundaries. Before we can do that, though, we need to discuss the boundary conditions that we are imposing on the B​FBF theory. Our guiding principle is that we should choose boundary conditions that reproduce the ones from the second order formulation of JT gravity. Essentially, we need to arrange that the boundary conditions should allow a wiggly boundary but not more.

The boundary conditions that are imposed in JT gravity in order to compute the partition function Z⁡(β)Z(\beta) are

gu​u|bdy=1ϵ2,ϕ|bdy=γϵ,ϵ→0.g_{uu}\big|_{\text{bdy}}=\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}},\hskip 20.0pt\phi\big|_{\text{bdy}}=\frac{\gamma}{\epsilon},\hskip 20.0pt\epsilon\rightarrow 0. (99)

The uu coordinate is a rescaled proper length coordinate along the boundary. It should run from zero to β\beta, so that the total length of the boundary is β/ϵ\beta/\epsilon. The invariant content of (99) is that that ϕ|bdy=γβ⋅length​(bdy)\phi|_{\text{bdy}}=\frac{\gamma}{\beta}\cdot\text{length}(\text{bdy}), but these equations also define a preferred coordinate uu along the boundary. This coordinate will be convenient below. As emphasized in [9], this type of boundary condition allows a “boundary graviton” mode corresponding to a wiggly boundary. This is typically described by giving the trajectory of the ϵ\epsilon-regularized boundary in Euclidean AdS2.2525 25 JT gravity localizes to exact Euclidean AdS2, but all that is really important for parametrizing the boundary this way is that the geometry is asymptotically Euclidean AdS2. To specify this, one can use e.g. global coordinates

d​s2=d​ρ2+sinh2⁡(ρ)​d​θ2ds^{2}=d\rho^{2}+\sinh^{2}(\rho)d\theta^{2} (100)

and then give a function θ⁡(u)\theta(u), which specifies the angle in the hyperbolic plane as a function of the boundary proper length coordinate uu. The function ρ⁡(u)\rho(u) is then fixed by (99). Instead of parametrizing things this way, we would rather have a formula for the asymptotic behavior of the metric, so that we can read off conditions that can be translated to the first-order formalism. To do this, we can use coordinates r,ur,u where rr is a coordinate that measures distance to the boundary (which is taken to r=∞r=\infty in the ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 limit), and uu is the coordinate we have already discussed. Then one can show that a wiggly boundary leads to a metric with the large rr behavior

d​s2=d​r2+(14​e2​r−Sch​(u)+…)​d​u2,Sch​(u)=Sch​(tan⁡θ⁡(u)2,u).ds^{2}=dr^{2}+\left(\tfrac{1}{4}e^{2r}-\text{Sch}(u)+...\right)du^{2},\hskip 20.0pt\text{Sch}(u)=\text{Sch}\left(\tan\frac{\theta(u)}{2},u\right). (101)

One way to check this is to note that this metric has R=−2R=-2 to the order we are working, and then to compute the extrinsic curvature of a constant rr surface for large rr, which is

K=12​gu​u​∂rgu​u=12​∂r(14​e2​r−Sch​(u)+…)14​e2​r−Sch​(u)+…=1+4​e−2​r​Sch​(u)+…K=\frac{1}{2}g^{uu}\partial_{r}g_{uu}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}\partial_{r}\left(\tfrac{1}{4}e^{2r}-\text{Sch}(u)+...\right)}{\tfrac{1}{4}e^{2r}-\text{Sch}(u)+...}=1+4e^{-2r}\text{Sch}(u)+... (102)

This agrees with the computation of the extrinsic curvature of the parametrized boundary in the fixed metric (100), as described in [9].2626 26 And the extrinsic curvature of the boundary curve specifies it uniquely, up to an S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) isometry of the entire geometry that is a gauge symmetry in this context. So, the summary of this discussion is that a to allow wiggly boundaries, we can impose that the metric should asymptotically take the form (101) with an arbitrary function Sch​(u)\text{Sch}(u) that is allowed to vary.

We would now like to translate this condition to the B​FBF theory. First of all, a standard minimal boundary condition for B​FBF theory would be to fix some linear combination of BB and AuA_{u} to zero

B+i​c​Au|bdy=0,c=const. to be fixed below.B+icA_{u}\big|_{\text{bdy}}=0,\hskip 20.0ptc=\text{const. to be fixed below}. (103)

The coefficient was taken to be purely imaginary so that the boundary condition is a real one after continuing the Euclidean boundary time uu to Lorentzian time. One can check that with this boundary condition, the action with an appropriate boundary term

I=−i∫ℳTr(BF)+i2∫∂ℳTr(BA).I=-i\int_{\mathcal{M}}{\rm Tr}(BF)+\frac{i}{2}\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}{\rm Tr}\left(BA\right). (104)

is stationary with respect to linear variations about a solution. The boundary condition (103) is closely related to a familiar boundary condition in three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory. There, some linear combination of the boundary components of the gauge field are typically set to zero. B​FBF theory is a dimensional reduction of Chern-Simons theory where the gauge field is taken to be independent of the third coordinate x3x^{3}, and where

A(3​d)=A+B​d​x3.A^{(3d)}=A+B\,dx^{3}. (105)

From the three-dimensional perspective, the boundary components of A(3​d)A^{(3d)} are AuA_{u} and BB, so (103) is indeed the usual type of condition. Chern-Simons theory with this type of boundary condition leads to a boundary theory that is a chiral WZW model [87, 88]. The analogous statement for B​FBF theory with Lie group GG is that the boundary theory is the quantum mechanics of a particle moving on the GG manifold [89]. However, this isn’t quite what we want. We are aiming for the Schwarzian boundary theory, which is a path integral over a quotient of diff​(S1)\text{diff}(S^{1}), whereas the above suggests that we will get a path integral over the larger space loop​(S​L​(2,ℝ))/S​L​(2,ℝ)\text{loop}(SL(2,\mathbb{R}))/SL(2,\mathbb{R}) [90].

The problem can be fixed [23, 91, 92, 90] by following the steps [93] used to impose the asymptotic boundary conditions for AdS3 [94] in the Chern-Simons formulation [95, 96] (see also [97, 98] for recent 3d discussion). Basically, we need to impose stronger boundary conditions, namely the asymptotic conditions (101). These conditions can be written in first-order variables as

e1=d​r,e2=(12​er−Sch​(u)​e−r)​d​u,ω=−(12​er+Sch​(u)​e−r)​d​u.e^{1}=dr,\hskip 20.0pte^{2}=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{r}-\text{Sch}(u)e^{-r}\right)du,\hskip 20.0pt\omega=-\left(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{r}+\text{Sch}(u)e^{-r}\right)du. (106)

In terms of the gauge field, this imposes the large rr behavior

A\displaystyle A =d​r2​(−1001)+d​u2​(0er−2​Sch​(u)​e−r0).\displaystyle=\frac{dr}{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right)+\frac{du}{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&e^{r}\\ -2\,\text{Sch}(u)e^{-r}&0\end{array}\right).

We emphasize that in these boundary conditions, Sch​(u)\text{Sch}(u) is an arbitrary function which is allowed to vary; this describes the freedom in AA at the displayed order in e−re^{-r}. We should check that the action for this quantity agrees with expectations from JT gravity. First, we can fix the constant in (103) by requiring that (106) is consistent with the large rr behavior of (99), which requires ϕ=γϵ=γ​er2\phi=\frac{\gamma}{\epsilon}=\gamma\frac{e^{r}}{2}. This fixes c=2​γc=2\gamma, so the boundary term becomes

I=γ∫duTr(Au2)=−γ∫duSch(u)I=\gamma\int du\,{\rm Tr}\left(A_{u}^{2}\right)=-\gamma\int du\,\text{Sch}(u) (111)

which is the same Schwarzian action one gets from the standard treatment of JT.

3.3.4 The boundary wiggles and symplectic form

We can now give a B​FBF theory description of the boundary wiggles and compute the measure from the symplectic form (88). In Chern-Simons theory, the boundary WZW modes arise from would-be gauge transformations that act nontrivially on the boundary. In B​FBF theory we are in the same situation: the physical mode describing the boundary wiggles is a transformation by a would-be gauge transformation that does not vanish at infinity, but instead limits to a function Θ⁡(u,r)\Theta(u,r) with some asymptotic rr dependence and arbitrary uu dependence.

In principle Θ⁡(u,r)\Theta(u,r), as an s​l​(2,ℝ)sl(2,\mathbb{R}) element, contains three independent functions. However, imposing that the transformation A→A+d​Θ+[A,Θ]A\rightarrow A+d\Theta+[A,\Theta] should preserve the condition (3.3.3) allows us to solve for the large rr behavior of two of the functions in terms of the third, so that the most general transformation has the large rr behavior

Θ⁡(u,r)→(12​ε′​(u)12​er​ε​(u)−e−r​[Sch​(u)​ε​(u)+ε′′​(u)]−12​ε′​(u))\Theta(u,r)\rightarrow\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\prime}(u)&\tfrac{1}{2}e^{r}\varepsilon(u)\\ -e^{-r}\left[\text{Sch}(u)\varepsilon(u)+\varepsilon^{\prime\prime}(u)\right]&-\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\prime}(u)\end{array}\right) (112)

for some function ε⁡(u)\varepsilon(u). This preserves (3.3.3) but induces the transformation

Sch​(u)→Sch​(u)+ε′′′​(u)+ε⁡(u)​Sch′​(u)+2​ε′​(u)​Sch​(u).\text{Sch}(u)\rightarrow\text{Sch}(u)+\varepsilon^{\prime\prime\prime}(u)+\varepsilon(u)\text{Sch}^{\prime}(u)+2\varepsilon^{\prime}(u)\text{Sch}(u). (113)

This transformation is the correct transformation of the Schwarzian derivative Sch​(f​(u),u)\text{Sch}(f(u),u) under an infinitesimal reparametrization acting on the right: f⁡(u)→f⁡(u+ε⁡(u))f(u)\rightarrow f(u+\varepsilon(u)). This identifies the mode (112) with an infinitesimal reparametrization, introducing a small wiggle.

We are finally in a position to evaluate the measure for the wiggles, by evaluating the symplectic form

Ω⁡(δ1​A,δ2​A)=2​α​∫ℳTr​(δ1​A∧δ2​A)\Omega(\delta_{1}A,\delta_{2}A)=2\alpha\int_{\mathcal{M}}\text{Tr}(\delta_{1}A\wedge\delta_{2}A) (114)

on a pair of configurations where δi​A=d​Θi+[A,Θi]\delta_{i}A=d\Theta_{i}+[A,\Theta_{i}] and Θi\Theta_{i} have the limiting behavior (112). For any formal gauge transformations Θi\Theta_{i}, the integrand in (114) is a total derivative, and a short calculation shows that the above can be written as a boundary integral

Ω⁡(δ1​A,δ2​A)=2​α​∫∂ℳTr⁡(Θ1​(d​Θ2+[A,Θ2])).\Omega(\delta_{1}A,\delta_{2}A)=2\alpha\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}{\rm Tr}\big(\Theta_{1}(d\Theta_{2}+[A,\Theta_{2}])\big). (115)

Now inserting the limiting form (112) and integrating by parts in uu, assuming that all functions including Sch​(u)\text{Sch}(u) are periodic, one finds

Ω⁡(δ1​A,δ2​A)=α​∫0βd​u​[ε1′​(u)​ε2′′​(u)−Sch​(u)​(ε1​(u)​ε2′​(u)−ε1′​(u)​ε2​(u))]\Omega(\delta_{1}A,\delta_{2}A)=\alpha\int_{0}^{\beta}du\bigg[\varepsilon_{1}^{\prime}(u)\varepsilon^{\prime\prime}_{2}(u)-\text{Sch}(u)\bigg(\varepsilon_{1}(u)\varepsilon_{2}^{\prime}(u)-\varepsilon_{1}^{\prime}(u)\varepsilon_{2}(u)\bigg)\bigg] (116)

which can also be written as

Ω=α2​∫0βd​u​[d​ε′​(u)∧d​ε′′​(u)−2​Sch​(u)​𝑑ε​(u)∧d​ε′​(u)].\Omega=\frac{\alpha}{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}du\bigg[d\varepsilon^{\prime}(u)\wedge d\varepsilon^{\prime\prime}(u)-2\,\text{Sch}(u)\,d\varepsilon(u)\wedge d\varepsilon^{\prime}(u)\bigg]. (117)

This is a multiple of the same (Kirillov-Kostant-Souriau) symplectic form that was assumed for the Schwarzian path integral in [22]. Here we have derived it from the bulk theory. Also, we have related the coefficient of the symplectic form for boundary wiggles to the coefficient of the Weil-Petersson form (67), because both are special cases of the form (88).

3.3.5 The path integral over the boundary wiggles

We will now evaluate the path integral over the boundary wiggles for the cases that are relevant for our problem. There are two cases, corresponding to a wiggly boundary on the disk, and a wiggly boundary at the big end of a hyperbolic “trumpet” geometry as shown below.

(118)

A useful simplification is that both path integrals are one-loop exact [22], so we can evaluate them exactly by just doing the path integral for small fluctuations.

We start with the disk. In this case, it is convenient to use the following coordinates for the hyperbolic disk

d​s2=d​ρ2+sinh2⁡(ρ)​d​θ2.ds^{2}=d\rho^{2}+\sinh^{2}(\rho)d\theta^{2}. (119)

The wiggly boundary can be described by giving θ⁡(u)\theta(u), where uu is a rescaled proper length coordinate along the boundary, running from zero to β\beta. The other coordinate ρ⁡(u)\rho(u) is determined by the condition that the induced metric for the boundary is gu​u=1ϵ2g_{uu}=\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}. The JT action reduces to the boundary extrinsic curvature term (65) in this case, which is −γ∫duSch(tanθ2,u)-\gamma\int du\,\text{Sch}(\tan\frac{\theta}{2},u) [9]. Evaluating the Schwarzian derivative explicitly and integrating by parts, one finds that the path integral we want is

ZSchdisk(β)=∫d​μ​[θ]S​L​(2,ℝ)exp[−γ2∫0βdu(θ′′2θ′2−θ′2)].Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{disk}}(\beta)=\int\frac{d\mu[\theta]}{SL(2,\mathbb{R})}\exp\left[-\frac{\gamma}{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}du\left(\frac{\theta^{\prime\prime 2}}{\theta^{\prime 2}}-\theta^{\prime 2}\right)\right]. (120)

The measure d​μ​[θ]d\mu[\theta] means the measure induced by the symplectic form (117). We are dividing by S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) for the following reason: the hyperbolic disk has an S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) isometry group. Acting with an isometry on the left panel of (118) moves the shaded droplet around in the hyperbolic space, but doesn’t change the geometry of the shaded region. So to avoid overcounting, we should integrate over wiggly boundaries only up to S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) equivalence [9].

Using the one-loop exactness of this integral, we can get the exact answer by doing the Gaussian integral for small fluctuations about the classical solution

θ⁡(u)=2​πβ​(u+ε⁡(u)).\theta(u)=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\left(u+\varepsilon(u)\right). (121)

At quadratic order, the action three modes ε=1,e±2​πβ​i​u\varepsilon=1,e^{\pm\frac{2\pi}{\beta}iu}. These zero modes correspond to linearized S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) transformations of the classical solution, and we can implement the quotient in (120) by not integrating over these modes. So we integrate over functions parametrized by

ε⁡(u)=∑|n|≥2e−2​πβ​i​n​u​(εn(R)+i​εn(I))\varepsilon(u)=\sum_{|n|\geq 2}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\beta}inu}\left(\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)}+i\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)}\right) (122)

where in order for ε⁡(u)\varepsilon(u) to be real, the real and imaginary parts satisfy εn(R)=ε−n(R)\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)}=\varepsilon_{-n}^{(R)} and εn(I)=−ε−n(I)\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)}=-\varepsilon_{-n}^{(I)}. One can view the independent variables are εn(R)\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)} and εn(I)\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)} for positive n≥2n\geq 2. It is straightforward to insert (122) into (117), along with the saddle point value of the Schwarzian Sch​(tan⁡π​uβ,u)=2​π2β2\text{Sch}(\tan\frac{\pi u}{\beta},u)=\frac{2\pi^{2}}{\beta^{2}} and get the symplectic form in terms of these variables

Ω\displaystyle\Omega =2​α​(2​π)3β2​∑n≥2(n3−n)​d​εn(R)∧d​εn(I).\displaystyle=2\alpha\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{\beta^{2}}\sum_{n\geq 2}(n^{3}-n)d\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)}\wedge d\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)}. (123)

After also working out the action in (120) to quadratic order in ε\varepsilon, one finds that the properly normalized path integral is

ZSchdisk​(β)\displaystyle Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{disk}}(\beta) =e2​π2​γβ​∏n≥22​α​(2​π)3β2​(n3−n)​∫d​εn(R)​d​εn(I)​e−(2​π)4​γ​(εn(R))2+(εn(I))2β3​(n4−n2)\displaystyle=e^{\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma}{\beta}}\prod_{n\geq 2}2\alpha\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{\beta^{2}}(n^{3}-n)\int d\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)}d\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)}e^{-(2\pi)^{4}\gamma\frac{(\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)})^{2}+(\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)})^{2}}{\beta^{3}}(n^{4}-n^{2})} (124)
=e2​π2​γβ​∏n≥2α​βγ​n=1α3/2​γ3/2(2​π)1/2​β3/2​e2​π2​γβ.\displaystyle=e^{\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma}{\beta}}\prod_{n\geq 2}\frac{\alpha\beta}{\gamma\,n}=\frac{1}{\alpha^{3/2}}\frac{\gamma^{3/2}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta^{3/2}}e^{\frac{2\pi^{2}\gamma}{\beta}}. (125)

In the last step, we regularized the product using e.g. zeta function regularization or by writing the product as an exponential of a sum of logs, introducing a smooth cutoff in the sum, and then discarding the divergent piece.

Next we consider the trumpet. There is actually a one-parameter family of trumpet geometries, labeled by the length of the geodesic at the small end of the trumpet. We take this length to be bb. The relevant geometry can be obtained by a piece of hyperbolic space in the coordinates

d​s2=d​σ2+cosh2⁡(σ)​d​τ2,τ∼τ+b.ds^{2}=d\sigma^{2}+\cosh^{2}(\sigma)d\tau^{2},\hskip 20.0pt\tau\sim\tau+b. (126)

The periodic identification of τ\tau breaks the S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) symmetry of the hyperbolic plane down to U⁡(1)U(1) translations in τ\tau. The wiggly boundary is described by a function τ⁡(u)\tau(u), and in this case the boundary action becomes −γ∫duSch(e−τ,u)-\gamma\int du\,\text{Sch}(e^{-\tau},u).2727 27 One way to derive this is to find the relation between the τ\tau and θ\theta coordinates at the boundary of the regular hyperbolic disk. This is cos⁡θ=tanh⁡(τ)\cos\theta=\tanh(\tau), which implies tan⁡θ2=e−τ\tan\frac{\theta}{2}=e^{-\tau}. The standard formula for the Lagrangian Sch​(tan⁡θ2,u)\text{Sch}(\tan\frac{\theta}{2},u) is then equal to Sch​(e−τ,u)\text{Sch}(e^{-\tau},u). After writing this out explicitly and integrating by parts, we find

ZSchtrumpet(β,b)=∫d​μ​[τ]U⁡(1)exp[−γ2∫0βdu(τ′′2τ′2+τ′2)].Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta,b)=\int\frac{d\mu[\tau]}{U(1)}\exp\left[-\frac{\gamma}{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}du\left(\frac{\tau^{\prime\prime 2}}{\tau^{\prime 2}}+\tau^{\prime 2}\right)\right]. (127)

This is also a one-loop exact integral [22], so we can get the exact answer by studying the Gaussian integral over small fluctuations about the saddle point:

τ⁡(u)=bβ​(u+ε⁡(u)).\tau(u)=\frac{b}{\beta}(u+\varepsilon(u)). (128)

One can again decompose ε\varepsilon into modes and work out the symplectic form, this time inserting into (117) the classical value Sch​(e−u​bβ,u)=−b22​β2\text{Sch}(e^{-\frac{ub}{\beta}},u)=-\frac{b^{2}}{2\beta^{2}}. The path integral becomes

ZSchtrumpet​(β,b)\displaystyle Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta,b) =e−γ​b22​β​∏n≥12​α​(2​π)3β2​(n3+b2(2​π)2​n)​∫d​εn(R)​d​εn(I)​e−(2​π)4​γ​(εn(R))2+(εn(I))2β3​(n4+b2(2​π)2​n2)\displaystyle=e^{-\frac{\gamma b^{2}}{2\beta}}\prod_{n\geq 1}2\alpha\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{\beta^{2}}\left(n^{3}+\tfrac{b^{2}}{(2\pi)^{2}}n\right)\int d\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)}d\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)}e^{-(2\pi)^{4}\gamma\frac{(\varepsilon_{n}^{(R)})^{2}+(\varepsilon_{n}^{(I)})^{2}}{\beta^{3}}\left(n^{4}+\tfrac{b^{2}}{(2\pi)^{2}}n^{2}\right)}
=e−γ​b22​β​∏n≥1α​βγ​n=1α1/2​γ1/2(2​π)1/2​β1/2​e−γ2​b2β.\displaystyle=e^{-\frac{\gamma b^{2}}{2\beta}}\prod_{n\geq 1}\frac{\alpha\beta}{\gamma n}=\frac{1}{\alpha^{1/2}}\frac{\gamma^{1/2}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta^{1/2}}e^{-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{b^{2}}{\beta}}. (129)

3.4 Putting it together: the contribution of genus gg in JT gravity

We are now in a position to put the pieces together – the Weil-Petersson volume of the bulk moduli space and the path integral over the wiggly boundary – and compute the genus gg partition function with nn boundaries, Zg,n​(β1,…,βn)Z_{g,n}(\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n}), introduced in (63). The formula is simply

Z0,1​(β)\displaystyle Z_{0,1}(\beta) =ZSchdisk​(β)\displaystyle=Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{disk}}(\beta)
Z0,2​(β1,β2)\displaystyle Z_{0,2}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) =α​∫0∞b​𝑑b​ZSchtrumpet​(β1,b)​ZSchtrumpet​(β2,b)\displaystyle=\alpha\int_{0}^{\infty}bdbZ_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta_{1},b)Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta_{2},b) (130)
Zg,n​(β1,…,βn)\displaystyle Z_{g,n}(\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n}) =αn​∫0∞b1​𝑑b​…​∫0∞bn​d​bn​Vg,nα​(b1,…,bn)​ZSchtrumpet​(β1,b1)​…​ZSchtrumpet​(βn,bn)\displaystyle=\alpha^{n}\int_{0}^{\infty}b_{1}db...\int_{0}^{\infty}b_{n}db_{n}V^{\alpha}_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n})Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta_{1},b_{1})...Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta_{n},b_{n})

where we have written the first two (which are special cases) separately.

Let’s explain this formula for the case Zg,1​(β)Z_{g,1}(\beta). In this case, the geometries that we integrate over have a trumpet connected to the rest of the space across a minimal geodesic of some length bb that should be integrated over:

(131)

For fixed bb, the path integral factorizes into an integral over the moduli of the internal part of the surface, and an integral over the wiggly boundary of the trumpet. Together, these factors give

Vg,nα​(b)​ZSchtrumpet​(β,b),V^{\alpha}_{g,n}(b)Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta,b), (132)

where we have written Vg,nαV_{g,n}^{\alpha} with α\alpha explicit to make clear the dependence on the normalization of the Weil-Petersson form (67). All that remains is to integrate over bb. In fact, there is both the length bb and a twist parameter τ\tau, and the measure is again the one that follows from the Weil-Petersson form (67). For this case, since twisting by bb leaves the surface invariant, the twist is bounded between zero and bb, so the total measure for the length parameter is

∫τΩ=α​𝑑b​∫0b𝑑τ=α​b​𝑑b\int_{\tau}\Omega=\alpha db\int_{0}^{b}d\tau=\alpha bdb (133)

and the final answer is

Zg,1​(β)=α​∫0∞b​𝑑b​Vg,nα​(b)​ZSchtrumpet​(β,b).Z_{g,1}(\beta)=\alpha\int_{0}^{\infty}bdb\,V^{\alpha}_{g,n}(b)Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}}(\beta,b). (134)

The logic for nn boundaries is similar.

Note that the α\alpha dependence of the entire expression is proportional to

αn⋅α3​g+n−3⋅α−n/2=α32​(2​g+n−2)=α−32​χ.\alpha^{n}\cdot\alpha^{3g+n-3}\cdot\alpha^{-n/2}=\alpha^{\frac{3}{2}(2g+n-2)}=\alpha^{-\frac{3}{2}\chi}. (135)

Here the first factor comes from the nn explicit factors of α\alpha in (130), and the second factor comes from the fact that Vg,nV_{g,n} involves an integral over 3​g+n−33g+n-3 pairs of internal variables, each carrying a factor of α\alpha form the form (67). The final factor comes from the α\alpha dependence of the nn factors of (129). Since the total α\alpha dependence is of the form α−32​χ\alpha^{-\frac{3}{2}\chi}, we can set α\alpha to one by a shift of S0S_{0} by 32​log⁡(α)\frac{3}{2}\log(\alpha).2828 28 Note that although the above calculation does not apply to the special cases (g,n)=(0,1)(g,n)=(0,1) or (0,2)(0,2), it is separately also true for those cases that the α\alpha dependence is α−32​χ\alpha^{-\frac{3}{2}\chi}.

3.4.1 Example: Z0,2Z_{0,2}

Although it is a somewhat special case from the perspective of the above formulas, it is interesting to work out the formula for Z0,2Z_{0,2} explicitly. This corresponds to the case where the two asymptotic boundaries are connected by a “double trumpet”

(136)

Explicitly, in this case one has

Z0,2​(β1,β2)\displaystyle Z_{0,2}(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) =∫0∞b​𝑑b​(γ1/2(2​π)1/2​β11/2​e−γ2​b2β1)​(γ1/2(2​π)1/2​β21/2​e−γ2​b2β2)\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}bdb\left(\frac{\gamma^{1/2}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta_{1}^{1/2}}e^{-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{b^{2}}{\beta_{1}}}\right)\left(\frac{\gamma^{1/2}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta_{2}^{1/2}}e^{-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{b^{2}}{\beta_{2}}}\right) (137)

If we continue β1→β1+i​t\beta_{1}\rightarrow\beta_{1}+it and β2→β2−i​t\beta_{2}\rightarrow\beta_{2}-it, and take t≫βt\gg\beta, we get the linearly growing “ramp” contribution to the spectral form factor

Z0,2​(β+i​t,β−i​t)→12​π​tβ1+β2.Z_{0,2}(\beta+it,\beta-it)\rightarrow\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{t}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}. (139)

The coefficient here agrees with the prediction of random matrix theory, but more is actually true. The whole function (138) agrees with random matrix theory. To see this, we compute the contribution to the correlator of resolvents (assuming E1,E2<0E_{1},E_{2}<0)
