=14​(−E1)1/2​(−E2)1/2​[(−E1)1/2+(−E2)1/2]2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4(-E_{1})^{1/2}(-E_{2})^{1/2}\left[(-E_{1})^{1/2}+(-E_{2})^{1/2}\right]^{2}}, (141)

which agrees with the universal answer (47) for double-scaled matrix integrals.

This expression can be continued to positive energy either through the upper half plane to E+i​ϵE+i\epsilon or through the lower half plane to E−i​ϵE-i\epsilon. The difference between these continuations gives the density of states (14), and one finds (using an obvious notation)

⟨ρ⁡(E1)​ρ​(E2)⟩0=R(++)+R(−−)−R(+−)−R(−+)(−2​π​i)2=−1(2​π)2​E1+E2E11/2​E21/2​(E1−E2)2\langle\rho(E_{1})\rho(E_{2})\rangle_{0}=\frac{R(++)+R(--)-R(+-)-R(-+)}{(-2\pi i)^{2}}=\frac{-1}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{E_{1}+E_{2}}{E_{1}^{1/2}E_{2}^{1/2}(E_{1}-E_{2})^{2}} (142)

Note that this expression is singular as E1E_{1} approaches E2E_{2}. This is not true for higher genus contributions to the same correlator. This is easy to check for the genus one contribution, by doing the integral with the explicit function V1,2V_{1,2} in (59).

3.4.2 Aside: these are not classical solutions

Except for the disk, none of the path integral configurations that we considered above are full solutions to the equations of motion of JT theory. The equation of motion of ϕ\phi is satisfied, since R+2=0R+2=0. But the equation of motion for the metric implies that ϵμ​ν​∂νϕ\epsilon^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\nu}\phi is a Killing vector [99], and except for the disk and double trumpet, the manifolds we consider here do not have isometries. For the double trumpet, a separate argument rules out a solution [11].

The basic point is that because of the e−b2/4βe^{-b^{2}/4\beta} factor in the trumpet partition function, there is pressure pushing bb to be small [100], which prevents us from finding a fully on-shell configuration. Of course, this is not a problem in the present context, since the JT theory is simple enough that we can simply do the integral over bb.

3.5 Correspondence with the matrix integral recursion relation

The agreement of R0,2R_{0,2} above with random matrix theory is an example of a more general fact, which is that all of the Zg,nZ_{g,n}, taken together, give a solution to Eynard’s recursion relation applied to double scaled matrix integrals (56).

As a first step, we should understand what the spectral curve function y⁡(z)y(z) is for this case. This can be obtained from the genus zero expression for the density of states as in (38). The genus zero density of states for the JT theory is obtained by writing Z0,1Z_{0,1} as an integral with some density of states

Z0,1​(β)=∫0∞d​E​ρ0​(E)​e−β​E.Z_{0,1}(\beta)=\int_{0}^{\infty}dE\rho_{0}(E)e^{-\beta E}. (143)

In our case, Z0,1=ZSchdiskZ_{0,1}=Z_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{disk}} was given in (125). After adjusting S0S_{0} to make α=1\alpha=1, one can check that this answer is reproduced by the function

ρ0​(E)=γ2​π2​sinh⁡(2​π​2​γ​E),\rho_{0}(E)=\frac{\gamma}{2\pi^{2}}\sinh(2\pi\sqrt{2\gamma E}), (144)

which implies

y⁡(z)=γ2​π​sin⁡(2​π​2​γ​z).y(z)=\frac{\gamma}{2\pi}\sin(2\pi\sqrt{2\gamma}\,z). (145)

We have already seen that R0,2R_{0,2} has the right form for a double-scaled matrix integral, so it remains to check the generic Rg,nR_{g,n} case. More precisely, we will check that Wg,nW_{g,n} defined in (54) satisfy (56). The quantities Wg,nW_{g,n} are in general related to Zg,nZ_{g,n} by an integral transform

Wg,n​(E1,…,En)=2n​z1​…​zn​∫0∞d​β1​…​d​βn​e−(β1​z12+…+βn​zn2)​Zg,n​(β1,…,βn).W_{g,n}(E_{1},...,E_{n})=2^{n}z_{1}...z_{n}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\beta_{1}...d\beta_{n}e^{-(\beta_{1}z_{1}^{2}+...+\beta_{n}z_{n}^{2})}Z_{g,n}(\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n}). (146)

For the JT gravity case (130), after inserting the explicit expression for ZSchtrumpetZ_{\text{Sch}}^{\text{trumpet}} in (129), one can do the integral over β\beta inside the integral over bb. Then, using the integral

2​z​∫0∞d​β​e−β​z2​γ1/2(2​π)1/2​β1/2​e−γ2​b2β=(2​γ)1/2​e−2​γ​b​z,2z\int_{0}^{\infty}d\beta e^{-\beta z^{2}}\frac{\gamma^{1/2}}{(2\pi)^{1/2}\beta^{1/2}}e^{-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{b^{2}}{\beta}}=(2\gamma)^{1/2}e^{-\sqrt{2\gamma}\,bz}, (147)

one finds that

Wg,n​(z1,…,zn)=(2​γ)n/2​∫0∞b1​d​b1​e−2​γ​b1​z1​…​∫0∞bn​d​bn​e−2​γ​bn​zn​Vg,n​(b1,…,bn).W_{g,n}(z_{1},...,z_{n})=(2\gamma)^{n/2}\int_{0}^{\infty}b_{1}db_{1}e^{-\sqrt{2\gamma}\,b_{1}z_{1}}...\int_{0}^{\infty}b_{n}db_{n}e^{-\sqrt{2\gamma}\,b_{n}z_{n}}V_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n}). (148)

If we take γ=12\gamma=\frac{1}{2}, then we land on the case discussed near eq. (60). Eynard and Orantin showed that Mirzakhani’s recursion relation implies that these functions indeed satisfy the recursion relation (56) for the spectral curve y=sin⁡(2​π​z)4​πy=\frac{\sin(2\pi z)}{4\pi}, which is just (145) for γ=12\gamma=\frac{1}{2}.

The case for general γ\gamma follows trivially from this. One simply shows that the recursion relation (56) behaves correctly under rescalings of energy. Concretely, if Wg,n​(z1,…,zn)W_{g,n}(z_{1},...,z_{n}) satisfy (56) with a given y⁡(z)y(z) then so do (2​γ)n/2​Wg,n​(2​γ​z1,…,2​γ​zn)(2\gamma)^{n/2}W_{g,n}(\sqrt{2\gamma}z_{1},...,\sqrt{2\gamma}z_{n}) with y⁡(z)→(2​γ)​y​(2​γ​z)y(z)\rightarrow(2\gamma)y(\sqrt{2\gamma}z).

4 Connection to minimal string theory

In the last section, we saw that the sum over topologies in JT gravity reproduces the genus expansion of a particular double-scaled matrix integral. This is reminiscent of previous connections between two-dimensional gravity and matrix integrals [34, 35, 36, 37],2929 29 For reviews see [38, 39]. which were motivated by thinking of the double-line graphs of matrix perturbation theory [74, 73] as a discretization of an integral over surfaces. This becomes precise in the double-scaled limit [17, 18, 19], and we will find evidence that the correspondence identified above between JT gravity and matrix integrals is related to a further limit of these models.

Let’s first briefly review the older story. In one presentation, one regards the sum over surfaces as a type of noncritical string theory called the “minimal string,” where the worldsheet theory is a minimal model CFT on a fluctuating geometry described by Liouville theory. Minimal model CFTs are labeled by a pair of relatively prime integers (p,p′)(p,p^{\prime}), and for general values of (p,p′)(p,p^{\prime}), the minimal string is dual to a multi-matrix integral. But for the special case of (2,p)(2,p), with pp an odd positive integer, one finds a single Hermitian matrix integral, and we will focus on this case. The (2,p)(2,p) minimal models are non-unitary, and have central charge c=−3​p+13−12pc=-3p+13-\frac{12}{p}. In order to get a c=0c=0 worldsheet theory, the minimal model is combined with the usual c=−26c=-26 ghosts, and a Liouville theory [101]3030 30 For reviews see [102, 38]. of central charge 3​p+13+12p3p+13+\frac{12}{p}. This can be accomplished by taking the Liouville theory 3131 31 Note that in the following action the only matter field operator appearing is the identity operator, coupling to the cosmological constant. To achieve this in the matrix realization of the nonunitary minimal string the negative dimension matter fields must be fine-tuned to zero. This is referred to as the “conformal background” [41].

I=14​π​∫d2​x​g^​((∇^​φ)2+(b−1+b)​φ​R^+4​π​μ​e2​b​φ),b=2p.I=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{\widehat{g}}\left((\widehat{\nabla}\varphi)^{2}+(b^{-1}+b)\varphi\widehat{R}+4\pi\mu e^{2b\varphi}\right),\hskip 20.0ptb=\sqrt{\frac{2}{p}}. (149)

The dictionary between this theory and the matrix integral is similar to what we discussed for JT gravity. In particular, matrix ensemble averages of ⟨Tr​(e−ℓ1​H)​…​Tr​(e−ℓn​H)⟩\langle\text{Tr}(e^{-\ell_{1}H})...\text{Tr}(e^{-\ell_{n}H})\rangle are given by the worldsheet path integral over surfaces with nn boundaries. The boundary conditions are fixed finite lengths ℓ1,…,ℓn\ell_{1},...,\ell_{n} for the Liouville sector, and the identity Cardy state for the minimal model.

Assuming that the minimal string is dual to some matrix model, one can determine the correct one by computing the disk partition function, interpreting it as the leading contribution to ⟨Tr​(e−ℓ​H)⟩\langle\text{Tr}(e^{-\ell H})\rangle, and reading off ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E).3232 32 More precisely, to compute ⟨Tr​(e−ℓ​H)⟩\langle\text{Tr}(e^{-\ell H})\rangle, one should consider a disk with a marked boundary, meaning that a base point on the boundary has been chosen, and we do not consider translations of the boundary time coordinate as a gauge symmetry. The difference is a factor of ℓ\ell: if we do not pick a base point on the boundary, we would be computing 1ℓ​⟨Tr​(e−ℓ​H)⟩\frac{1}{\ell}\langle\text{Tr}(e^{-\ell H})\rangle. This computation was first done by [41], using a minisuperspace approximation to Liouville, which was shown to be exact, as in [103]. It was later redone in [53], using formulas from the bootstrap solution of the Liouville boundary problem [47]. In this approach, one uses, as an intermediate step, the FZZT boundary condition, which corresponds to an unmarked boundary in Liouville with fixed boundary cosmological constant μB\mu_{B}. For this problem, expressions for one-point functions are known [47]. By an integral transform, one can change from FZZT boundary conditions to a marked boundary with fixed length ℓ\ell. The resulting one-point function of the cosmological constant operator with these boundary conditions is given in Eq. (2.44) of [47] as

Wb​(ℓ)=(const.)​μ1−b22​b2​K1−b2b2​(κ​ℓ),κ2=μsin⁡(π​b2).W_{b}(\ell)=(\text{const.})\mu^{\frac{1-b^{2}}{2b^{2}}}K_{\frac{1-b^{2}}{b^{2}}}(\kappa\ell),\hskip 20.0pt\kappa^{2}=\frac{\mu}{\sin(\pi b^{2})}. (150)

This one-point function can be interpreted as the derivative with respect to the cosmological constant μ\mu of the disk partition function, which is then given by integrating:

W⁡(ℓ)=∫d​μ​Wb​(ℓ)=(const.)​1ℓ​μ12​b2​K1b2​(κ​ℓ).W(\ell)=\int d\mu\,W_{b}(\ell)=(\text{const.})\frac{1}{\ell}\mu^{\frac{1}{2b^{2}}}K_{\frac{1}{b^{2}}}(\kappa\ell). (151)

To determine the relevant matrix ensemble, we set b=2/pb=\sqrt{2/p} and interpret (151) as ⟨Tr​(e−ℓ​H)⟩\langle\text{Tr}(e^{-\ell H})\rangle, and then compute the inverse Laplace transform to obtain the leading density of eigenvalues. Before doing this, it is convenient to adjust a boundary counterterm to multiply (151) by a factor of eκ​ℓe^{\kappa\ell}, which will have the effect of setting the ground state energy to zero. Then, using

ess​K1b2​(s)=b2​∫0∞d​t​e−s​t​sinh⁡(1b2​arccosh​(1+t))\frac{e^{s}}{s}K_{\frac{1}{b^{2}}}(s)=b^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\,e^{-st}\sinh\left(\frac{1}{b^{2}}\text{arccosh}(1+t)\right) (152)

one finds that

eκ​ℓ​W​(ℓ)=∫0∞d​E​ρ0​(E)​e−ℓ​Ee^{\kappa\ell}W(\ell)=\int_{0}^{\infty}dE\rho_{0}(E)e^{-\ell E} (153)

with

ρ0​(E)\displaystyle\rho_{0}(E) =(const.)​sinh⁡[p2​arccosh​(1+Eκ)]\displaystyle=(\text{const.})\sinh\left[\frac{p}{2}\text{arccosh}\left(1+\frac{E}{\kappa}\right)\right] (154)
=E​(a0+a1​E+a2​E2+…+ap−12​Ep−12).\displaystyle=\sqrt{E}\left(a_{0}+a_{1}E+a_{2}E^{2}+...+a_{\frac{p-1}{2}}E^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\right). (155)

This gives the leading density of eigenvalues in the matrix model dual to the (2,p)(2,p) minimal string. In the second line we wrote a schematic form for the function in the case of interest where pp is an odd integer. The coefficients aka_{k} are positive numbers.

We would now like to understand the relationship of this to JT gravity.3333 33 We are grateful to Nathan Seiberg for emphasizing this question. For large pp, the central charge of the Liouville theory is large, and the fluctuations about the classical solution will be small. The classical solution of Liouville theory is hyperbolic space, and by working in units with 4​π​μ=1b24\pi\mu=\frac{1}{b^{2}}, we can arrange that the radius of curvature of the classical solution is one, so R=−2R=-2, as in our conventions for JT gravity. It seems plausible that this theory could be related to JT gravity. However, since both are supposed to be dual to matrix integrals, we can compare them by comparing the ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) function that specifies the matrix integral. And, indeed, it is easy to check that if we take p→∞p\rightarrow\infty with E=2​πp​EJTE=\frac{2\pi}{p}E_{\text{JT}} held fixed, we land on the JT gravity spectral curve:

sinh⁡[p2​arccosh​(1+Eκ)]→sinh⁡(2​π​EJT).\sinh\left[\frac{p}{2}\text{arccosh}\left(1+\frac{E}{\kappa}\right)\right]\rightarrow\sinh\left(2\pi\sqrt{E_{\text{JT}}}\right). (156)

The agreement of these spectral curves suggests that JT gravity is in some sense the p→∞p\rightarrow\infty limit of the (2,p)(2,p) minimal string.3434 34 A more complete description of this correspondence will be forthcoming in [42]. We will use this correspondence below to import intuition from the minimal string on the role of FZZT and ZZ branes in Liouville theory.

5 Nonperturbative effects

The effects we have discussed so far in this paper are perturbative from the perspective of a matrix integral. More precisely, they are perturbative in the expansion parameter 1/L1/L, or e−S0e^{-S_{0}} in the double-scaled case. From the perspective of JT gravity, or the collective field description of the SYK model, these are nonperturbative effects, because the quantity e−S0e^{-S_{0}} is itself nonperturbatively small relative to the GNG_{N} or 1N\frac{1}{N} expansion:

gravity: e−S0=e−#GN,SYK: e−S0=e−#​N.\text{gravity: }\,e^{-S_{0}}=e^{-\frac{\#}{G_{N}}},\hskip 60.0pt\text{SYK: }\,e^{-S_{0}}=e^{-\#\,N}. (157)

In matrix integrals these perturbative effects come from smooth fluctuations around the large LL density of states ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E). The perturbative series describing these fluctuations are typically divergent, with the coefficient at genus gg behaving like (2​g)!(2g)!, indicating the existence of nonperturbative effects of order exp⁡(−c​L)\exp(-cL), or exp⁡(−c​eS0)\exp(-ce^{S_{0}}) in the double scaled case (here cc can be complex).

Indeed, below we will derive the following formula, which summarizes the leading perturbative (i.e. genus zero) and leading nonperturbative effects in the density of eigenvalues:

⟨ρ⁡(E)⟩≈{eS0​ρ0​(E)−14​π​E​cos⁡(2​π​eS0​∫0Ed​E′​ρ0​(E′))E>01−8​π​Eexp(−2eS0∫0−Edxy(x))E<0.\langle\rho(E)\rangle\approx\begin{cases}e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}(E)-\frac{1}{4\pi E}\cos\Big(2\pi e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{E}dE^{\prime}\rho_{0}(E^{\prime})\Big)&E>0\cr\frac{1}{-8\pi E}\exp\Big(\hskip-2.0pt-\hskip-2.0pt2e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{-E}dx\,y\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\Big)&E<0.\end{cases} (158)

Let’s explain some of the qualitative features of this formula. One feature that is easy to understand concerns the density of eigenvalues in the “classically forbidden” region E<0E<0. This is zero to all orders in perturbation theory, and the main nonzero contribution comes from the exponentially small probability of a single eigenvalue being located at E<0E<0. The weighting for such a configuration is controlled by the “effective potential” Veff​(E)V_{\text{eff}}(E) that the eigenvalue feels: the sum of the actual potential V⁡(E)V(E) and the Vandermonde repulsion from the remaining eigenvalues. In the forbidden region we have from (22)

Veff′​(E)\displaystyle V^{\prime}_{\text{eff}}(E) =L​V′​(E)−2​eS0​R0,1​(E)=−2​eS0​y​(−E)\displaystyle=LV^{\prime}(E)-2e^{S_{0}}R_{0,1}(E)=-2e^{S_{0}}y(\sqrt{-E}) (159)
Veff​(E)\displaystyle V_{\text{eff}}(E) =2​eS0​∫0−Ed​x​y​(x)\displaystyle=2e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{-E}dx\,y\left(\sqrt{x}\right) (160)

and so in the forbidden region (158) can be rewritten as

⟨ρ⁡(E)⟩≈1−8​π​E​exp⁡(−Veff​(E)).\langle\rho(E)\rangle\approx\frac{1}{-8\pi E}\exp\left(-V_{\text{eff}}(E)\right)~. (161)

This simple picture only makes sense if Veff​(E)>0V_{\text{eff}}(E)>0 in the forbidden region, indicating stability of the tree level distribution ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E). We will assume this for now to simplify our presentation. For JT gravity it actually isn’t true, as we will discuss in section 5.5.

The oscillating behavior of (158) in the allowed region is in some respects more dramatic. The nonperturbative cosine term in (158) is rapidly oscillating, but is not particularly small, of order one in powers of eS0e^{S_{0}}. This is smaller than the tree level term eS0​ρ0e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}, but it is larger than the first perturbative (genus one) correction, which we haven’t displayed in (158), but which would be proportional to e−S0e^{-S_{0}}. So the nonperturbative correction isn’t small, but it is rapidly oscillating as a function of EE, on the scale of the separation between individual eigenvalues. This is clearly visible in Figure 1.

For integrated observables that are sufficiently smooth in energy, such a term will give small effects. But in special observables they can be important. For example, oscillating nonperturbative terms in the two-eigenvalue correlation function are needed in order to explain the “plateau” in the spectral form factor. More generally, the oscillating nonperturbative term can be understood as a consequence of the underlying discreteness of the energy levels, as the oscillations are on the scale of the separation between adjacent levels.

The kinds of nonperturbative effects discussed here have been given a “bulk” interpretation as D-branes in minimal string theories described by double scaled matrix integrals. One eigenvalue instantons correspond to “ZZ branes,” an analog of D-instantons. The allowed region oscillations are probed by “FZZT branes,” an analog of probe D0 flavor branes.

In this section, we will give a heuristic derivation of (158) and then interpret it in the context of JT gravity by analogy to the minimal string identification. This is particularly interesting since in that context, the effects are doubly-nonperturbative from the perspective of ordinary gravitational perturbation theory in GNG_{N}.

5.1 The determinant

In order to discuss nonperturbative effects in matrix integrals, it is convenient to start out by working with determinants instead of resolvents.3535 35 We are grateful to Juan Maldacena for this suggestion. In these quantities, the nonperturbative effects contribute at leading order, and are therefore easier to examine. In particular, we define the quantity

ψ⁡(E)≡det(E−H)​e−L2​V​(E).\psi(E)\equiv\det(E-H)e^{-\frac{L}{2}V(E)}. (162)

As we will discuss later, this operator can be interpreted as the insertion of a “brane” [57, 55].

A useful general fact is that the expectation value of ψ⁡(E)\psi(E) in the matrix integral is equal to PL​(E)​e−L2​V​(E)P_{L}(E)e^{-\frac{L}{2}V(E)}, where Pn​(E)P_{n}(E) is the degree nn monic polynomial from the family of polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to the measure e−L​V​(E)e^{-LV(E)}. In the double-scaled limit, the polynomial index nn is replaced by a continuous parameter n/Ln/L, and the orthogonal functions satisfy a pair of linear differential equations. For large eS0e^{S_{0}}, these equations can be solved using WKB methods, and a “one loop” solution at large eS0e^{S_{0}} is [104, 55]

⟨ψ(E)⟩∼Az1/2exp[eS0∫0zdE(z′)y(z′)]+Bz1/2exp[−eS0∫0zdE(z′)y(z′)].\langle\psi(E)\rangle\sim\frac{A}{z^{1/2}}\exp\left[e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{z}dE(z^{\prime})y(z^{\prime})\right]+\frac{B}{z^{1/2}}\exp\left[-e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{z}dE(z^{\prime})y(z^{\prime})\right]. (163)

where E=−z2E=-z^{2}. This is written in terms of the spectral curve coordinate yy (38). The coefficients A,BA,B are arbitrary so far, and as we will see, they can depend on the angle of EE in the complex plane.

5.1.1 Airy

A useful example to have in mind is the case where ρ0=1π​E\rho_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{E} and the corresponding spectral curve is y2=−Ey^{2}=-E. In this case, it is possible to write the exact answer for ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle by representing it as the effect of integrating out an additional “matter field” in the fundamental representation. This motivates the interpretation of ψ⁡(E)\psi(E) as a probe ‘‘flavor’’ brane.3636 36 See for example [55]. This kind of construction is used extensively in the quantum chaos literature. For reviews see [105, 106, 67, 68].

We begin with the Gaussian matrix potential V⁡(x)=2a2​x2V(x)=\frac{2}{a^{2}}x^{2}, which has the leading order density of states given by the Wigner semicircle:

ρ0total​(E)=eS0π​a2−E22​a,−a<E<a.\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E)=\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{a^{2}-E^{2}}{2a}},\hskip 20.0pt-a<E<a. (164)

For this to be normalized, L=eS0​(a/2)3/2L=e^{S_{0}}(a/2)^{3/2}. For this theory, one can write the determinant det(E−H)\det(E-H) as an integral over Grassmann vectors χi\chi_{i} and χ¯i\overline{\chi}_{i} and perform the Gaussian integral over HH to arrive at an integral over the Grassmann variables that only depends on the combination ∑iχ¯i​χi\sum_{i}\overline{\chi}_{i}\chi_{i},

⟨det(E−H)⟩=∫d​χi​d​χ¯i​eE​χ¯i​χi−a28​L​(χ¯i​χi)2.\langle\det(E-H)\rangle=\int d\chi_{i}d\overline{\chi}_{i}e^{E\overline{\chi}_{i}\chi_{i}-\frac{a^{2}}{8L}(\overline{\chi}_{i}\chi_{i})^{2}}. (165)

We can introduce an auxiliary variable ss so that χi\chi_{i} and χ¯i\overline{\chi}_{i} can be simply integrated out,

⟨det(E−H)⟩\displaystyle\langle\det(E-H)\rangle =2​Lπ​a2​∫d​s​d​χi​d​χ¯i​e(E+i​s)​χ¯i​χi−2​La2​s2\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{\pi a^{2}}}\int ds\,d\chi_{i}d\overline{\chi}_{i}e^{(E+is)\overline{\chi}_{i}\chi_{i}-\frac{2L}{a^{2}}s^{2}} (166)
=2​Lπ​a2​∫d​s​(E+i​s)L​e−2​La2​s2.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{\pi a^{2}}}\int ds(E+is)^{L}e^{-\frac{2L}{a^{2}}s^{2}}. (167)

The final line is an integral representation for the Hermite polynomial (a28​L)L/2​HL​(2​L​E/a).(\frac{a^{2}}{8L})^{L/2}H_{L}(\sqrt{2L}E/a). The Hermite polynomials are the orthogonal polynomials for the Gaussian measure, so this is an example of the general result mentioned above. We see that in this case ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle is a harmonic oscillator wavefunction, and so satisfies a Schrodinger equation (with ℏ=1L\hbar=\frac{1}{L}). For this simple potential the WKB estimates described in (163) follow from a standard WKB analysis of of this Schrodinger equation.3737 37 We will not use the Schrodinger equation perspective directly, but it is a convenient way to obtain the leading exponential behavior of (163). See e.g.  section 4.3 of [32] for recent discussion. To obtain the theory ρ0​(E)=1π​E\rho_{0}(E)=\frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{E}, we study this Gaussian theory near the lower edge of the eigenvalue distribution. This corresponds to studying the wavefunction near its left classical turning point. To do this, we replace Eold=−a+EnewE_{\text{old}}=-a+E_{\text{new}} so that the support of ρ0\rho_{0} is 0<Enew<2​a0<E_{\text{new}}<2a. Then we send a→∞a\rightarrow\infty holding Enew=EE_{\text{new}}=E fixed. One can take this limit in the integral representation (166).

After multiplying by e−L2​V​(E)e^{-\frac{L}{2}V(E)} as in (162), one finds3838 38 We change variables to s→−i​a2+a2e−S0/3ss\rightarrow-\frac{ia}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{a}{2}}e^{-S_{0}/3}s before taking a→∞a\rightarrow\infty. Also, as the overall normalization in ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle can be rescaled by a constant shift of the potential, we will choose things so that the constant of proportionality in (168) is one.

⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩∝12​π​∫−∞∞d​s​ei3​s3+i​ξ​s=Ai​(ξ),ξ=−e2​S03​E.\langle\psi(E)\rangle\propto\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}ds\;e^{\frac{i}{3}s^{3}+i\xi s}=\text{Ai}(\xi),\hskip 20.0pt\xi=-e^{\frac{2S_{0}}{3}}E. (168)

The leading asymptotics of the Airy function on the real axis can be obtained from a standard saddle point analysis of this integral. There are two saddle points, and in the allowed region ξ<0\xi<0, the defining contour is deformable to the union of the two associated steepest-descent contours. In the forbidden region, ξ>0\xi>0, the defining contour is deformable to the steepest descent contour associated to only one of the saddles. This leads to the leading large ξ\xi asymptotics

Ai​(ξ)∼{1π​(−ξ)1/4​cos⁡(−π4+23​(−ξ)3/2)ξ<012​π​ξ1/4​exp⁡(−23​ξ3/2)ξ>0.\text{Ai}(\xi)\sim\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}(-\xi)^{1/4}}\cos\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\tfrac{2}{3}(-\xi)^{3/2}\right)&\xi<0\\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}\xi^{1/4}}\exp\left(-\tfrac{2}{3}\xi^{3/2}\right)&\xi>0.\end{cases} (169)

This is consistent with the general formula (163) applied to the case y2=−Ey^{2}=-E, and it determines the A,BA,B coefficients in both the forbidden and allowed regions.

In this paper we are concerned with matrix integrals whose spectral curve approaches the Airy curve y2=−Ey^{2}=-E at small EE, up to a rescaling. We will determine the A,BA,B coefficients in general by demanding that the results join onto the Airy results for small EE. This prescription is consistent with rigorous results for unscaled matrix models [107].

5.1.2 Disks and Cylinders

We now describe another technique for obtaining semiclassical formulas like (163).3939 39 See for example [57, 54, 108, 32]. This technique is not rigorous, but it does have two advantages. First, it makes direct contact with the quantities used in topological recursion. Second, and more importantly, it is directly connected to the D-brane interpretation of these nonperturbative effects.

The essence of the technique is very simple. It is based on the identity

det(E−H)=exp⁡(Tr​log⁡(E−H)).\det(E-H)=\exp\Big({\rm Tr}\log(E-H)\Big). (170)

We would like to take the expectation value of the RHS in the matrix ensemble, using the general formula

⟨eX⟩=exp⁡(⟨X⟩+12​⟨X2⟩conn.+…),\langle e^{X}\rangle=\exp\left(\langle X\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\langle X^{2}\rangle_{\text{conn.}}+...\right), (171)

where in our case X=Tr​log⁡(E−H)X={\rm Tr}\log(E-H). In a matrix integral, the higher connected correlators are suppressed by powers of eS0e^{S_{0}}. So, in a leading approximation, we can keep only the first term in (171), and we evaluate it to leading order. This can be done by integrating the genus-zero resolvent:

⟨Tr​log⁡(E−H)⟩g=0=eS0​∫Ed​E′​R0,1​(E′).\langle{\rm Tr}\log(E-H)\rangle_{g=0}=e^{S_{0}}\int^{E}dE^{\prime}R_{0,1}(E^{\prime}). (172)

This combines nicely with the explicit factor of e−L2​V​(E)e^{-\frac{L}{2}V(E)} in (162). Using eS0​y=eS0​R0,1​(E)−L2​V′​(E)e^{S_{0}}y=e^{S_{0}}R_{0,1}(E)-\frac{L}{2}V^{\prime}(E), we have the leading formula

⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩=e−L2​V​(E)​⟨det(E−H)⟩≃exp⁡(eS0​∫Ed​E′​y),\langle\psi(E)\rangle=e^{-\frac{L}{2}V(E)}\langle\det(E-H)\rangle\simeq\exp\left(e^{S_{0}}\int^{E}dE^{\prime}\,y\right), (173)

which matches the exponential factors in (163).

This approach is analogous to Polchinski’s calculation [46] of D-brane amplitudes, of order e−1/gse^{-1/g_{s}}, as an expansion in disconnected worldsheets of disk topology, that is in powers of 1/gs1/g_{s}. We will give a corresponding brane interpretation of the effects in (173). Anticipating this discussion, we will refer to the term in the exponential in (173) as the disk amplitude.

For the discussion below, we will need to be more precise about the choice of branch. Because yy is multivalued in the EE plane, it is convenient to view the disk amplitude as a function of zz, where E=−z2E=-z^{2}:

Disk​(z)≡eS0​∫0zy⁡(z′)​𝑑E​(z′).\text{Disk}(z)\equiv e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{z}y(z^{\prime})dE(z^{\prime}). (174)

For the Airy spectral curve y2=−Ey^{2}=-E, or alternatively y=zy=z, this is

Disk​(z)=eS0​∫0zz⋅(−2​z​𝑑z)=−2​z33​eS0.\text{Disk}(z)=e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{z}z\cdot(-2zdz)=-\frac{2z^{3}}{3}e^{S_{0}}. (175)

For the JT gravity curve, it is

Disk​(z)=eS0​∫0zsin⁡(2​π​z)4​π⋅(−2​z​𝑑z)=−sin⁡(2​π​z)−2​π​z​cos⁡(2​π​z)8​π3​eS0.\text{Disk}(z)=e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\sin(2\pi z)}{4\pi}\cdot(-2zdz)=-\frac{\sin(2\pi z)-2\pi z\cos(2\pi z)}{8\pi^{3}}e^{S_{0}}. (176)

In order to insert these expressions in (173), we have to decide which branch of z⁡(E)z(E) to use. In principle, we have this choice in each factor of ⟨Tr​log⁡(E−H)⟩g=0\langle{\rm Tr}\log(E-H)\rangle_{g=0} that appears when we expand out (170). In order to determine the branch, we need to supply additional input. The known general form (163) can be reproduced if we choose the same branch for all terms in the expansion of the exponential, and possibly also choose the other choice in another complete sum. This gives the two exponentials in (163). Additional information has to be supplied to fix their coefficients. In our case joining onto the Airy limit will determine this.

In order to reproduce the prefactor powers in (163), we need to include the order-one terms in (171). For Hermitian matrix integrals, the only term of order one comes from the connected two-point function. It will be convenient to view this as a function of separate E1,E2E_{1},E_{2} arguments:

⟨Tr​log⁡(E1−H)​Tr​log⁡(E2−H)⟩conn.=∫E1d​E1′​∫E2d​E2′​R0,2​(E1′,E2′)+𝒪⁡(e−2​S0).\langle{\rm Tr}\log(E_{1}-H){\rm Tr}\log(E_{2}-H)\rangle_{\text{conn.}}=\int^{E_{1}}dE_{1}^{\prime}\int^{E_{2}}dE_{2}^{\prime}\;R_{0,2}(E_{1}^{\prime},E_{2}^{\prime})+{\cal O}(e^{-2S_{0}}). (177)

Anticipating the brane discussion, we will refer to the leading term on the RHS as the cylinder, and we will regard it as a function of zz:

Cyl​(z1,z2)\displaystyle\text{Cyl}(z_{1},z_{2}) ≡∫∞z1d​E​(z1′)​∫∞z2d​E​(z2′)​R0,2​(E⁡(z1′),E⁡(z2′))\displaystyle\equiv\int_{\infty}^{z_{1}}dE(z_{1}^{\prime})\int_{\infty}^{z_{2}}dE(z_{2}^{\prime})\;R_{0,2}(E(z_{1}^{\prime}),E(z_{2}^{\prime})) (178)
=∫∞z1∫∞z2d​z1′​d​z2′(z1′+z2′)2=−log⁡(z1+z2)+∞.\displaystyle=\int_{\infty}^{z_{1}}\int_{\infty}^{z_{2}}\frac{dz_{1}^{\prime}dz_{2}^{\prime}}{(z_{1}^{\prime}+z_{2}^{\prime})^{2}}=-\log(z_{1}+z_{2})+\infty. (179)

In the second line, we used (47) and did the integral, assuming z1,z2>0z_{1},z_{2}>0. The infinite additive constant is independent of z1,z2z_{1},z_{2}, and it reflects an ambiguity in the normalization of ψ⁡(E)\psi(E) in the double-scaled limit. For the moment, we simply add a constant to the potential in order to cancel the ∞\infty. In the better-defined ratio of determinants that we will consider below, it will cancel automatically.

In terms of the disk and cylinder quantities, for a given choice of branch, we can write the RHS of (171) to one-loop accuracy as a function of zz

Ψ⁡(z)≡exp⁡[Disk​(z)+12​Cyl​(z,z)]=12​z​exp⁡[Disk​(z)].\Psi(z)\equiv\exp\left[\text{Disk}(z)+\frac{1}{2}\text{Cyl}(z,z)\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2z}}\exp\left[\text{Disk}(z)\right]. (180)

We expect to be able to express ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle in general in terms of a linear combination of the two branches Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z) and Ψ⁡(−z)\Psi(-z). By matching to the Airy case (168) and using the asymptotics of the Airy function (169), we find that specific linear combination has to be

⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩∝{Ψ⁡(z)+Ψ⁡(−z)E>0Ψ⁡(z)E<0.\langle\psi(E)\rangle\propto\begin{cases}\Psi(z)+\Psi(-z)&E>0\cr\Psi(z)&E<0.\end{cases} (181)

In this expression, we have z2=−Ez^{2}=-E as always. Because of the 1/2​z1/\sqrt{2z} in (180), we have to specify a branch for the prefactor. The correct prescription from matching to Airy is to take Ψ⁡(ei​π2​E)+Ψ⁡(e−i​π2​E)\Psi(e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E})+\Psi(e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E}) on the first line, and Ψ⁡(−E)\Psi(\sqrt{-E}) on the second line.

5.2 The inverse determinant

We would like to understand the origin of nonperturbative effects in more familiar quantities like the average density, the pair density correlation function, or in resolvents. The orthogonal polynomial approach to matrix integrals allows one to write all such quantities in terms of orthogonal polynomials [72]. So in principle having determined the orthogonal polynomial from the ⟨det(E−H)⟩\langle\det(E-H)\rangle we have all that we need. But we would like to attempt a more direct, if more formal, calculation.

An important intermediate tool is the insertion of

ψ~​(E)≡eL2​V​(E)det(E−H).\widetilde{\psi}(E)\equiv\frac{e^{\frac{L}{2}V(E)}}{\det(E-H)}. (182)

The operator ψ~​(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E) is interpreted as the insertion of a ‘‘ghost brane,’’ which is a term used to mean an object that totally cancels a brane if it is inserted at the same point.4040 40 See for example [57, 108, 32]. In some of these papers this object is referred to as an antibrane. We are using the term ghost brane in the sense of [109]. The ghost brane is a more complicated object than the brane. Before double scaling ⟨1/det(E−H)⟩\langle 1/\det(E-H)\rangle is the Hilbert transform4141 41 More precisely ⟨1/det(E−H)⟩L+1\langle 1/\det(E-H)\rangle_{L+1} is the Hilbert transform of e−L​V​(E)​⟨det(E−H)⟩Le^{-LV(E)}\langle\det(E-H)\rangle_{L}. of ⟨det(E−H)⟩\langle\det(E-H)\rangle with respect to the measure e−L​V​(E)e^{-LV(E)} [72]. This procedure defines two independent functions, depending on whether the energy argument is above or below the real axis. Of course, both functions can be continued in the complex EE plane, and they define two separate entire functions. We will refer to them as ⟨ψ~±​(E)⟩\langle\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E)\rangle, where the plus subscript means that the formula gives the actual ghost brane answer for EE in the upper half-plane, and the minus subscript means that it agrees in the lower half-plane.

The double scaled version of ⟨ψ~​(E)⟩\langle\widetilde{\psi}(E)\rangle also obeys a differential equation [110] which yields a semiclassical expansion of the same general form as (163). To understand the more subtle determination of coefficients in this case we turn again to the Airy example and then proceed to a formal disk and cylinder calculation.

5.2.1 Airy

We start with the Airy case, with spectral curve y2=−Ey^{2}=-E. One can compute ⟨ψ~⟩\langle\widetilde{\psi}\rangle using the same technique we used for ⟨ψ⟩\langle\psi\rangle. Instead of introducing Grassmann flavor fields we introduce bosonic fields ϕi,ϕ¯i\phi_{i},\bar{\phi}_{i} to implement 1/det(E−H)1/\det(E-H). After mimicking the procedure that led us to the Airy integral, and adjusting the arbitrary overall normalization, we find (see A.1.1)

⟨ψ~±​(E)⟩=∫𝒞±d​r​e13​r3−ξ​r,ξ=−e23​S0​E.\langle\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E)\rangle=\int_{\mathcal{C}_{\pm}}dr\;e^{\frac{1}{3}r^{3}-\xi r},\hskip 20.0pt\xi=-e^{\frac{2}{3}S_{0}}E. (183)

As explained in appendix A.1.1, the contour 𝒞±\mathcal{C}_{\pm} starts at r=−∞r=-\infty and ends at r=e±i​π3⋅∞r=e^{\pm i\frac{\pi}{3}}\cdot\infty. By comparing to the contour integral definitions of the Airy function, we see that the exact answer for this integral is

⟨ψ~±​(E)⟩=π​Bi​(ξ)±i​π​Ai​(ξ).\langle\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E)\rangle=\pi\text{Bi}(\xi)\pm i\pi\text{Ai}(\xi). (184)

As in the case of the brane, the overall normalization of this quantity is not significant.

5.2.2 Disks and Cylinders

We would now like to write a candidate general formula in terms of the disk and cylinder function. We use the same formula (171), but now with X=−Tr​log⁡(E−H)X=-{\rm Tr}\log(E-H). At one-loop order, this is equal to

Ψ~​(z)≡exp⁡[−Disk​(z)+12​Cyl​(z,z)]=12​z​exp⁡[−Disk​(z)]\widetilde{\Psi}(z)\equiv\exp\left[-\text{Disk}(z)+\frac{1}{2}\text{Cyl}(z,z)\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2z}}\exp\left[-\text{Disk}(z)\right] (185)

At one loop, one would expect to be able to write ⟨ψ~⟩\langle\widetilde{\psi}\rangle in terms of a linear combination of the two branches Ψ~​(±z)\widetilde{\Psi}(\pm z). Matching to (184) determines the linear combination, up to an overall constant multiple, as

⟨ψ~±​(E)⟩∼{Ψ~​(z)E>0Ψ~​(z)+12​Ψ~​(−z)E<0.\langle\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E)\rangle\sim\begin{cases}\widetilde{\Psi}(z)&E>0\cr\widetilde{\Psi}(z)+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{\Psi}(-z)&E<0.\end{cases} (186)

In these expressions, we mean that zz is continued through the lower half-plane for ψ~+\widetilde{\psi}_{+} and through the upper half plane for ψ~−\widetilde{\psi}_{-}. So in the upper line we have Ψ~​(e∓i​π2​E)\widetilde{\Psi}(e^{\mp i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E}) and in the lower line we have Ψ~​(−E)+12​Ψ~​(e∓i​π​−E)\widetilde{\Psi}(\sqrt{-E})+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{\Psi}(e^{\mp i\pi}\sqrt{-E}). We expect (186) to be valid for a general spectral curve that limits to the Airy curve near the origin.

5.3 The resolvent

We will now combine the brane and ghost brane computations in order to get (158). The key formula for this section relates the resolvent to the derivative of a dipole of a brane and ghost brane4242 42 See for example [105, 67, 68, 108].

Tr​1E−H=∂Edet(E−H)det(E′−H)|E′→E.{\rm Tr}\frac{1}{E-H}=\partial_{E}\frac{\det(E-H)}{\det(E^{\prime}-H)}\bigg|_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}~. (187)

Though the above way of writing this relation will be more suitable for calculations, the following, more trivial-looking formula may also be helpful to think about

Tr​1E−H=Tr⁡(1E−H)​det(E−H)det(E′−H)|E′→E.{\rm Tr}\frac{1}{E-H}={\rm Tr}\left(\frac{1}{E-H}\right)\frac{\det(E-H)}{\det(E^{\prime}-H)}\bigg|_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}~. (188)

The introduction of these determinants may seem unnecessary. However, if we include the ratio of determinants for E≠E′E\neq E^{\prime} and calculate using the formal method of the previous sections we find in addition to the perturbative series for the resolvent there are nonperturbative pieces that survive in the limit E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E.

5.3.1 Airy

As always, we start with the Airy case y2=−Ey^{2}=-E. Modifying the techniques for the brane and ghost brane, we show in appendix A.1.2 that

⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~±​(E′)⟩\displaystyle\big\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E^{\prime})\big\rangle =−∫𝒞±d​r​d​s2​π(r+is)exp[13r3+i3s3+e2​S03(E′r−iEs)]\displaystyle=-\int_{\mathcal{C_{\pm}}}\frac{drds}{2\pi}(r+is)\exp\Big[\tfrac{1}{3}r^{3}+\tfrac{i}{3}s^{3}+e^{\tfrac{2S_{0}}{3}}(E^{\prime}r-iEs)\Big] (189)
=πe−2​S03(∂E−∂E′)Ai(ξ)(Bi(ξ′)±iAi(ξ′)),(ξ,ξ′)=−e2​S03(E,E′).\displaystyle=\pi e^{-\frac{2S_{0}}{3}}(\partial_{E}-\partial_{E^{\prime}})\text{Ai}(\xi)\big(\text{Bi}(\xi^{\prime})\pm i\text{Ai}(\xi^{\prime})\big),\hskip 20.0pt(\xi,\xi^{\prime})=-e^{\frac{2S_{0}}{3}}(E,E^{\prime}).

By contrast to the brane and the ghost brane computations, this dipole quantity has a well-defined and meaningful normalization. Taking another derivative with respect to EE, using the definition of the Airy function Ai′′​(ξ)=ξ​Ai​(ξ)\text{Ai}^{\prime\prime}(\xi)=\xi\text{Ai}(\xi), and setting E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E, we find an exact formula for the resolvent:

⟨R±​(E)⟩−L​V′​(E)2=π​e2​S03​[−Ai′​(ξ)​(Bi′​(ξ)±i​Ai′​(ξ))+ξ​Ai​(ξ)​(Bi​(ξ)±i​Ai​(ξ))].\langle R^{\pm}(E)\rangle-\frac{LV^{\prime}(E)}{2}=\pi e^{\frac{2S_{0}}{3}}\left[-\text{Ai}^{\prime}(\xi)\big(\text{Bi}^{\prime}(\xi)\pm i\text{Ai}^{\prime}(\xi)\big)+\xi\text{Ai}(\xi)\big(\text{Bi}(\xi)\pm i\text{Ai}(\xi)\big)\right]. (190)

Note that like the ghost brane, the resolvent defines two separate entire functions, as discussed in [55]. Taking the difference between the two along the real axis, we recover (50).

One point to note is the following. The saddle point structure of the integral (189) is the same as for the product of the integrals for ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle and ⟨ψ~​(E′)⟩\langle\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime})\rangle. This means that the asymptotics of ⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~​(E′)⟩\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime})\rangle is to leading order the same as the asymptotics of ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩​⟨ψ~​(E′)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle\langle\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime})\rangle. At first sight this may seem problematic; ⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~​(E′)⟩\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime})\rangle should be exactly one as E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E, while the product ⟨ψ​(E)⟩​⟨ψ~​(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle\langle\widetilde{\psi}(E)\rangle is not equal to one. The one-loop correction away from the product structure of (189) is critical for ensuring the correct behavior at E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E, as we will see in a moment.

5.3.2 Disks and cylinders

We would now like to reproduce the asymptotics of this formula with a formal disk-and-cylinder approach. To do this, we write

det(E−H)det(E′−H)=exp⁡[∫E′Ed​E′′​R​(E′′)]\frac{\det(E-H)}{\det(E^{\prime}-H)}=\exp\bigg[\int_{E^{\prime}}^{E}dE^{\prime\prime}R(E^{\prime\prime})\bigg] (191)

and then apply the formula (171). A nice feature of the ratio of determinants is that although the determinant and the inverse determinant do not by themselves have a natural normalization, their product does. This is because the arbitrary constant in the potential cancels out. And, correspondingly, the total one-loop factor

C⁡(z,z′)≡12​(Cyl​(z,z)+Cyl​(z′,z′))−Cyl​(z,z′)=log⁡z+z′2​z​z′C(z,z^{\prime})\equiv\frac{1}{2}\Big(\text{Cyl}(z,z)+\text{Cyl}(z^{\prime},z^{\prime})\Big)-\text{Cyl}(z,z^{\prime})=\log\frac{z+z^{\prime}}{2\sqrt{zz^{\prime}}} (192)

is finite without any subtraction of infinite terms. By analogy to the previous formulas (180) and (185), we expect to write a one-loop formula for the brane-ghost brane pair in terms of the function

Ψ⁡(z,z′)=z+z′2​z​z′​exp⁡(Disk​(z)−Disk​(z′)).\Psi(z;z^{\prime})=\frac{z+z^{\prime}}{2\sqrt{zz^{\prime}}}\exp\Big(\text{Disk}(z)-\text{Disk}(z^{\prime})\Big). (193)

We separate the arguments by a semicolon to emphasize that this function is not symmetric. The first argument refers to the determinant, and the second to the inverse determinant.

We find that the exact Airy expression can be matched to the leading asymptotics

⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~±​(E′)⟩≈{Ψ⁡(z,z′)+Ψ⁡(−z,z′)E,E′>0Ψ⁡(z,z′)+12​Ψ​(z,−z′)E,E′<0.\big\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E^{\prime})\big\rangle\approx\begin{cases}\Psi(z;z^{\prime})+\Psi(-z;z^{\prime})&E,E^{\prime}>0\cr\Psi(z;z^{\prime})+\frac{1}{2}\Psi(z;-z^{\prime})&E,E^{\prime}<0.\end{cases} (194)

The branch prescriptions for the two arguments are the same as in the respective determinant and inverse determinant cases. Explicitly,

⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~±​(E′)⟩≈{Ψ⁡(ei​π2​E,e∓i​π2​E′)+Ψ⁡(e−i​π2​E,e∓i​π2​E′)E,E′>0Ψ⁡(−E,−E′)+12​Ψ​(−E,e∓i​π​−E′)E,E′<0.\big\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E^{\prime})\big\rangle\approx\begin{cases}\Psi(e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E};e^{\mp i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E^{\prime}})+\Psi(e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E};e^{\mp i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E^{\prime}})&E,E^{\prime}>0\cr\Psi(\sqrt{-E};\sqrt{-E^{\prime}})+\frac{1}{2}\Psi(\sqrt{-E};e^{\mp i\pi}\sqrt{-E^{\prime}})&E,E^{\prime}<0.\end{cases} (195)

Unlike in the previous cases, the normalization here is meaningful. As a simple check, we can take the limit E′=EE^{\prime}=E. Using (193), we find that

Ψ⁡(z,z)=1,Ψ⁡(z,−z)=0,\Psi(z,z)=1,\hskip 20.0pt\Psi(z,-z)=0, (196)

so (194) reduces to one in the limit E′=EE^{\prime}=E. This is expected because ψ⁡(E)​ψ~​(E)=1\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E)=1 exactly.

Now, to compute the resolvent we take the derivative ∂E=−12​z∂z\partial_{E}=-\frac{1}{2z}\partial_{z} and then set E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E. Again using (193), and also using that Disk​(z)\text{Disk}(z) is odd in zz, one finds

∂zΨ⁡(z,z′)|z′=z=∂zDisk​(z),∂zΨ⁡(z,z′)|z′=−z=12​−z2​exp⁡[2​Disk​(z)].\partial_{z}\Psi(z;z^{\prime})\Big|_{z^{\prime}=z}=\partial_{z}\text{Disk}(z),\hskip 20.0pt\partial_{z}\Psi(z;z^{\prime})\Big|_{z^{\prime}=-z}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-z^{2}}}\exp\big[2\,\text{Disk}(z)\big]. (197)

This is an interesting expression. In the coincidence limit when the arguments are on the same sheet, the derivative of the brane-ghost brane function (193) reduces to a simple object, the derivative of the disk. But when the zz arguments are on opposite sheets, we get a nontrivial expression with an exponentiated disk amplitude. This is the source of the nonperturbative effects in this way of calculating the resolvent.

Multiplying by −12​z-\frac{1}{2z} to convert the zz derivative to an EE derivative, and then plugging into (195) and taking care with the branches, we find

⟨R±​(E)⟩≈{∓eS0​y​(i​E)±i4​E​exp⁡[±2​Disk​(i​E)]E>0eS0​y​(−E)∓i−8​E​exp⁡[2​Disk​(−E)]E<0.\langle R^{\pm}(E)\rangle\approx\begin{cases}\mp e^{S_{0}}y(i\sqrt{E})\pm\frac{i}{4E}\exp\big[\pm 2\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E})\big]&E>0\cr e^{S_{0}}y(\sqrt{-E})\mp\frac{i}{-8E}\exp\big[2\text{Disk}(\sqrt{-E})\big]&E<0.\end{cases} (198)

Given this expression for the resolvent, we can find the one-loop approximation to the density of eigenvalues by using R+−R−=−2​π​i​ρR^{+}-R^{-}=-2\pi i\rho. Using y⁡(i​E)=i​π​ρ0​(E)y(i\sqrt{E})=i\pi\rho_{0}(E) for E>0E>0, we find

⟨ρ⁡(E)⟩≈{eS0​ρ0​(E)−14​π​E​cos⁡(2​π​eS0​∫0Ed​E′​ρ0​(E′))E>01−8​π​Eexp(−2eS0∫0−Edxy(x))E<0.\langle\rho(E)\rangle\approx\begin{cases}e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}(E)-\frac{1}{4\pi E}\cos\big(2\pi e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{E}dE^{\prime}\rho_{0}(E^{\prime})\big)&E>0\cr\frac{1}{-8\pi E}\exp\big(-2e^{S_{0}}\int_{0}^{-E}dx\,y(\sqrt{x})\big)&E<0.\end{cases} (199)

as claimed in (158).

Although it is more complicated, one can follow a similar procedure to calculate a nonperturbative correction to the two-resolvent correlator, and extract a generalization of the sine kernel formula for the pair correlation function ⟨ρ⁡(E)​ρ​(E′)⟩\langle\rho(E)\rho(E^{\prime})\rangle. In the appendix A.2, we find that by writing each resolvent as a derivative of a ratio of determinants and calculating to one-loop order, we find for E,E′>0E,E^{\prime}>0

⟨ρ⁡(E)​ρ​(E′)⟩⊃cos⁡(2​π​∫EE′d​E′′​ρ0total​(E′′))2​π2​(E−E′)2,|E−E′|≪1.\langle\rho(E)\rho(E^{\prime})\rangle\supset\frac{\cos\big(2\pi\int_{E}^{E^{\prime}}dE^{\prime\prime}\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E^{\prime\prime})\big)}{2\pi^{2}(E-E^{\prime})^{2}},\hskip 20.0pt|E-E^{\prime}|\ll 1. (200)

Adding the contribution from the leading perturbative cylinder geometry between the two resolvents and approximating the integral in the above formula to leading order in E−E′E-E^{\prime}, we find the familiar sine kernel expression for the pair correlation function. While the nonperturbative correction and cylinder are separately divergent as E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E, this expression is finite in that limit (although there is also a delta function contact term, see (262) for more detail).

5.4 Connection to JT gravity

We would like to understand how to interpret the above computations in the context of JT gravity. We will start by thinking about ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle, using the representation of the determinant as det(E−H)=exp⁡(Tr​log⁡(E−H))\det(E-H)=\exp({\rm Tr}\log(E-H)). Expanding out the exponential, one has to compute expectation values of arbitrary powers of Tr​log⁡(E−H){\rm Tr}\log(E-H). These are related by an integral transform to an expectation value of products of partition functions Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n}), which we know how to compute in JT gravity. As described before, for ⟨Z⁡(β1)​…​Z​(βn)⟩\langle Z(\beta_{1})...Z(\beta_{n})\rangle, one sums over surfaces with nn boundaries with lengths proportional to β1,…,βn\beta_{1},...,\beta_{n}.

The boundary condition required to compute Tr​log⁡(E−H){\rm Tr}\log(E-H) is a type of fixed energy boundary condition and it can be obtained as an integral transform of the fixed length boundary condition that defines Z⁡(β)=Tr​e−β​HZ(\beta)={\rm Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}. Naively, the relation is

Trlog(E−H)=−∫ϵ∞d​ββeβ​EZ(β)+const.{\rm Tr}\log(E-H)=-\int_{\epsilon}^{\infty}\frac{d\beta}{\beta}e^{\beta E}Z(\beta)+\text{const}. (201)

This expression is quite natural from the perspective of quantum gravity. The integral over β\beta is an integral over the length of the boundary, and the eβ​Ee^{\beta E} weighting amounts to a boundary cosmological constant. The measure factor of 1β\frac{1}{\beta} is familiar in string theory. It means that we consider the boundary to have no marked point, so configurations that differ by a translation of the boundary time coordinate should not be counted independently.4343 43 The integral to compute Tr​1E−H{\rm Tr}\frac{1}{E-H} has no such factor, and corresponds to a marked boundary. In the context of the minimal string, the boundary condition implied by (201) is simply the FZZT boundary condition in Liouville, with μB∝−E\mu_{B}\propto-E.

The following is a technical remark. Eq. (201) works for contributions with genus g>0g>0, but for the disk topology, the integral has an exponential divergence at β=0\beta=0. This reflects the divergence in Tr​log⁡(E−H){\rm Tr}\log(E-H) in a double-scaled matrix integral. In the quantity ψ⁡(E)\psi(E), this is cured by subtracting the bare potential L2​V​(E)\frac{L}{2}V(E). In JT gravity, a prescription that effectively subtracts this is as follows. The function Z⁡(β)Z(\beta) is a double-valued function, due to a branch point at β=0\beta=0. The two branches differ by a minus sign, so we can rewrite the integrand in (201) as one-half of the difference of the two branches. The integral can then be interpreted as the discontinuity across a branch cut. A way to define the integral in general is to deform the contour slightly to pass around the branch point at the origin, avoiding the singularity. This prescription is equivalent to the naive one for g>0g>0 and it also gives the correct answer (subtracting the potential) for g=0g=0. In order to converge at infinity, the integral has to be done along a ray that is oriented in an appropriate half-plane, depending on the phase of EE.

In any case, an insertion of Tr​log⁡(E−H){\rm Tr}\log(E-H) amounts to a boundary in JT gravity of a particular kind. To compute ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle we sum over configurations with an arbitrary number of such boundaries. These boundaries can be connected to each other or disconnected. See figure 2 for an example configuration.

So ψ⁡(E)\psi(E) is fundamentally a ‘‘many universe’’ quantity, whose computation involves disconnected spacetime geometries.4444 44 In the introduction we used the term “baby universe” to refer to a disconnected spatial universe. Here we are referring to disconnected spacetimes, which would be the histories of such “baby universes.”

This is analogous to the mathematics of D-branes as described in [46]. The Tr​log⁡(E−H){\rm Tr}\log(E-H) boundary condition is interpreted as the worldsheet boundary associated to a D-brane. ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle is then the D-brane partition function, involving a sum over many disconnected worldsheets ending at the same type of boundary condition. In this analogy, the D-brane is labeled by the argument EE, and the multivaluedness reflects the branched structure of the semiclassical space of D-branes [55]. In the Liouville minimal string case, the relevant D-branes are called FZZT branes [47], and they are defined by a boundary condition similar to (201). So the mathematics is the same but the interpretation is different: we view the two-dimensional geometry as spacetime, rather than a string worldsheet.4545 45 It would be interesting to explore the D-brane interpretation of ⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩\langle\psi(E)\rangle in JT gravity further, including understanding the “target space” in which this D-brane lives. The description outlined in Section 4 of JT gravity as a limit of the minimal string might provide a way of addressing this issue.

The computation of ⟨ψ~⟩\langle\widetilde{\psi}\rangle is similar to that of ⟨ψ⟩\langle\psi\rangle: it is also a many-universe quantity. One obvious difference is a minus sign associated to each boundary, which comes from writing det(E−H)−1=exp⁡(−Tr​log⁡(E−H))\det(E-H)^{-1}=\exp(-{\rm Tr}\log(E-H)). A less obvious difference is that the sum over branches has to be treated differently than for ⟨ψ⟩\langle\psi\rangle. We do not have a derivation of this branch prescription from JT gravity, but we can follow the rules outlined in the matrix integral discussion above.

The calculation of the “dipole” partition function ⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~±​(E′)⟩\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E^{\prime})\rangle is also similar. For a given choice of branches, we sum over all geometries with any number of brane or ghost brane boundaries. In the disk-and-cylinder approximation, the disconnected spacetimes exponentiate to form the combination Ψ⁡(z,z′)\Psi(z,z^{\prime}). For coincident E′=EE^{\prime}=E, the ghost brane perfectly cancels the brane, thanks to (196).

The JT interpretation of the resolvent is more interesting. In (198), we got the resolvent by differentiating the dipole partition function, and then setting E′=EE^{\prime}=E. For the present discussion, it is convenient to think about this procedure using the formula (188):

R⁡(E)=limE′→ER⁡(E)​ψ​(E)​ψ~​(E′).R(E)=\lim_{E^{\prime}\rightarrow E}R(E)\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime}). (202)

To calculate this, we sum over geometries with a single resolvent boundary in addition to the brane and ghost brane boundaries, see figure 3.4646 46 A key point is that the resolvent boundary must be on the same branch as the brane boundary; we do not sum over separate branch choices for the resolvent. This can easily be seen to follow from the requirement that we match with the version of the calculation where we take the EE derivative of the dipole partition function. In the sum over geometries, there is a class in which the resolvent does not connect to any of the brane boundaries. These sum up to the factorized expectation value ⟨R±​(E)⟩​⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~±​(E′)⟩\langle R^{\pm}(E)\rangle\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E^{\prime})\rangle. Taking the limit E′→EE^{\prime}\rightarrow E, the brane and ghost brane cancel and we recover the perturbative series for the resolvent.

The leading correction to factorization comes from a geometry where the resolvent is connected to one of the branes by a cylinder diagram. By a calculation similar to the one in (178), we find the cylinder between the resolvent and the brane is

⟨R⁡(E)​Tr​log⁡(E′−H)⟩conn.=12​z​(z+z′).\langle R(E){\rm Tr}\log(E^{\prime}-H)\rangle_{\text{conn.}}=\frac{1}{2z(z+z^{\prime})}. (203)

The cylinder to the ghost brane is minus the same thing. Combining these two, and with the right sum over branches, we have at leading order

⟨R⁡(E)​ψ​(E1)​ψ~​(E2)⟩−⟨R⁡(E)⟩​⟨ψ⁡(E1)​ψ~​(E2)⟩=∑branchesz2−z12​z​(z+z1)​(z+z2)​Ψ​(z1,z2).\langle R(E)\psi(E_{1})\widetilde{\psi}(E_{2})\rangle-\langle R(E)\rangle\langle\psi(E_{1})\widetilde{\psi}(E_{2})\rangle=\sum_{\text{branches}}\frac{z_{2}-z_{1}}{2z(z+z_{1})(z+z_{2})}\Psi(z_{1},z_{2}). (204)

Let’s first consider this function for the case where E1=E2≠EE_{1}=E_{2}\neq E. Then the explicit cylinder factor vanishes if z1,z2z_{1},z_{2} are on the same sheet, and from (193) the function Ψ\Psi vanishes if z1,z2z_{1},z_{2} are on opposite sheets, so we find zero. However, when we obtain the resolvent as a limit of the derivative of the brane-ghost brane dipole, we are effectively setting E=E1E=E_{1} before taking the limit E2=E1E_{2}=E_{1}. In this case the answer still vanishes if z1,z2z_{1},z_{2} are on the same sheet, but if they are on opposite sheets, a factor in the denominator of (204) cancels the zero in Ψ⁡(z,−z)\Psi(z,-z) and we get a nonzero answer, proportional to exp⁡[2​Disk​(z)]\exp[2\,\text{Disk}(z)]. In this term, the sum over an infinite number of disconnected spacetimes remains!

This surprising result would be natural if we were studying a different problem, a string theory where the worldsheet is described by JT gravity – the “JT string.” Then the infinite number of spacetimes would just be the infinite number of worldsheets connected to a D-brane, as in the minimal string theory calculations that motivated the above analysis. But this result is highly unnatural from the point of view of gravity, where the resolvent is a “single-spacetime” object, at least at the perturbative level of the sum over geometries. Could it be that there is a different gravitational theory that does not include the nonperturbative effects discussed above?

The gravitational sum over geometries is divergent. If we make the plausible assumption that it is a resurgent asymptotic series then, as we will see in section 5.6, the perturbation series itself contains information about nonperturbative effects. That information is consistent with the results of the D-brane approach. So, perhaps the right question is whether there is another method of calculating these effects that is natural from the single-spacetime gravitational point of view – although it might be less efficient than the D-brane method that is natural in the JT string. SYK model considerations, discussed in section 6.3, hint at the existence of such a method. Then the question would become, what does the existence of these two different approaches mean for quantum gravity?

5.5 Nonperturbative instability and ZZ brane

Up to this point we have made the simplifying assumption that Veff​(E)>0V_{\text{eff}}(E)>0 in the forbidden region, meaning that the most likely position for an eigenvalue is in the allowed region where ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) is supported. But in some cases Veff​(E)V_{\text{eff}}(E) can become negative, indicating that the density ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) is not the dominant contribution to the matrix integral. Another eigenvalue density, perhaps with multiple regions of support, could dominate.

In fact, for JT gravity the situation is more extreme. The JT spectral curve, y=sin⁡(2​π​z)4​πy=\frac{\sin(2\pi z)}{4\pi} gives the effective potential

Veff​(E)=eS04​π3​[sin⁡(2​π​−E)−2​π​−E​cos⁡(2​π​−E)],E<0.V_{\text{eff}}(E)=\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{4\pi^{3}}\left[\sin(2\pi\sqrt{-E})-2\pi\sqrt{-E}\cos(2\pi\sqrt{-E})\right],\hskip 20.0ptE<0. (205)

We give a plot of this function in figure 4.

As we enter the forbidden region, the potential initially rises, reaching a local maximum value at E=−14E=-\frac{1}{4}, before decreasing and becoming negative. It then oscillates repeatedly, with regions that are more and more negative. The consequence is that this model is nonperturbatively ‘‘unstable.’’4747 47 A similar situation applies in the (2,p)(2,p) minimal string: there the potential oscillates a finite number of times, passing through zero p−12\frac{p-1}{2} times before eventually going to either positive infinity (a metastable situation) or negative infinity (an unstable situation).

To give the model a nonperturbative definition, we must choose a contour other than the real axis for the integral over eigenvalues. We choose a contour so that the integral converges and so that the perturbative series which involves expanding around the ρ0​(E)\rho_{0}(E) saddle point is actually asymptotic to the true value of the integral. For example the contour can extend along the real axis from positive infinity down to E=−14E=-\frac{1}{4}, and then follow this steepest descent contour either upwards or downwards into the complex EE plane and out to infinity, see figure 4. Any linear combination of these contours (suitably normalized) would also produce the same asymptotic series and be a viable nonperturbative completion of the theory, so such a completion is not unique.

A special role is played by the saddle point at E=−14E=-\frac{1}{4}. In the matrix integral literature, such saddle points are known as one-eigenvalue instantons. In the minimal string, they are related to boundary conditions in Liouville known as ZZ branes. We will study this in matrix integral language in the next section. First, we will give a somewhat tentative JT gravity interpretation.

An important point is that in the minimal string, ZZ branes are interpreted in a fundamentally different way than FZZT branes. As we have seen, FZZT branes correspond to observables that one can insert into the matrix integral partition function. By contrast, ZZ branes are non-optional: they are like instantons that occur as part of the matrix integral, and will contribute a small amount to any computation.

Let’s first study the effect of a ZZ brane on the matrix integral partition function, 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. As discussed in section 3.2, 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has an asymptotic series given by the sum over closed surfaces. The ZZ brane correction amounts to allowing surfaces to end in a particular boundary associated to the ZZ brane. This boundary condition can be described in the minimal string as a difference of two FZZT boundary conditions [51]:

|ZZ⟩=|FZZT​(zZZ)⟩−|FZZT​(−zZZ)⟩|\text{ZZ}\rangle=|\text{FZZT}(z_{\text{ZZ}})\rangle-|\text{FZZT}(-z_{\text{ZZ}})\rangle (206)

Here we are using the notation that |FZZT​(z)⟩|\text{FZZT}(z)\rangle is the boundary state associated to an insertion of Tr​log⁡(E−H)−L​V​(E)2{\rm Tr}\log(E-H)-\frac{LV(E)}{2}, with the understanding that zz encodes both the energy via z2=−Ez^{2}=-E and also the choice of branch. This can be rewritten as

|ZZ⟩=∫−zZZzZZd​E​(z′)​|R⁡(z′)⟩|\text{ZZ}\rangle=\int_{-z_{\text{ZZ}}}^{z_{\text{ZZ}}}dE(z^{\prime})|R(z^{\prime})\rangle (207)

where |R⁡(z)⟩|R(z)\rangle is the boundary state associated to an insertion of R⁡(E)−L​V′​(E)2R(E)-\frac{LV^{\prime}(E)}{2}. The zz coordinate of the ZZ brane is determined by the condition that it be a stationary point of the effective potential, so that y⁡(z)=0y(z)=0. At such points, the two branches of the spectral curve meet, and the integral in (207) can be understood as a closed contour on the spectral curve, see [53]. Concretely, for the ZZ brane associated to the local maximum of VeffV_{\text{eff}} at E=−14E=-\frac{1}{4}, we have zZZ=12z_{\text{ZZ}}=\frac{1}{2}.

In the matrix integral partition function, we propose to include surfaces that end on the ZZ brane by taking

𝒵→𝒵⋅[1+(const.)⋅e2​Disk​(zZZ)].\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}\cdot\left[1+(\text{const.})\cdot e^{2\text{Disk}(z_{\text{ZZ}})}\right]. (208)

Let’s explain this formula. First of all, the term involving the 11 is just the original series for the matrix partition function. The correction represents the possibility that a ZZ brane is ‘‘present.’’4848 48 A familiar subtlety in this type of expression is that the series without the ZZ brane is asymptotic, with a nonperturbative ambiguity that is of the order of the correction. Depending on the Borel contour, we could view the correction term as just arising from the resummation of the perturbative series. However, as with other instantons, the ZZ brane gives a semiclassical interpretation to this correction. In this term, any number of surfaces can connect to the ZZ brane: the exponential factor is the disk amplitude associated to the boundary state (206), after we remember that Disk(−z)=−(-z)=-Disk(z)(z). Note that Disk(zZZ)<0(z_{\text{ZZ}})<0. Formally, the constant should include the one-loop contribution that comes from the exponentiated cylinder diagram connecting the ZZ brane to itself. Using (207), this cylinder diagram is

∫−zZZzZZd​E​(z1)​𝑑E​(z2)​R0,2​(E⁡(z1),E⁡(z2))=∫−zZZzZZd​z1​d​z2(z1+z2)2\int_{-z_{\text{ZZ}}}^{z_{\text{ZZ}}}dE(z_{1})dE(z_{2})R_{0,2}(E(z_{1}),E(z_{2}))=\int_{-z_{\text{ZZ}}}^{z_{\text{ZZ}}}\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}+z_{2})^{2}} (209)

but the integral appears to be infinite or ambiguous. It may be possible to resolve this directly, but we will leave the constant arbitrary, and see that it can be matched to a matrix integral computation below. We will find that the constant is imaginary, and that it depends on the contour choice described above.

Let’s now discuss the contribution of the ZZ brane to the resolvent. To discuss this correction, we do not need to represent the resolvent as a brane-ghost brane dipole. We can simply treat it in the naive way as a single boundary. At leading order, the contribution of the ZZ brane reflects the possibility of this resolvent boundary connecting to the ZZ brane boundary via a cylinder diagram. This leads to

⟨R⁡(z)⟩→⟨R⁡(z)⟩+zZZz​1−z2+zZZ2⋅(const.)⋅e2​Disk​(zZZ).\langle R(z)\rangle\rightarrow\langle R(z)\rangle+\frac{z_{\text{ZZ}}}{z}\frac{1}{-z^{2}+z_{\text{ZZ}}^{2}}\cdot(\text{const.})\cdot e^{2\text{Disk}(z_{\text{ZZ}})}. (210)

In this expression, the constant and exponential factors are the same as in (208). The prefactor is simply the cylinder diagram between a resolvent boundary and the ZZ state (207):

∫−zZZzZZd​E​(z′)​R0,2​(E⁡(z),E⁡(z′))=∫−zZZzZZ−2​z′​d​z′4​z​z′​(z+z′)2=zZZz​1−z2+zZZ2.\int_{-z_{\text{ZZ}}}^{z_{\text{ZZ}}}dE(z^{\prime})R_{0,2}(E(z),E(z^{\prime}))=\int_{-z_{\text{ZZ}}}^{z_{\text{ZZ}}}\frac{-2z^{\prime}dz^{\prime}}{4zz^{\prime}(z+z^{\prime})^{2}}=\frac{z_{\text{ZZ}}}{z}\frac{1}{-z^{2}+z_{\text{ZZ}}^{2}}. (211)

We see that indeed the expression has a pole when the energy argument EE of the resolvent agrees with the energy associated to the ZZ brane, −zZZ2=−14-z_{\text{ZZ}}^{2}=-\frac{1}{4}. This is consistent with the interpretation of the ZZ brane as an eigenvalue sitting at the local maximum of the potential.

Finally, we emphasize that the ZZ brane effects are numerically very small, because 2​Disk​(zZZ)=−eS04​π22\,\text{Disk}(z_{\text{ZZ}})=-\frac{e^{S_{0}}}{4\pi^{2}}, so the contribution is double-exponentially suppressed. However, these effects are significant because they encode the large orders behavior of the asymptotic series. We will discuss this next.

5.6 Large order behavior

In this section we will use the density of eigenvalues in the forbidden region to predict the large genus asymptotics of the Weil-Petersson volumes, following a similar approach for other problems described by topological recursion in [111, 112, 61]. In doing this, we are assuming that the matrix integral dual to JT gravity is resurgent, so that it can be analyzed by Borel transform techniques. We will start by reviewing these.

In general, given a formal series

A⁡(u)≃∑n=0∞ak​ukA(u)\simeq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{k}u^{k} (212)

where the coefficients grow asymptotically as ak∼k!a_{k}\sim k!, one can define a related convergent series called the Borel transform of AA:

A^​(t)=∑k=1∞akΓ⁡(k)​tk−1.\widehat{A}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_{k}}{\Gamma(k)}t^{k-1}. (213)

This sum will have a finite radius of convergence under our growth assumption for aka_{k}. One can then define a third function, sometimes called the Borel sum of AA, or inverse Borel transform of A^\widehat{A}, by

A~(u)=a0+∫𝒞e−t/uA^(t)dt.\widetilde{A}(u)=a_{0}+\int_{\mathcal{C}}e^{-t/u}\widehat{A}(t)dt. (214)

Here, the contour 𝒞\mathcal{C} starts at the origin and ends at infinity and is chosen so that the integral is convergent. By substituting in (213) and doing the tt integral, one can show that A~\widetilde{A} has an asymptotic series that matches AA. Therefore A~\widetilde{A} is a candidate nonperturbative completion of AA, although in general there will be multiple choices depending on the contour 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

The closest singularity to the origin of the Borel transform A^​(t)\widehat{A}(t) encodes the large orders asymptotics of the original series aka_{k}. To see this, one can write a dispersion relation for aka_{k} by starting with a contour integral around the origin

ak=Γ⁡(k)2​π​i​∮0d​ttk​A^​(t)a_{k}=\frac{\Gamma(k)}{2\pi i}\oint_{0}\frac{dt}{t^{k}}\widehat{A}(t) (215)

and then deforming the contour outwards in the complex tt plane. For large kk, the closest singularity to the origin will dominate the answer.

5.6.1 Large Genus Asymptotics of Vg,0V_{g,0}

We would like to apply (215) to predict the large genus behavior of Weil-Petersson volumes. We start by considering the perturbative series for the matrix partition function 𝒵\mathcal{Z} for JT gravity, which involves a sum over closed surfaces of arbitrary genus. As discussed in section 3.2, the partition functions of these closed surfaces evaluate to the Weil-Petersson volumes with no boundary. So the matrix integral free energy has a perturbative series

ℱ⁡(e−S0)=log⁡𝒵≃∑g=0∞e(2−2​g)​S0​Vg,0.\mathcal{F}(e^{-S_{0}})=\log\mathcal{Z}\simeq\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}e^{(2-2g)S_{0}}V_{g,0}. (216)

The genus zero and one cases have to be defined specially, but we are interested in the large genus behavior, so this will not be important. The series (216) is asymptotic due to the (2​g)!(2g)! growth of the volumes Vg,0V_{g,0}. In order to apply the Borel transform formalism, we should think in terms of a series indexed by k=2​g−2k=2g-2 instead of gg, so that the growth is k!k!. Explicitly, one can write

ℱ⁡(e−S0)≃∑k=−2∞fk​e−k​S0,fk={0k​ oddVk+22,0k​ even.\mathcal{F}(e^{-S_{0}})\simeq\sum_{k=-2}^{\infty}f_{k}e^{-kS_{0}},\hskip 20.0ptf_{k}=\begin{cases}0&k\text{ odd}\\ V_{\frac{k+2}{2},0}&k\text{ even}.\end{cases} (217)

Now, we switch perspective to the matrix integral. We start with a conventional matrix integral with finite LL. Then 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is an integral over LL eigenvalues. We can can organize this into integrals over the allowed region E>0E>0 and the forbidden region E<0E<0:

𝒵\displaystyle\mathcal{Z} =∫Ad​λ1​∫Ad​λ2​…​∫Ad​λL​μ​({λi})+L​∫Fd​λ1​∫Ad​λ2​…​∫Ad​λL​μ​({λi})+…\displaystyle=\int_{A}d\lambda_{1}\int_{A}d\lambda_{2}\dots\int_{A}d\lambda_{L}\;\mu(\{\lambda_{i}\})+L\int_{F}d\lambda_{1}\int_{A}d\lambda_{2}\dots\int_{A}d\lambda_{L}\;\mu(\{\lambda_{i}\})+\dots (218)
=𝒵(0)+𝒵(1)+…\displaystyle=\mathcal{Z}^{(0)}+\mathcal{Z}^{(1)}+\dots (219)

Here μ⁡({λi})\mu(\{\lambda_{i}\}) denotes the measure, including both the Vandermonde and the potential. We will refer to 𝒵(1)\mathcal{Z}^{(1)} as the “one-instanton” contribution to 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. The nonperturbative expression for the free energy will be

ℱ=log⁡𝒵=log⁡𝒵(0)+𝒵(1)𝒵(0)+…\mathcal{F}=\log\mathcal{Z}=\log\mathcal{Z}^{(0)}+\frac{\mathcal{Z}^{(1)}}{\mathcal{Z}^{(0)}}+... (220)

where 𝒵(1)𝒵(0)\frac{\mathcal{Z}^{(1)}}{\mathcal{Z}^{(0)}} is the one-instanton contribution to the free energy. From (218), we can recognize this quantity simply as

𝒵(1)𝒵(0)=∫Fd​λ​⟨ρ⁡(λ)⟩\frac{\mathcal{Z}^{(1)}}{\mathcal{Z}^{(0)}}=\int_{F}d\lambda\,\langle\rho(\lambda)\rangle (221)

after integrating over the other eigenvalues λ2,…,λL\lambda_{2},...,\lambda_{L}. This generalizes in a trivial way to a double-scaled theory.

The main idea is to recognize the integral over λ\lambda in (221) as a contribution to an inverse Borel transform integral for the free energy ℱ\mathcal{F}

ℱ⁡(e−S0)=∫𝒞d​t​exp⁡(−eS0​t)​ℱ^​(t)\mathcal{F}(e^{-S_{0}})=\int_{\mathcal{C}}dt\,\exp(-e^{S_{0}}t)\,\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(t) (222)

with some mapping between tt and λ\lambda. This relationship can be fixed by interpreting the exponential term in the density of eigenvalues, given by (161), as exp⁡(−eS0​t)\exp(-e^{S_{0}}t). In other words t=Veff​(λ)eS0t=\frac{V_{\text{eff}}(\lambda)}{e^{S_{0}}}. To determine the large genus asymptotics via (215), we need to know ℱ^​(t)\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(t) near the closest singularity to the origin. This singularity is associated to the saddle point in the effective potential at λ=−14\lambda=-\frac{1}{4}. Expanding (205) near this point, and matching (221) to (222), we find

t≈14​π2−12​(λ+14)2,ℱ^​(t)≈12​π​2​(14​π2−t).t\approx\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}(\lambda+\tfrac{1}{4})^{2},\hskip 20.0pt\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(t)\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{2(\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}-t)}}. (223)

So, in particular, ℱ^​(t)\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(t) has a branch point singularity at t=14​π2t=\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}.

We now apply (215). Since the perturbative series for ℱ\mathcal{F} is an even function of e−S0e^{-S_{0}}, the same will be true for ℱ^\widehat{\mathcal{F}}, and the integral will vanish for odd kk. For even kk, we will get the contribution from the branch point described in (223), together with an equal contribution from the reflection under t→−tt\rightarrow-t. For large gg, this leads to

Vg,0≈2⋅Γ⁡(2​g−2)2​π​i∫14​π2∞d​tt2​g−2disc[ℱ^(t)]≈(4​π2)2​g−5221/2​π3/2Γ(2g−52).V_{g,0}\approx 2\cdot\frac{\Gamma(2g{-}2)}{2\pi i}\int_{\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{t^{2g-2}}\text{disc}\left[\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(t)\right]\approx\frac{(4\pi^{2})^{2g-\frac{5}{2}}}{2^{1/2}\pi^{3/2}}\Gamma(2g-\tfrac{5}{2}). (224)

In the final step, we substituted in (223) and did the integral. This expression is expected to be accurate at order one, which means that it will have multiplicative corrections of the form (1+a1g+a2g2+…)(1+\frac{a_{1}}{g}+\frac{a_{2}}{g^{2}}+...). And, indeed, at this level of precision (224) matches a conjecture due to Zograf [69].4949 49 Parts of this conjecture have been established rigorously [31, 70, 45].

We now move on to discuss the large genus asymptotics of Vg,1​(b)V_{g,1}(b), for which we will find a new formula. We start by defining a generating function of the volumes for g≥1g\geq 1:

V⁡(b,e−S0)≃∑g=1∞e(1−2​g)​S0​Vg,1​(b)=∑n=0∞e−n​S0​vn​(b).V(b,e^{-S_{0}})\simeq\sum_{g=1}^{\infty}e^{(1-2g)S_{0}}V_{g,1}(b)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-nS_{0}}v_{n}(b). (225)

Here vn=0v_{n}=0 for even nn and vn​(b)=Vn+12,1​(b)v_{n}(b)=V_{\frac{n+1}{2},1}(b) for odd nn. In terms of this quantity, the expectation value of the resolvent is given by (dropping the genus zero piece)

⟨R(−z2)⟩=−12​z∫0∞bdbV(b,eS0)e−z​b.\langle R(-z^{2})\rangle=-\frac{1}{2z}\int_{0}^{\infty}\hskip-5.0ptb\,db\,V(b,e^{S_{0}})e^{-zb}. (226)

In appendix A.3, we compute the nonperturbative contribution to the resolvent that results from integrating one eigenvalue in the classically forbidden region. The result is

⟨R⁡(E)⟩(1)=∫Fd​λ​⟨ρ⁡(λ)⟩E−λ​λE.\langle R(E)\rangle^{(1)}=\int_{F}d\lambda\frac{\langle\rho(\lambda)\rangle}{E-\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{E}}. (227)

V(1)​(b,e−S0)\displaystyle V^{(1)}(b,e^{-S_{0}}) =2b​∫Fd​λ​⟨ρ⁡(λ)⟩​sinh⁡(−λ​b)\displaystyle=\frac{2}{b}\int_{F}d\lambda\,\langle\rho(\lambda)\rangle\sinh(\sqrt{-\lambda}b) (228)
=∫Fd​z2​π​sinh⁡(b​z)b​z​e−eS0​t​(z).\displaystyle=\int_{F}\frac{dz}{2\pi}\frac{\sinh(bz)}{bz}e^{-e^{S_{0}}t(z)}. (229)

In the second line, we substituted in the formula for the density of eigenvalues in the forbidden region (161) and changed variables to λ=−z2\lambda=-z^{2}. The function t⁡(z)t(z) is

t⁡(z)=2​∫0z2d​x​sin⁡(2​π​x)4​π=sin⁡(2​π​z)−2​π​z​cos⁡(2​π​z)4​π3.t(z)=2\int_{0}^{z^{2}}\hskip-5.0ptdx\,\frac{\sin(2\pi\sqrt{x})}{4\pi}=\frac{\sin(2\pi z)-2\pi z\cos(2\pi z)}{4\pi^{3}}. (230)

Similarly to the discussion of the free energy, we would like to interpret the integral in (229) as an inverse Borel transform V⁡(b,e−S0)=∫d​t​e−eS0​t​V^​(b,t)V(b,e^{-S_{0}})=\int dte^{-e^{S_{0}}t}\widehat{V}(b,t) and thus determine V^\widehat{V}. In making this correspondence, the mapping between tt and zz will be (230). Then, to predict the large-orders behavior we need to compute (for odd nn)

Vn+12,1​(b)\displaystyle V_{\frac{n+1}{2},1}(b) ≈2⋅Γ⁡(n)2​π​i∫14​π2∞d​ttndisc[V^(b,t)].\displaystyle\approx 2\cdot\frac{\Gamma(n)}{2\pi i}\int_{\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{t^{n}}\text{disc}\left[\widehat{V}(b,t)\right]. (231)

This integral is over a contour in the tt plane that surrounds the branch cut along the positive tt axis. In the free energy case, we computed ℱ^​(t)\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(t) approximately by inverting (230) near the singularity at t=14​π2t=\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}, which maps to z=12z=\frac{1}{2}. However, in the present case we will need to know the behavior for more general values of tt. Because it is difficult to invert (230) in general, it turns out to be more convenient to work in terms of the zz variable. In terms of this coordinate, one finds that the integral (231) becomes

Vg,1​(b)≈Γ⁡(2​g−1)π​i​∫𝒞d​z2​π​sinh⁡(b​z)b​z​1t​(z)2​g−1.V_{g,1}(b)\approx\frac{\Gamma(2g-1)}{\pi i}\int_{\mathcal{C}}\frac{dz}{2\pi}\frac{\sinh(bz)}{bz}\frac{1}{t(z)^{2g-1}}. (232)

More precisely, we expect multiplicative corrections (1+a1/g+a2/g2+…)(1+a_{1}/g+a_{2}/g^{2}+...) where the coefficients a1,a2,…a_{1},a_{2},... are bounded functions of bb. For small values of b/gb/g, the saddle point is close to z=12z=\frac{1}{2}, and for large values of b/gb/g, it is close to the origin.
