These checks give us some confidence in our understanding of nonperturbative effects in the matrix integral dual to JT gravity. As a side note, it would be possible to use a similar method to predict the large gg behavior of Vg,n​(b1,…,bn)V_{g,n}(b_{1},...,b_{n}). It is also interesting to consider the possibility that the large genus limit of any expansion described by topological recursion can be obtained in a similar way, by using the one-eigenvalue sector of a formal matrix integral with spectral curve yy, see [111, 112, 61] for some related work.

6 Discussion

6.1 Disordered but kk-local theories like SYK

The SYK model is a type of sparse random matrix ensemble, and there is numerical evidence that certain aspects of the model are well described by random matrix statistics. However, it is not a random matrix ensemble in the sense of section 2, and so in general we do not expect the JT gravity results in this paper to match the behavior of SYK.

One reason is the following. Varying the SYK couplings Ja1​…​aqJ_{a_{1}...a_{q}} will “rattle around” the fine-grained structure of the spectrum, as in a true random-matrix ensemble. However, because the number of variable parameters is relatively small, of order NqN^{q}, one also expects there to be some “global” features of the spectrum with relatively large 1/Nq1/N^{q} fluctuations. These features include the overall normalization of the Hamiltonian, as well as other low-order moments [20, 116, 117]. They lead to relatively large connected correlations in ⟨Z⁡(β1)​Z​(β2)⟩\langle Z(\beta_{1})Z(\beta_{2})\rangle of order 1/Nq1/N^{q}. Taken at face value, these represent a large departure from random matrix statistics, and one without a clear JT gravity interpretation. However, we note that these modes can be reduced or eliminated by “unfolding” the spectrum sample-by-sample [117], so we will not dwell on this point.

There is another reason. It seems possible that the collective field description of SYK involves analogs of the JT geometries discussed in this paper. For example, the ramp saddle point [13] is analogous to the double trumpet considered here. However, even for these contributions, one expects differences from JT gravity. As a crude model, one can consider the effect of free bulk matter fields on the JT gravity computation. The measure for the genus gg moduli space will now include the matter determinant as well as the Weil-Petersson measure. At higher genus this leads to a dramatic effect: the portion of moduli space with long thin tubes will be exponentially divergent, due to the negative Casimir energy on the small circle. This is essentially the tachyon divergence familiar from string theory.

In the full SYK theory we expect that this divergence will be preempted by a first order Hawking-Page transition, very similar to the situation discussed by Maldacena and Qi [11]. There, before a cylinder becomes long and thin, it disconnects into two disks, describing disconnected Euclidean black holes. This mechanism could effectively remove the dangerous part of moduli space, but in doing so it will change the JT gravity answer significantly.

So, in general, we do not expect the JT gravity results in this paper to match those of SYK, or indeed any kk-local theory. An important exception is for the short-ranged spectral correlators that are subject to random matrix universality (probed e.g. by the late-time spectral form factor). These are described by the universal ramp saddle point of [13], together with D-brane effects for the plateau. As we have seen, the D-brane contribution in JT is determined by the disk and cylinder amplitude. The matter field correction to the disk contribution determines the correction to the leading order density of states. For short range spectral correlations the cylinder is far from the transition point and so the matter fields should not change its energy dependence.5050 50 The matter field corrections to the cylinder do limit the range of agreement of eigenvalue pair correlations with random matrix theory to energy differences less than a “Thouless energy” of order 1/log⁡N1/\log N [13]. So we expect a close relative of the the D-brane effects described in JT to explain the sine kernel result with a modified SYK density of states. This clearly deserves more work.

6.2 Non-disordered theories

So far all the comments in this paper have concerned averaged systems. Some of the deepest questions in this subject concern the fine-grained behavior of the energy eigenvalues of gauge/gravity dual systems that are not averaged – large NN Super Yang-Mills theory (SYM) is the canonical example. In trying to apply the ideas of this paper to such a system one encounters an immediate problem. Consider for example the double-trumpet:

(236)

This contributes to the connected correlator ⟨Z⁡(β1)​Z​(β2)⟩−⟨Z⁡(β1)⟩​⟨Z⁡(β2)⟩\langle Z(\beta_{1})Z(\beta_{2})\rangle-\langle Z(\beta_{1})\rangle\langle Z(\beta_{2})\rangle. But in a non-disordered theory, Z⁡(β)Z(\beta) is a fixed function rather than an observable in an ensemble, and such a correlator would not make sense [118, 119].

We are not sure what to say about this, but there is a well understood example of quantum chaos that may be instructive. This is the semiclassical quantum dynamics of classically chaotic systems with a few degrees of freedom.5151 51 For a review see [67], especially the ArXiv version. These systems are studied using the Feynman path integral representation (or actually its refinement known as the Gutzwiller trace formula) for Tre−iHT/ℏ{\rm Tr}e^{-iHT/\hbar} as a sum over periodic paths aa:

Tre−iHT/ℏ∼∑aeiℏ​Sa.{\rm Tr}e^{-iHT/\hbar}\sim\sum_{a}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S_{a}}~. (237)

Here SaS_{a} is the classical action. To study the spectral form factor one uses two copies,

Trei​H​T/ℏTre−iHT/ℏ∼∑a,beiℏ​Sae−iℏ​Sb.{\rm Tr}e^{iHT/\hbar}~{\rm Tr}e^{-iHT/\hbar}\sim\sum_{a,b}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S_{a}}e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}S_{b}}~. (238)

Note that this factorizes into the product of the result for each copy. Semiclassically the long time behavior is determined by long periodic classical orbits. In a chaotic system the details of such orbits are extremely complicated and the resulting behavior in (238) is erratic.5252 52 The results will resemble Figure 10 in [20].

But this signal simplifies after averaging, for instance over a time window. For long orbits the phases in the orbit sum in (238) are very large and after any appreciable averaging most terms in the double sum over a,ba,b cancel. The only surviving terms for times in the ramp region are those with a=ba=b up to a time translation. For these terms the action precisely cancels. This pairing is Berry’s “diagonal approximation” [120], and gives the ramp. This pattern is a close analog of the double cone [13], which is a continuation of the geometry (236). The two systems, decoupled without averaging, become correlated into a connected “geometry” after averaging. Factorization is destroyed by suppressing the a≠ba\neq b terms.5353 53 The potential for averaging to make such connected geometries, and the link to Coleman’s ideas, were pointed out in [118].

The role of essentially random phases in creating these connections calls to mind the work of Coleman [121, 122] on Euclidean wormholes.5454 54 This work was motivated by [123, 124, 100]. See also, [125, 126, 127, 128, 129]. Here Euclidean wormholes result from integration over random couplings. Operator insertions with Gaussian random coefficients on the same or different “universes” are paired by Wick contraction and fattened by an OPE into wormholes. In our setup we might imagine “forming” the wormholes in Figure 2 by averaging over erratic phases as in Figure 7. Figure 2 would be an open “many-universe” analog of the closed “many-universe” configurations that are summed up in this approach [122, 126, 127, 128]. This sum also produces results doubly exponential in 1/GN1/G_{N}, for analogous reasons.

Perhaps we have a choice about the bulk description of spectral statistics for non-disordered systems: an unaveraged description with simple topology but with exceedingly detailed and complicated information about microstates, like the individual orbits aa, and their intricate and rapidly fluctuating phases; or an averaged description made up of simpler geometrical objects. But the price for this simplicity seems to be third quantization, wormholes, and branes.

6.3 Other open questions

  1. 1.

    What is the result for the cylinder amplitude that connects a ZZ brane to itself?

  2. 2.

    Is it possible to recover the description of the matrix integral in terms of eigenvalues, starting with the bulk JT gravity description? A possible hint is the McGreevy-Verlinde proposal [50] for the c=1c=1 string. As refined in [52] this proposal asserts that the LL unstable ZZ branes, combined with the tachyonic stretched strings between them, form the matrix of the matrix quantum mechanics.

  3. 3.

    Is there another way to get the nonperturbative effects without summing over disconnected geometries? SYK may give a useful perspective. The determinant approach from section 5 should work, but it involves infinitely many SYK replicas as an intermediate step. As an alternative, it should be possible in principle to get the full spectral form factor (including the plateau) by doing the exact G,ΣG,\Sigma path integral with two replicas. Can the plateau be obtained this way in practice?

  4. 4.

    We have emphasized the doubly exponential character of the brane effects, of order exp⁡(c​e1/GN)\exp(ce^{1/G_{N}}) or exp⁡(c​eNSYK)\exp(ce^{N_{\text{SYK}}}). This suggests two layers of asymptotic expansion. Consider the SYK spectral form factor expressed as a two replica G,ΣG,\Sigma integral. Away from the Schwarzian limit where certain quantities become one loop exact, we expect to have an asymptotic expansion in 1/N1/N. Presumably its Borel transform has singularities corresponding to various e−Ne^{-N} effects. Perhaps the higher genus surfaces present in the JT limit persist in some fashion and determine some of these effects. If this is the case then these e−Ne^{-N} effects themselves will form another asymptotic series, whose Borel plane singularities will contain the doubly exponential effects. Can we find a simpler problem with a similar two-layer structure?5555 55 This is unlike the more familiar pattern, where the sum over e−Ne^{-N} instantons is convergent, see e.g. [130]. There is a field theory example where such phenomena occur [131], due to IR “renormalon” effects.

  5. 5.

    Another natural set of observables in JT gravity are correlators of probe bulk matter fields. Some preliminary remarks about higher genus corrections to them were made in [13] and a systematic treatment has been initiated in [132]. One interesting aspect of these observables is that they probe matrix elements as well as energies and so give information about the random matrix character of eigenstates, i.e. ETH. Higher order OTOCs may be especially interesting to study in this regard.

  6. 6.

    Are there theories of quantum gravity in higher dimensions that are dual to ensemble averages of boundary theories, rather than specific boundary theories?

  7. 7.

    In cases where the boundary theory is fixed, what prevents us from including the contribution of connected geometries? See [118, 119]. These papers considered actual solutions to the bulk equations of motion. By contast, the gravity configurations considered in this paper are not solutions: there is no on-shell configuration for the dilaton (more physically, the action is not stationary with respect to bb, as in [100]). If we are willing to consider such geometries in higher dimensions, the problem could be even worse than envisioned in [118, 119].

  8. 8.

    The disk and cylinder geometries are the ingredients required to determine the ramp and plateau. These seem to have a natural extension to higher dimensions: the Euclidean black hole solution and, when continued to Minkowski signature, the double cone portion of the eternal AdS-Schwarzschild geometry [13]. Do these provide an explanation of spectral statistics in suitably averaged higher dimensional gauge/gravity dual systems?

  9. 9.

    The branched structure of the spectral curve was important for getting the nonperturbative effects. What is the meaning of this spectral curve in gravity?

We will close the paper with the following comment. In an ensemble average of quantum systems, unitarity of time evolution is not as dramatic as for an individual system (e.g. there are no recurrences). But it still means something. For example, it implies that the spectral form factor cannot decay to zero at late time. So Maldacena’s version of the black hole information problem [133] can be formulated for disordered theories.

Concretely, an analog of Maldacena’s puzzle for disordered theories is to explain in bulk language the late time behavior of the spectral form factor. For the case where the bulk dual is JT gravity, the nonperturbative effects discussed in this paper provide a type of answer.5656 56 The ideas discussed in [129] may be related. Of course, we did not derive the effects from bulk reasoning: in section 5 we were essentially reinterpreting the rules of a matrix integral in JT language. A clearer bulk understanding of these rules, or perhaps a different version of them, would be valuable.

Appendix A Some details on nonperturbative effects

A.1 The Airy ghost brane and dipole

A.1.1 Integral representation for ghost brane

We begin with the Gaussian model5757 57 For related work in this context see [134]. described by V⁡(H)=2a2​H2V(H)=\frac{2}{a^{2}}H^{2}. Instead of introducing Grassmann flavor fields we introduce bosonic fields ϕi\phi_{i} to implement 1/det(E−H)1/\det(E-H).5858 58 The opposite statistics of these fields motivates the name “ghost brane.” Another point of view derives from the field theory on the spectral curve discussed in [104, 57, 32]. Performing the Gaussian integral over HH, we find an integrand that depends only on ∑iϕ¯i​ϕi\sum_{i}\overline{\phi}_{i}\phi_{i}. We then introduce an auxiliary variable rr that renders the integral over the ϕi\phi_{i} and ϕ¯i\overline{\phi}_{i} Gaussian, allowing us to integrate them out. The result is the integral

⟨det(E±i​ϵ−H)−1⟩=2​Lπ​a2​∫−∞∞d​r​(E±i​ϵ+r)−L​e−2​La2​r2.\langle\det(E\pm i\epsilon-H)^{-1}\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2L}{\pi a^{2}}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dr(E\pm i\epsilon+r)^{-L}e^{-\frac{2L}{a^{2}}r^{2}}. (239)

Before we discuss the saddle point structure of this integral, we will verify that this integral representation reproduces the expected discontinuity across the real axis. First, we shift r→r∓i​ϵr\rightarrow r\mp i\epsilon so that the the pole is on the real axis, and the contour for rr runs either just above or just below the real axis. The discontinuity of the integral is the integral over the difference of the two contours. The two contours can be joined at infinity to form a loop, which we can shrink to surround the pole at r=−Er=-E. We recognize the resulting integral as the familiar contour integral representation for the L−1L-1’th Hermite Polynomial. Up to a constant of proportionality, we find

disc​[⟨ψ~​(E)⟩L]∝i​⟨ψ⁡(E)⟩L−1.\text{disc}\big[\langle\widetilde{\psi}(E)\rangle_{L}\big]\propto i\langle\psi(E)\rangle_{L-1}. (240)

Here we are defining the LL and L−1L-1 ensembles as described around (264).

Now we move on to a saddle point analysis of (239). There are two saddle points, r=r±r=r_{\pm}. We will focus on the case E<0E<0 because we are ultimately interested in double-scaling near E=−aE=-a. Then the behavior of the integral depends on how EE compares to −a-a:

  1. 1.

    For E<−aE<-a, the two saddle points are on the real axis. The steepest descent contour for r−r_{-} runs along the real axis, while the steepest descent contour for r+r_{+} passes vertically through r+r_{+}. We may deform the defining contour into two portions of these steepest descent contours. The first segment comes in from r=−∞r=-\infty, passes through r−r_{-}, then reaches r+r_{+}. Here we go either upwards or downwards along the steepest descent contour for r+r_{+}. Which way we go is determined by the i​ϵi\epsilon prescription in (239), which requires the rr contour to go either below or above the pole, see figure 8. Schematically,

    ⟨det(E±i​ϵ−H)−1⟩∼e−L​I​(r−)±i2​e−L​I​(r−),E<−a.\langle\det(E\pm i\epsilon-H)^{-1}\rangle\sim e^{-LI(r_{-})}\pm\frac{i}{2}e^{-LI(r_{-})},\hskip 20.0ptE<-a. (241)

    Here e−L​I​(r±)e^{-LI(r_{\pm})} is the integrand evaluated on the saddle point r±r_{\pm}. In the above expression we have ignored the contributions of one-loop factors except to emphasize the i2\frac{i}{2}.

  2. 2.

    For E>−aE>-a, the defining contour can be deformed into just one of the steepest descent contours. Again, the choice is determined by the i​ϵi\epsilon prescription. The leading order saddle point approximation gives

    ⟨det(E±i​ϵ−H)−1⟩∼e±i​π4−L​I​(r±),−a<E<a.\langle\det(E\pm i\epsilon-H)^{-1}\rangle\sim e^{\pm i\frac{\pi}{4}-LI(r_{\pm})},\hskip 20.0pt-a<E<a. (242)

So far, we have discussed the standard Gaussian matrix integral. To get the double-scaled theory, we multiply (239) by eL2​V​(E)e^{\frac{L}{2}V(E)}, shift E→E−aE\rightarrow E-a, shift r→a2+a2​e−S03​rr\rightarrow\frac{a}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{a}{2}}e^{-\frac{S_{0}}{3}}r, and take the limit a→∞a\rightarrow\infty, holding fixed eS0=(2/a)3/2​Le^{S_{0}}=(2/a)^{3/2}L. This leads to (183), up to a constant of proportionality. This limit scales away the pole in (239), but it leaves a remnant: the integrand grows along the positive real axis. Because of this, the integration contour has to go to infinity in the right half-plane at a finite angle either above or below the real axis, ending at e±i​π3⋅∞e^{\pm i\frac{\pi}{3}}\cdot\infty. In taking the double-scaled limit, this choice matches onto the choice of whether the contour goes above or below the pole on the real axis, and is therefore determined by the ±i​ϵ\pm i\epsilon prescription.

A.1.2 Integral representation for dipole

We start again with the potential V⁡(H)=2a2​H2V(H)=\frac{2}{a^{2}}H^{2}. By writing the ratio of determinants as an integral over Grassmann vectors χi,χ¯i\chi_{i},\;\overline{\chi}_{i} and bosonic vectors ϕi,ϕ¯i\phi_{i},\;\overline{\phi}_{i}, we find an integral that depends only on the matrix

S^=(∑iϕ¯i​ϕi∑iϕ¯i​χi∑iχ¯i​ϕi∑iχ¯i​χi).\widehat{S}=\begin{pmatrix}\sum_{i}\overline{\phi}_{i}\phi_{i}&\sum_{i}\overline{\phi}_{i}\chi_{i}\cr\sum_{i}\overline{\chi}_{i}\phi_{i}&\sum_{i}\overline{\chi}_{i}\chi_{i}\end{pmatrix}. (243)

Defining the supertrace Str​(M^)≡M^11−M^22\text{Str}(\widehat{M})\equiv\widehat{M}_{11}-\widehat{M}_{22}, we have

⟨det(E−H)det(E′±i​ϵ−H)⟩=∫∏i=1L[d​χi​d​χ¯i​d​ϕ¯i​d​ϕi2​π]​exp⁡[a28​L​Str​(S^2)−ϕ¯i​ϕi​(E′±i​ϵ)+χ¯i​χi​E].\bigg\langle\frac{\det(E-H)}{\det(E^{\prime}\pm i\epsilon-H)}\bigg\rangle=\int\prod_{i=1}^{L}\bigg[\frac{d\chi_{i}d\overline{\chi}_{i}d\overline{\phi}_{i}d\phi_{i}}{2\pi}\bigg]\exp\bigg[\frac{a^{2}}{8L}\text{Str}(\widehat{S}^{2})-\overline{\phi}_{i}\phi_{i}(E^{\prime}\pm i\epsilon)+\overline{\chi}_{i}\chi_{i}E\bigg]. (244)

We can introduce an auxiliary matrix SS which has bosonic diagonal elements and Grassmann off-diagonal elements to render the integral over the χi,χ¯i\chi_{i},\;\overline{\chi}_{i} and ϕi,ϕ¯i\phi_{i},\;\overline{\phi}_{i} Gaussian,

S=(S11S12S21i​S22).S=\begin{pmatrix}S_{11}&S_{12}\cr S_{21}&i\;S_{22}\end{pmatrix}. (245)

Defining the matrix ℰ=diag​(E′±i​ϵ,E)\mathcal{E}=\text{diag}(E^{\prime}\pm i\epsilon,E) and performing the Gaussian integral we are led to an integral just over the matrix SS,

⟨det(E−H)det(E′±i​ϵ−H)⟩=∫d​S11​d​S22​d​S12​d​S212​π​exp⁡[−L​Str​log⁡(ℰ+S)−2​La2​Str​(S2)].\bigg\langle\frac{\det(E-H)}{\det(E^{\prime}\pm i\epsilon-H)}\bigg\rangle=\int\frac{dS_{11}dS_{22}dS_{12}dS_{21}}{2\pi}\exp\bigg[-L\;\text{Str}\log(\mathcal{E}+S)-\frac{2L}{a^{2}}\text{Str}(S^{2})\bigg]. (246)

To take the double scaled limit we multiply this by exp⁡[L​V⁡(E′)−V⁡(E)2]\exp[L\frac{V(E^{\prime})-V(E)}{2}], shift E,E′E,E^{\prime} by aa, shift the matrix S→a2+a2​SS\rightarrow\frac{a}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{a}{2}}S, then take the limit a→∞a\rightarrow\infty keeping eS0e^{S_{0}} fixed. We find

⟨ψ⁡(E)​ψ~​(E′±i​ϵ)⟩=∫𝒞±d​S11​d​S22​d​S12​d​S212​π​exp⁡[eS0​Str​(13​S3+ℰ​S)].\big\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime}\pm i\epsilon)\big\rangle=\int_{\mathcal{C_{\pm}}}\frac{dS_{11}dS_{22}dS_{12}dS_{21}}{2\pi}\;\exp\Big[e^{S_{0}}\text{Str}\big(\tfrac{1}{3}S^{3}+\mathcal{E}S\big)\Big]. (247)

The contours for S11,S22S_{11},S_{22} are the same as the contours for r,sr,s in the respective ghost brane and brane computations. To obtain the formula (189), we simply integrate out the Grassmann variables S12S_{12} and S21S_{21}. This leads to

⟨ψ(E)ψ~(E′±iϵ)⟩=−eS0∫𝒞±d​S11​d​S222​π(S11+iS22)exp[eS0(13S113+i3S223+E′S11−iES22)].\big\langle\psi(E)\widetilde{\psi}(E^{\prime}\pm i\epsilon)\big\rangle=-e^{S_{0}}\int_{\mathcal{C_{\pm}}}\frac{dS_{11}dS_{22}}{2\pi}(S_{11}+iS_{22})\exp\Big[e^{S_{0}}\big(\tfrac{1}{3}S_{11}^{3}+\tfrac{i}{3}S_{22}^{3}+E^{\prime}S_{11}-iES_{22}\big)\Big]. (248)

After relabeling S11=e−S03​rS_{11}=e^{-\frac{S_{0}}{3}}r, S22=e−S03​sS_{22}=e^{-\frac{S_{0}}{3}}s, we find (189). Note that for this Airy case, apart from the factor of (S11+i​S22)(S_{11}+iS_{22}), this is the product of the brane and ghost brane answers. This correction term can be obtained by differentiating with respect to E,E′E,E^{\prime}.

This calculation is a simple application of a central technique in the modern treatment of quantum chaos [105, 106, 67, 68, 135, 136]. In this approach correlators of arbitrary numbers of determinants and inverse determinants are represented by higher dimensional versions of S^\widehat{S}. The integral over S^\widehat{S} is then treated as a nonlinear sigma model whose target is embedded in a superspace. Its “pion” perturbative excitations produce the long range energy correlations. A nonperturbative saddle point, the analog of a baryon, produces the D-brane effects. In this context the saddle point is called the “Altshuler-Andreev” instanton [137].

This approach offers a framework to demonstrate random matrix universality. “All” one needs to do is show that the system being studied produces the necessary pattern of symmetry breaking in the effective sigma model. It would be interesting to explore this approach in the gravity context.

A.2 Density pair correlation function

We want to calculate the density pair correlation function ⟨ρ⁡(E1)​ρ​(E2)⟩\langle\rho(E_{1})\rho(E_{2})\rangle for |E1−E2|≪1|E_{1}-E_{2}|\ll 1, E1,E2>0E_{1},E_{2}>0. To do so, we compute the resolvent correlator using the formula

⟨R±(E1)R±′(E2)⟩=∂E1∂E2⟨ψ(E1)ψ(E2)ψ~±(E3)ψ~±′(E4)⟩|E1=E3,E2=E4\big\langle R^{\pm}(E_{1})R^{\pm^{\prime}}(E_{2})\big\rangle=\partial_{E_{1}}\partial_{E_{2}}\big\langle\psi(E_{1})\psi(E_{2})\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm}(E_{3})\widetilde{\psi}_{\pm^{\prime}}(E_{4})\big\rangle\big|_{E_{1}=E_{3},\;E_{2}=E_{4}} (249)

and then extract the density correlator using

(−2​π​i)2​⟨ρ​ρ⟩=⟨R+​R+⟩+⟨R−​R−⟩−⟨R+​R−⟩−⟨R−​R+⟩.(-2\pi i)^{2}\langle\rho\rho\rangle=\langle R^{+}R^{+}\rangle+\langle R^{-}R^{-}\rangle-\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle-\langle R^{-}R^{+}\rangle. (250)

This computation involves many different cases, and we will simplify our task somewhat by restricting to the pieces that are singular as E2→E1E_{2}\rightarrow E_{1}. The one-loop function, including the exponentiated disks and cylinders, is

Ψ⁡(z1,z2,z3,z4)=(z1+z3)​(z1+z4)​(z2+z3)​(z2+z4)4⋅z1​z2​z3​z4​(z1+z2)​(z3+z4)​eDisk​(z1)+Disk​(z2)−Disk​(z3)−Disk​(z4).\Psi(z_{1},z_{2};z_{3},z_{4})=\frac{(z_{1}+z_{3})(z_{1}+z_{4})(z_{2}+z_{3})(z_{2}+z_{4})}{4\cdot\sqrt{z_{1}z_{2}z_{3}z_{4}}(z_{1}+z_{2})(z_{3}+z_{4})}e^{\text{Disk}(z_{1})+\text{Disk}(z_{2})-\text{Disk}(z_{3})-\text{Disk}(z_{4})}. (251)

The branch prescription is determined by the prescription for the dipole (195). In the allowed region, the rule is to sum over both branches for the brane operators, but to take only the branch z=e∓i​π2​Ez=e^{\mp i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E} for the ghost brane operator associated to R±R^{\pm}. In all cases, we will evaluate the contribution to the resolvent, which is

∂E1∂E2Ψ=−12​z1​∂z1−12​z2​∂z2Ψ⁡(z1,z2,z3,z4)\partial_{E_{1}}\partial_{E_{2}}\Psi=\frac{-1}{2z_{1}}\partial_{z_{1}}\frac{-1}{2z_{2}}\partial_{z_{2}}\Psi(z_{1},z_{2};z_{3},z_{4}) (252)

where z12=z32=−E1z_{1}^{2}=z_{3}^{2}=-E_{1} and z22=z42=−E2z_{2}^{2}=z_{4}^{2}=-E_{2} with a choice of branch in the square root that has to be specified. The singular terms arise from the action of derivatives on the prefactor (cylinder) expressions, so we do not need to differentiate the disk functions. We will now go through the cases.

  1. 1.

    First, we consider the computation of ⟨R+​R+⟩\langle R^{+}R^{+}\rangle, so z3=e−i​π2​E1z_{3}=e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E_{1}} and z4=e−i​π2​E2z_{4}=e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E_{2}}. The computation for ⟨R−​R−⟩\langle R^{-}R^{-}\rangle can be treated similarly. There are four branch choices. In the two cases (z1,z2)=±(z3,z4)(z_{1},z_{2})=\pm(z_{3},z_{4}), one finds no singular contribution. In the case (z1,z2)=(−z3,z4)(z_{1},z_{2})=(-z_{3},z_{4}), one finds

    ⟨R+​R+⟩⊃i4​E1​E2​(E1−E2)​e2​Disk​(i​E1).\langle R^{+}R^{+}\rangle\supset\frac{i}{4\sqrt{E_{1}E_{2}}(E_{1}-E_{2})}e^{2\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E_{1}})}. (253)

    This is singular at E1=E2E_{1}=E_{2}, but the singularity cancels when we include the term from (z1,z2)=(z3,−z4)(z_{1},z_{2})=(z_{3},-z_{4}), which is obtained from the above by switching 1↔21\leftrightarrow 2. So, in summary, thre are no singular terms in ⟨R+​R+⟩\langle R^{+}R^{+}\rangle or ⟨R−​R−⟩\langle R^{-}R^{-}\rangle.

  2. 2.

    Next, we consider ⟨R+​R−⟩\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle, so z3=e−i​π2​E1z_{3}=e^{-i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E_{1}} and z4=ei​π2​E2z_{4}=e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{E_{2}}. The case ⟨R−​R+⟩\langle R^{-}R^{+}\rangle follows from complex conjugation, or by interchanging 1↔21\leftrightarrow 2.

    1. (a)

      If both z1=z3z_{1}=z_{3} and z2=z4z_{2}=z_{4}, we find the singular term

      ⟨R+​R−⟩⊃−14​E1​E2​(E1−E2)2.\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle\supset\frac{-1}{4\sqrt{E_{1}E_{2}}(\sqrt{E_{1}}-\sqrt{E_{2}})^{2}}. (254)

      This is simply the singularity that is present for the resolvent in the perturbative theory, coming from the double trumpet (141).

    2. (b)

      If z1=−z3z_{1}=-z_{3} and z2=z4z_{2}=z_{4}, we find

      ⟨R+​R−⟩⊃−i4​E1​E2​(E1−E2)​e2​Disk​(i​E1).\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle\supset\frac{-i}{4\sqrt{E_{1}E_{2}}(E_{1}-E_{2})}e^{2\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E_{1}})}. (255)
    3. (c)

      If z1=z3z_{1}=z_{3} and z2=−z4z_{2}=-z_{4}, we find

      ⟨R+​R−⟩⊃−i4​E1​E2​(E1−E2)​e−2​Disk​(i​E2).\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle\supset\frac{-i}{4\sqrt{E_{1}E_{2}}(E_{1}-E_{2})}e^{-2\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E_{2}})}. (256)
    4. (d)

      If z1=−z3z_{1}=-z_{3} and z2=−z4z_{2}=-z_{4}, we find

      ⟨R+​R−⟩⊃116​E1​E2​(E1+E2)2(E1−E2)2​e2​Disk​(i​E1)−2​Disk​(i​E2)\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle\supset\frac{1}{16E_{1}E_{2}}\frac{(\sqrt{E_{1}}+\sqrt{E_{2}})^{2}}{(\sqrt{E_{1}}-\sqrt{E_{2}})^{2}}e^{2\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E_{1}})-2\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E_{2}})} (257)

    So, we see that for ⟨R+​R−⟩\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle and ⟨R−​R+⟩\langle R^{-}R^{+}\rangle, all terms are singular. The term (254) has a double pole at E1=E2E_{1}=E_{2}, but no single pole. The terms (255) and (256) have single poles at E1=E2E_{1}=E_{2}, but the coefficient is rapidly oscillating as a function of energy. For our purposes, the most interesting term is (257). This contains a double pole that cancels the double pole in (254), and it also contains a single pole with a coefficient proportional to the derivative of the disk amplitude.

One can now add the contributions for ⟨R+​R−⟩\langle R^{+}R^{-}\rangle and ⟨R−​R+⟩\langle R^{-}R^{+}\rangle together to compute ⟨ρ​ρ⟩\langle\rho\rho\rangle, as in (250). In doing so, it is important to treat the poles carefully, giving a small ±\pm imaginary part to the energy argument of R±R^{\pm}. With this prescription, the poles discussed above lead to δ⁡(E1−E2)\delta(E_{1}-E_{2}) contact terms in ⟨ρ​ρ⟩\langle\rho\rho\rangle. One finds that the term (257) and its analog in ⟨R−​R+⟩\langle R^{-}R^{+}\rangle lead to the contribution

⟨ρ⁡(E1)​ρ​(E2)⟩⊃\displaystyle\langle\rho(E_{1})\rho(E_{2})\rangle\supset 132​π2​E1​E2​(E1+E2)2(E1−E2)2​cos⁡[2​π​eS0​∫E2E1d​E​ρ0​(E)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{32\pi^{2}E_{1}E_{2}}\frac{(\sqrt{E_{1}}+\sqrt{E_{2}})^{2}}{(\sqrt{E_{1}}-\sqrt{E_{2}})^{2}}\cos\big[2\pi e^{S_{0}}\hskip-5.0pt\int_{E_{2}}^{E_{1}}\hskip-5.0ptdE\rho_{0}(E)\big] (258)
+ρ0total​(E1)​δ​(E1−E2).\displaystyle\hskip 20.0pt+\rho^{\text{total}}_{0}(E_{1})\delta(E_{1}{-}E_{2}).

In writing this expression, we used that

∂EDisk​(i​E)=i​π​eS0​ρ0​(E)=i​π​ρ0total​(E).\partial_{E}\text{Disk}(i\sqrt{E})=i\pi e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}(E)=i\pi\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E). (259)

The pole from (255) and (256) corrects the coefficient of the delta function in this expression slightly, by adding the leading oscillating correction to the density of eigenvalues (199). The perturbative term (254) adds a term that cancels the double pole in the first line of (258).

Away from E1,E2=0E_{1},E_{2}=0, we may simplify our expressions to find the universal sine kernel formula for the connected pair correlation function in regions of large density. Expanding the integral ∫E2E1d​E​ρ0​(E)≈ρ0​(E2)​(E1−E2)\int_{E_{2}}^{E_{1}}dE\rho_{0}(E)\approx\rho_{0}(E_{2})(E_{1}-E_{2}), keeping only the singular parts as E2→E1E_{2}\rightarrow E_{1} in (258), and subtracting a double pole to account for the perturbative term (254), we find that for non-coincident points,

⟨ρ⁡(E1)​ρ​(E2)⟩conn.\displaystyle\langle\rho(E_{1})\rho(E_{2})\rangle_{\text{conn}.} ⊃−12​π2​(E1−E2)2+12​π2​(E1−E2)2​cos⁡[2​π​eS0​ρ0​(E2)​(E1−E2)]\displaystyle\supset-\frac{1}{2\pi^{2}(E_{1}-E_{2})^{2}}+\frac{1}{2\pi^{2}(E_{1}-E_{2})^{2}}\cos\big[2\pi e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}(E_{2})(E_{1}-E_{2})\big] (260)
=−sin2⁡[π​eS0​ρ0​(E2)​(E1−E2)]π2​(E1−E2)2,E1,E2>0,|E1−E2|≪1.\displaystyle=-\frac{\sin^{2}\big[\pi e^{S_{0}}\rho_{0}(E_{2})(E_{1}-E_{2})]}{\pi^{2}(E_{1}-E_{2})^{2}},\hskip 20.0ptE_{1},E_{2}>0,\;|E_{1}{-}E_{2}|\ll 1. (261)

The full sine-kernel approximation to the pair correlation also includes the leading factorized piece ρ0total​(E1)​ρ0total​(E2)\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E_{1})\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E_{2}). In our present setup, this arises from a nonsingular but large contribution to ⟨R+​R+⟩\langle R^{+}R^{+}\rangle and ⟨R−​R−⟩\langle R^{-}R^{-}\rangle in which the derivatives in (252) act on the disk amplitudes. Including this piece, and the delta function at coincident points, one finds

⟨ρ⁡(E1)​ρ​(E2)⟩≈ρ0total​(E1)​ρ0total​(E2)+ρ0total​δ​(E1−E2)−sin2⁡[π​ρ0total​(E2)​(E1−E2)]π2​(E1−E2)2.\langle\rho(E_{1})\rho(E_{2})\rangle\approx\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E_{1})\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E_{2})+\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}\delta(E_{1}{-}E_{2})-\frac{\sin^{2}\big[\pi\rho_{0}^{\text{total}}(E_{2})(E_{1}{-}E_{2})]}{\pi^{2}(E_{1}{-}E_{2})^{2}}. (262)

A.3 Forbidden contribution to the resolvent

In this appendix, we will derive the formula (227) from the perspective of a matrix integral. As a setup for the calculation, suppose that we divide the region of integration of the matrix eigenvalues into two pieces, an “allowed” region and a “forbidden” region, such that the probability of an eigenvalue being in the forbidden region is very small (in practice, this means that we should put the division a finite distance into the E<0E<0 region). Suppose that, as a first step, we compute everything by doing the integrals over eigenvalues in the allowed region, including the integrals in the matrix partition function that normalizes expectation values. The question is: what do we have to add to the computation of the resolvent in order to accurately describe the contribution of one eigenvalue being in the forbidden region?

We will get a simple formula for double-scaled matrix integrals, but we will start out with an unscaled matrix integral with LL eigenvalues. It will be useful to define two un-normalized measures, one for LL eigenvalues and one for L−1L-1:

μL​(λ)\displaystyle\mu_{L}(\lambda) =Δ2(λ1,…,λL)e−L∑j=1LV(λj)\displaystyle=\Delta^{2}(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{L})e^{-L\sum_{j=1}^{L}V(\lambda_{j})} (263)
μ~L−1​(λ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mu}_{L-1}(\lambda) =Δ2(λ1,…,λL−1)e−(L−1)∑j=1L−1V~(λj)\displaystyle=\Delta^{2}(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{L-1})e^{-(L-1)\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}\widetilde{V}(\lambda_{j})} (264)

where Δ\Delta is the Vandermonde determinant, and

(L−1)​V~​(x)=L​V​(x).(L-1)\widetilde{V}(x)=LV(x). (265)

A useful relation is that the measure for LL eigenvalues is a product of the measure for L−1L-1 eigenvalues times the square of the determinant operator, viewed as an operator in the (L−1)(L-1)-eigenvalue theory:

μL​(λ1​…​λL)=μ~L−1​(λ1​…​λL−1)​ψ2​(λL).\mu_{L}(\lambda_{1}...\lambda_{L})=\widetilde{\mu}_{L-1}(\lambda_{1}...\lambda_{L-1})\psi^{2}(\lambda_{L}). (266)

This implies, for example, that we can write a formula for the density of eigenvalues in the LL ensemble in terms of the determinant operator in the L−1L-1 ensemble:

⟨ρ⁡(E)⟩L=L​𝒵L−1𝒵L​⟨ψ2​(E)⟩L−1.\langle\rho(E)\rangle_{L}=\frac{L\mathcal{Z}_{L-1}}{\mathcal{Z}_{L}}\langle\psi^{2}(E)\rangle_{L-1}. (267)

We can use this to write a formula for the matrix integral partition function

𝒵L=𝒵L(0)+𝒵L(1)+…\mathcal{Z}_{L}=\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}+\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(1)}+... (268)

Here the first term represents the contribution with all eigenvalues integrated in the allowed region:

𝒵L(0)=∫Ad​μL​(λ).\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}=\int_{A}d\mu_{L}(\lambda). (269)

The second term represents the contribution with one eigenvalue in the forbidden region:

𝒵L(1)=L​∫Ad​μ~L−1​∫Fd​λL​ψ2​(λL)=𝒵L−1(0)​L​∫Fd​λL​⟨ψ2​(λL)⟩L−1(0).\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(1)}=L\int_{A}d\widetilde{\mu}_{L-1}\int_{F}d\lambda_{L}\psi^{2}(\lambda_{L})=\mathcal{Z}_{L-1}^{(0)}L\int_{F}d\lambda_{L}\langle\psi^{2}(\lambda_{L})\rangle_{L-1}^{(0)}. (270)

The subscript on the expectation value in the last term means that we are working in the L−1L-1 eigenvalue ensemble defined by μ~L−1\widetilde{\mu}_{L-1}, and we are in the zero-instanton sector, where all eigenvalues are integrated in the allowed region.

Similarly, we can write a formula for an un-normalized version of the resolvent:

∫A+Fd​μL​(λ)E−λ1\displaystyle\int_{A+F}\frac{d\mu_{L}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda_{1}} =∫Ad​μL​(λ)E−λ1+∫Fd​λL​ψ2​(λL)​∫Ad​μ~L−1​(λ)​(L−1E−λ1+1E−λL).\displaystyle=\int_{A}\frac{d\mu_{L}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda_{1}}+\int_{F}d\lambda_{L}\psi^{2}(\lambda_{L})\int_{A}d\widetilde{\mu}_{L-1}(\lambda)\left(\frac{L-1}{E-\lambda_{1}}+\frac{1}{E-\lambda_{L}}\right). (271)

In the second term on the RHS, we are including the possibility that one of the LL eigenvalues is in the forbidden region. This could be any of the eigenvalues. In L−1L-1 of the LL possible cases, this special eigenvalue is not the eigenvalue λ1\lambda_{1} that appears in the denominator in the LHS. In one of the LL cases, it is that eigenvalue. The two possibilities are represented in the two terms in parentheses.

We can rewrite the second term in (271) as an expectation value in the L−1L{-}1 ensemble:

∫A+Fd​μL​(λ)E−λ1\displaystyle\int_{A+F}\frac{d\mu_{L}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda_{1}} =∫Ad​μL​(λ)E−λ1+𝒵L−1(0)​∫Fd​λ​⟨ψ2​(λ)​(R⁡(E)+1E−λ)⟩L−1(0).\displaystyle=\int_{A}\frac{d\mu_{L}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda_{1}}+\mathcal{Z}_{L-1}^{(0)}\int_{F}d\lambda\left\langle\psi^{2}(\lambda)\left(R(E)+\frac{1}{E-\lambda}\right)\right\rangle_{L-1}^{(0)}. (272)

The properly normalized resolvent is L/𝒵LL/\mathcal{Z}_{L} times this expression. Using (268) and (270), we find that at one-eigenvalue-instanton precision, this is

⟨R⁡(E)⟩L\displaystyle\langle R(E)\rangle_{L} =⟨R⁡(E)⟩L(0)​(1−𝒵L(1)𝒵L(0))+L​𝒵L−1(0)𝒵L(0)​∫Fd​λ​⟨ψ2​(λ)​(R⁡(E)+1E−λ)⟩L−1(0)\displaystyle=\langle R(E)\rangle_{L}^{(0)}\left(1-\frac{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(1)}}{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}}\right)+L\frac{\mathcal{Z}_{L-1}^{(0)}}{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}}\int_{F}d\lambda\left\langle\psi^{2}(\lambda)\left(R(E)+\frac{1}{E-\lambda}\right)\right\rangle_{L-1}^{(0)} (273)
=⟨R⁡(E)⟩L(0)+L​𝒵L−1(0)𝒵L(0)​∫Fd​λ​[⟨ψ2​(λ)​R​(E)⟩L−1,conn.(0)+⟨ψ2​(λ)E−λ⟩L−1(0)]\displaystyle=\langle R(E)\rangle_{L}^{(0)}+L\frac{\mathcal{Z}_{L-1}^{(0)}}{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}}\int_{F}d\lambda\left[\Big\langle\psi^{2}(\lambda)R(E)\Big\rangle_{L-1,\text{conn.}}^{(0)}+\left\langle\frac{\psi^{2}(\lambda)}{E-\lambda}\right\rangle_{L-1}^{(0)}\right] (274)
+𝒵L(1)𝒵L(0)​(⟨R⁡(E)⟩L−1(0)−⟨R⁡(E)⟩L(0)).\displaystyle\hskip 64.0pt+\frac{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(1)}}{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}}\left(\langle R(E)\rangle_{L-1}^{(0)}-\langle R(E)\rangle_{L}^{(0)}\right). (275)

Here we are defining ⟨ψ2​R⟩conn.=⟨ψ2​R⟩−⟨ψ2⟩​⟨R⟩\langle\psi^{2}R\rangle_{\text{conn.}}=\langle\psi^{2}R\rangle-\langle\psi^{2}\rangle\langle R\rangle.

So far, the discussion has been for a regular (unscaled) matrix integral. But in a double-scaled theory, we get a somewhat simpler expression. One reason is that in a double-scaled theory, the difference of expectation values on the final line (275) vanishes. Intuitively, this is because in a double-scaled matrix integral, LL is taken to infinity, so changing it by one has no effect on normalized quantities. Another nice feature of the double-scaled case is that we can write a simple leading-order formula for the connected correlator ⟨ψ2​R⟩conn.\langle\psi^{2}R\rangle_{\text{conn.}}. We use

⟨R⁡(E⁡(z))​Tr​log⁡(E⁡(z1)−H)⟩conn.=∫∞z1d​E​(z′)​R0,2​(E⁡(z),E⁡(z′))=12​z​(z+z1)\langle R(E(z))\,{\rm Tr}\log(E(z_{1})-H)\rangle_{\text{conn.}}=\int_{\infty}^{z_{1}}dE(z^{\prime})R_{0,2}(E(z),E(z^{\prime}))=\frac{1}{2z(z+z_{1})} (276)

to find that

⟨ψ2​(E⁡(z1))​R​(E⁡(z))⟩L−1,conn.(0)=1z⁡(z+z1)​⟨ψ2​(E⁡(z1))⟩L−1(0).\Big\langle\psi^{2}(E(z_{1}))R(E(z))\Big\rangle_{L-1,\text{conn.}}^{(0)}=\frac{1}{z(z+z_{1})}\Big\langle\psi^{2}(E(z_{1}))\Big\rangle_{L-1}^{(0)}. (277)

This term combines nicely with the ⟨ψ2​(λ)/(E−λ)⟩\langle\psi^{2}(\lambda)/(E-\lambda)\rangle term in (274) and we find

⟨R⁡(E)⟩\displaystyle\langle R(E)\rangle =⟨R⁡(E)⟩(0)+L​𝒵L−1(0)𝒵L(0)​∫Fd​λ​⟨ψ2​(λ)⟩L−1​λE​1E−λ.\displaystyle=\langle R(E)\rangle^{(0)}+L\frac{\mathcal{Z}_{L-1}^{(0)}}{\mathcal{Z}_{L}^{(0)}}\int_{F}d\lambda\langle\psi^{2}(\lambda)\rangle_{L-1}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{E}}\frac{1}{E-\lambda}. (278)

Finally, using (267), we find

⟨R⁡(E)⟩=⟨R⁡(E)⟩(0)+∫Fd​λ​⟨ρ⁡(λ)⟩​λE​1E−λ.\displaystyle\langle R(E)\rangle=\langle R(E)\rangle^{(0)}+\int_{F}d\lambda\,\langle\rho(\lambda)\rangle\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{E}}\frac{1}{E-\lambda}. (279)

This expression answers the question we posed at the beginning of this appendix.

When one applies this to the contour in figure 4, one finds a distinct semiclassical contribution from the saddle point at λ=−14\lambda=-\frac{1}{4}. In the leading semiclassical approximation, this gives a pole at E=−14E=-\frac{1}{4}. This agrees with the ZZ brane result in (210), although here we get a prediction for the (imaginary!) numerical coefficient after plugging in (161).
